fspl.name: Free Space Path Loss
fspl.purpose: Tells you how much signal, in dB, is lost as it travels through open space between a transmitter and a receiver, based on the frequency and the distance.
fspl.whyHere: It's the first step in any link budget. Use it to estimate how much signal a point-to-point or outdoor link loses before you add antennas and cables into the picture.
howToUse: Enter the frequency and pick its unit (GHz or MHz).
Enter the distance and pick its unit (km, mi, or m).
Read the path loss in dB. The result stays blank ("—") until both fields hold valid positive numbers.

inputs.name: Frequency
inputs.range: must be > 0

inputs.name: Distance
inputs.range: must be > 0

fspl.algorithm: Path loss in dB is 20 × log10(frequency in GHz) + 20 × log10(distance in km) + 92.45. That 92.45 is the fixed constant for the kilometer-and-GHz version of the formula. Frequency in MHz is divided by 1000 to get GHz; miles are multiplied by 1.60934 and meters divided by 1000 to get kilometers. The answer is rounded to one decimal place, and if either value is zero or less the result blanks out.
fieldNotes: This is free space only. No obstructions, no ground reflection, no atmospheric effects. Real links always lose more, so treat this as a best-case floor, not a prediction.
The reference card lists anchor values (2.4 GHz at 1 km = 100.1 dB, 6 GHz at 1 km = 108.0 dB).
fspl.source: Calculated live from the frequency and distance you enter using the standard free space path loss formula.

wavelength.name: Wavelength
wavelength.purpose: Converts a frequency into its wavelength, shown in meters, centimeters, millimeters, feet, and inches all at once.
wavelength.whyHere: Sizing antenna elements, setting ground-plane and spacing rules, and the quarter-wave and half-wave rules of thumb all depend on wavelength. Handy quick reference when you're laying out antennas.
howToUse: Enter the frequency and pick its unit (MHz or GHz).
Read the wavelength in all five units at once.

inputs.name: Frequency
inputs.range: must be > 0

wavelength.algorithm: Wavelength in meters is 300 divided by the frequency in MHz. The 300 comes from the speed of light (about 3 × 10⁸ meters per second) scaled for the MHz-and-meter form. From there: centimeters is meters × 100, millimeters is meters × 1000, feet is meters × 3.28084, and inches is feet × 12. Frequency in GHz is multiplied by 1000 to get MHz. Results show as meters to 4 decimals, centimeters to 2, millimeters to 1, feet to 4, and inches to 3.
fieldNotes: This uses the speed of light rounded to 3 × 10⁸ m/s (the 300 constant) rather than the exact 299792458. The tiny difference doesn't matter for antenna work.
This is free-space wavelength; it does not apply the velocity factor of cable or dielectric material.
wavelength.source: Calculated live from the frequency you enter using the speed of light.

antenna-length.name: Antenna Length
antenna-length.purpose: A frequency, wavelength, and antenna-element calculator: enter a frequency (or a wavelength) and get the full wavelength plus the half-wave dipole and quarter-wave vertical physical lengths (adjusted for velocity factor) in meters, feet, and inches, right alongside the classic 468/f and 234/f rules of thumb.
antenna-length.whyHere: Cutting a dipole or a ground-plane vertical means turning a frequency into a length. This shows both the physics length (wavelength × velocity factor) and the field rules of thumb side by side, so you can see how velocity factor and end-effect change the cut.
howToUse: Use the toggle to choose whether you're entering a Frequency (MHz/GHz) or a Wavelength (m).
Type the value, then set the velocity factor (default 0.95 for thin bare wire; lower for insulated wire or tubing).
Read the full wavelength, then the half-wave dipole and quarter-wave vertical lengths in m / ft / in, each beside its rule-of-thumb figure.

inputs.name: Frequency or wavelength
inputs.range: must be > 0

inputs.name: Velocity factor
inputs.range: 0 < VF <= 1 (default 0.95)

antenna-length.algorithm: Wavelength in meters is 299.792458 divided by the frequency in MHz (and the reverse gives frequency from wavelength). A half-wave dipole's physical length is half the wavelength times the velocity factor; a quarter-wave vertical is a quarter of the wavelength times the velocity factor. The field rules of thumb, in feet, are 468 divided by the frequency in MHz for a dipole and 234 divided by the frequency in MHz for a quarter-wave. Physical length is always the electrical length times the velocity factor. This uses the exact speed of light (299.792458), not the rounded 300.
antenna-length.example: 14.2 MHz gives a wavelength of 21.112 m; a half-wave dipole at velocity factor 0.95 is 10.03 m / 32.9 ft, and the 468 rule gives 32.96 ft. At 146 MHz a quarter-wave vertical (velocity factor 0.95) is about 19.2 in. At 2400 MHz a quarter-wave is about 2.97 cm.
fieldNotes: The 468 and 234 rules of thumb already build in a typical end-effect shortening, so they read a little shorter than the pure half- or quarter-wavelength.
Velocity factor is the ratio of physical to electrical length; 0.95 suits thin bare wire, while insulated wire and tubing run lower.
This is element-length math only; it does not model feedpoint impedance, height above ground, or matching.
antenna-length.source: Calculated live from the frequency or wavelength and velocity factor you enter, using the speed of light and the standard antenna-length formulas.

maidenhead-grid.name: Maidenhead Grid Square
maidenhead-grid.purpose: Turn a latitude/longitude into a Maidenhead (QTH) locator at 4, 6, or 8 characters, decode a locator back into its square center and corner bounds, and measure the great-circle distance and bearing between two grid squares.
maidenhead-grid.whyHere: Grid squares are the amateur-radio shorthand for position, and the distance and bearing between two squares is exactly the aiming math for a point-to-point Wi-Fi or microwave link. One tool covers both.
howToUse: To Grid: enter latitude and longitude in decimal degrees and pick a precision (4 / 6 / 8 characters). The result shows the locator plus the square center and corners.
To Lat/Lon: enter a 4/6/8-character locator (for example JO62qm) to get its center latitude/longitude and bounds.
Distance: enter two locators to get the great-circle distance (km/mi) and initial bearing between their centers.

inputs.name: Locator
inputs.range: field A-R, subsquare A-X, the rest 0-9

maidenhead-grid.algorithm: The locator system divides the globe into ever-smaller cells, longitude first, then latitude, one level at a time. The first pair (the Field, letters A-R) covers 20° of longitude and 10° of latitude; the second pair (the Square, digits 0-9) covers 2° and 1°; the third pair (the Subsquare, letters a-x) covers 5 and 2.5 arc-minutes; the fourth pair (Extended, digits 0-9) covers 0.5 and 0.25 arc-minutes. Decoding runs this in reverse to the southwest corner, then adds half a cell to land on the center. Distance and bearing use the standard spherical (haversine and forward-bearing) formulas with an Earth radius of 6371 km.
maidenhead-grid.example: 37.75, -122.45 gives CM87 (San Francisco Bay). 52.5 N, 13.4 E gives JO62 (Berlin). 48.14666, 11.60833 gives JN58td (Munich). CM87 to JO62 is about 9100 km.
fieldNotes: A locator names a rectangular square, not a single point; a longer locator means a smaller square. Decoding returns the square's center.
Exactly +180 longitude or +90 latitude is nudged one step inside so it stays in the last cell. A coordinate sitting on a square boundary (for example longitude -122.0) falls into the higher square.
Distance and bearing are measured from the square centers, so they are only as precise as the locators you give.
maidenhead-grid.source: Calculated on your device from the coordinates or locators you enter, using standard Maidenhead and great-circle math.

hear-frequency.name: Hear the Frequency
hear-frequency.purpose: Turn a frequency into a real-time tone so you can build RF intuition by ear: pitch is frequency, an octave is a doubling, twelve equal-tempered semitones span an octave, harmonics are whole-number multiples, and the same logarithmic instinct underlies both octaves and dB.
hear-frequency.whyHere: RF frequencies are millions of times too high to hear, but the rules that govern them (ratios, octaves, harmonics, logarithmic compression) are the same ones your ear already knows. Hearing them makes the RF math intuitive instead of abstract.
howToUse: Type a frequency in Hz (20 to 20,000) and press Play. Higher number, higher pitch.
Press x2 or div 2 to jump one octave up or down and hear the same note higher or lower; a sounding tone retunes smoothly without a click.

Tap the piano keys C4 to C5, or a preset, to hear named notes; switch between Sine / Square / Triangle to hear timbre. Use the interval explorer to compare any two frequencies (including Wi-Fi bands) as a ratio in octaves and semitones.

inputs.name: Frequency
inputs.range: playback limited to about 20 to 20,000 (the audible range)

inputs.name: Waveform
inputs.range: sine default; sine forced above 5 kHz to avoid aliasing

inputs.name: Volume
inputs.range: defaults to 50%

hear-frequency.algorithm: Note pitches come from 12-tone equal temperament: each note is 440 Hz times 2 raised to the power of the number of semitones away from A4 (the note 440 Hz, ISO 16), divided by 12. One octave is a doubling (12 semitones); one semitone is the 12th root of 2, about 1.05946. The nearest note and how many cents off come from comparing the frequency to 440 Hz on a base-2 scale. Any interval ratio maps to a number of octaves (base-2 log of the ratio) and semitones (12 times that). Harmonics are whole-number multiples: 2f, 3f, 4f, and so on. The tones are generated live as you play.
hear-frequency.example: 440 Hz is A4. Press x2 and you get 880 Hz, which is A5, the same note one octave up. Middle C is 261.63 Hz, and its octave C5 is 523.25 Hz. The step from 2.4 to 4.8 GHz is exactly 1 octave; 2.4 to 6 GHz is about 1.32 octaves (a major third into the next octave).
fieldNotes: An octave is NOT a dB. An octave is a base-2 frequency ratio; a dB is a base-10 power ratio (10 × log10 of a power ratio, or 20 × log10 of an amplitude ratio). Both are logarithmic, which is the real bridge, but they are not the same unit.

Audio harmonics are wanted; RF harmonics usually are not. The whole-number-multiple math (2f, 3f, and so on) is identical, but in music the overtones create timbre, while in a transmitter they are spurious emissions a filter suppresses.
Equal temperament is a compromise: the piano's evenly spaced ratios approximate the pure whole-number harmonic ratios, and the idea that C# equals Db holds true only in equal temperament.
Band labels like 2.4 / 5 / 6 GHz name spans, not single tones, so octave math on one number is illustrative, not a claim about exact channel edges.
No sound? Check that the device isn't muted and the volume is up (especially on iOS, where the hardware mute switch silences playback).
hear-frequency.source: Tones are generated live on your device from the frequency you enter, using standard equal-temperament music math.

modulation-simulator.name: Modulation Simulator
modulation-simulator.purpose: Shows how bits become a radio wave. Each group of bits picks one point on the I/Q plane, and that point sets the amplitude and phase of the carrier for one symbol. Add noise and watch the receiver decide which point was sent, measure the EVM, and count the symbol and bit errors.
modulation-simulator.whyHere: Every Wi-Fi data rate is a modulation plus a coding rate. Seeing BPSK next to 4096-QAM makes it plain why higher orders carry more bits per symbol and why they need a much cleaner signal to work.
howToUse: Pick a modulation, from BPSK (1 bit per symbol) to 4096-QAM (12 bits per symbol).
Press Step to send one symbol, or Play to keep sending at the chosen speed. The simulator always opens paused. Use +100 to send a batch at once and Reset to clear the points and counts.
Move the SNR slider (0 to 45 dB) to add or remove noise. Received points spread around the ideal points, and a point that crosses a decision boundary is decided wrong and marked with an X.
Choose Random bits, or Your text to send a message as UTF-8 bits and read back what the receiver decoded.
Up to 16-QAM every point shows its bits. Above that, tap or hover a point to see them.
Read the waveform strip: the thin solid trace is I cos, the thin dashed trace is -Q sin, and the bold trace is their sum, the carrier actually sent. The bits for each symbol sit above it.

On a computer or tablet, Present opens this simulator full screen for a projector: Space plays or pauses, the Right arrow steps, R resets, Up and Down move the SNR, F switches full screen, ? lists the keys and Esc exits.

inputs.name: Modulation
inputs.range: 7 choices

inputs.name: SNR
inputs.range: 0 to 45 in 0.5 dB steps

inputs.name: Bits to send
inputs.range: text up to 120 characters

modulation-simulator.algorithm: Square QAM with M points puts half the bits on I and half on Q. Each axis takes the odd levels -(sqrt(M)-1) to +(sqrt(M)-1) and is Gray coded, so neighboring points differ by one bit. BPSK uses I only, at -1 and +1. Every constellation is scaled by the 802.11 factor 1/sqrt(2(M-1)/3) so average symbol energy is 1. The carrier for a symbol is I cos(wt) - Q sin(wt), which equals A cos(wt + phase) with A = sqrt(I squared + Q squared) and phase = atan2(Q, I). Noise is Gaussian on each axis with standard deviation sqrt(1 / (2 x SNR)), SNR as a linear ratio. The receiver picks the nearest ideal point. With noise alone, RMS EVM is 1 / sqrt(SNR), so EVM in dB equals minus the SNR in dB; the measured value comes from the simulated points.
modulation-simulator.example: 16-QAM at 25 dB SNR gives an EVM of -25 dB, about 5.6%. That meets both 16-QAM transmit limits (-16 and -19 dB) and the 64-QAM rate 3/4 limit of -25 dB, but misses 64-QAM rate 5/6 at -27 dB. Typing the letter A sends 8 bits; in 64-QAM that is 2 symbols, with 4 zero bits padding the second.
fieldNotes: The drawing is slowed down. It shows 3 carrier cycles per symbol; a real Wi-Fi carrier runs billions of cycles per second.

The required EVM table is the 802.11 transmitter accuracy requirement: how cleanly a radio must build each point. It is not a receiver sensitivity threshold. Meets or misses compares the limit with the EVM the current SNR produces.
Changing the modulation, the SNR, the bit source or the message clears the received points and counts, so every reading belongs to one setting.
Measured EVM from a handful of symbols wanders. Send a few hundred and it settles close to the theoretical value.
The Wireless Classroom is designed for tablets and computers, and on a phone some views are cramped.
modulation-simulator.source: Constellations, Gray mapping and scaling follow the IEEE 802.11 modulation mapping; transmit EVM limits are from the 802.11 transmit modulation accuracy tables. Noise and decisions are simulated on your device.

teaching.teaches: a group of bits picks one point on the I/Q plane, higher orders pack more bits into points that sit closer together, and so they need a cleaner signal to decode.

controls.control: **Modulation** (select: BPSK, QPSK, 16-QAM, 64-QAM, 256-QAM, 1024-QAM, 4096-QAM, each with its bits per symbol)
controls.does: Picks the constellation. Default 16-QAM. The line under it gives the point count, bits per symbol and the amendment that first used it.
controls.why: Higher orders carry more bits per symbol and need a cleaner signal. Seeing BPSK next to 4096-QAM makes that plain (help, `whyHere`).

controls.control: **Play** / **Pause**
controls.does: Sends one symbol per tick at the chosen speed. The simulator always opens paused.
controls.why: Paused by default so nothing moves until you ask. Play lets the cloud build up while you talk.

controls.control: **Step**
controls.does: Sends exactly one symbol.
controls.why: One symbol is one point, one amplitude and one phase on the carrier strip. Step is how you show that mapping slowly, and it is the suggested path when reduced motion is on.

controls.does: Sends 100 symbols at once.
controls.why: Measured EVM from a handful of symbols wanders, and a few hundred settle close to theory (help, `fieldNotes`). +100 gets you there in two presses.

controls.control: **Reset**
controls.does: Clears the received points and counts. Disabled when nothing has been sent.
controls.why: Starts a fresh reading. Every other change clears the points too, so each reading belongs to one setting (help, `fieldNotes`).

controls.control: **Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)** slider, 0 to 45 dB in 0.5 dB steps, default 25 dB
controls.does: Sets the Gaussian noise added to each received point.
controls.why: The one noise control: the received cloud spreads, points cross decision boundaries and are marked wrong.

controls.control: **Speed (symbols per second)**: 1/s, 4/s, 20/s. Default 4/s.
controls.does: Sets how fast Play sends.
controls.why: 1/s is slow enough to narrate each symbol on the carrier strip; 20/s fills the constellation fast enough to see the cloud's shape.

controls.control: **Bits to send**: Random, Your text
controls.does: Random bits, or the UTF-8 bits of a typed message.
controls.why: The tool calls for both. Typed text makes the errors land in something the class can read, and shows the zero-padding of the last symbol.

controls.control: **Message** (text field, up to 120 characters, default "Hello, Wi-Fi"; appears with Your text)
controls.does: The message to send. Shows bytes, bits, symbols and padding, then Progress, Received so far and Last full copy.
controls.why: Lets the room watch a readable message break as the SNR drops.

controls.control: Tap or hover a point on the constellation (64-QAM and above)
controls.does: Shows that point's bits.
controls.why: Up to 16-QAM every point is labeled. Above that the labels would overlap, so labels show on hover or tap only.

controls.control: **Present** (title bar)
controls.does: Opens the presenter layout over the same state.
controls.why: See the shelf intro.

demo: Set up: 16-QAM, SNR 25 dB, Random bits. Press +100 twice. The cloud sits tight on each point, EVM measured is close to -25 dB, and there are no symbol errors.
Ask the room: "Same SNR, but I switch to 256-QAM. How many errors?"

Reveal: switch to 256-QAM and press +100. Errors appear at once, because the same noise now crosses boundaries that are four times closer on each axis. Press Up and watch the errors thin out; by our arithmetic they become rare somewhere past 30 dB.

Optional follow-up: switch to Your text, drop the SNR until "Hello, Wi-Fi" arrives garbled, then open the EVM card. 16-QAM at 25 dB meets both 16-QAM limits and the 64-QAM rate 3/4 limit of -25 dB, and misses 64-QAM rate 5/6 at -27 dB (help, `example`).
teaching.pairsWith: Rate vs Range (where each MCS stops working), the MCS Index card in Course Handouts, and Fourier and FFT mode 4, which puts these same constellations on every subcarrier.
teaching.leftOut: no coding (the coding rates appear only in the EVM limits table), no OFDM (one carrier, one symbol at a time), and only white Gaussian noise: no phase noise, fading or interference. The carrier strip draws 3 cycles per symbol; a real carrier runs billions per second. EVM limits are transmitter accuracy, not receiver sensitivity.

medium-access-simulator.name: Medium Access Simulator
medium-access-simulator.purpose: Shows how Wi-Fi stations share one channel. Each station waits for a quiet medium, counts down a random backoff in 9 µs slots, and transmits when the count reaches zero. You watch it happen slot by slot: collisions, the contention window doubling, EDCA priority, hidden nodes and RTS/CTS.
medium-access-simulator.whyHere: Wi-Fi is half duplex and shared, so airtime runs out long before the PHY rate does. Watching the waiting and the collisions shows why a 54 Mbps link delivers about 31 Mbps to one station, less as stations are added, and why voice traffic gets through first.
howToUse: Press Play to run the clock, or Step to move one 9 µs slot at a time. The simulation starts paused. Reset replays the same run from time zero.

Read the timeline. The top lane is the medium as the AP hears it, and each station has its own lane. Hatched blocks are DIFS, AIFS or EIFS waits, outlined cells are backoff slots with the count inside, filled gray cells are a frozen count, lime blocks are data frames, green blocks are ACKs and red blocks are frames lost to a collision. Zoom changes the time scale; while paused, drag the timeline sideways to look back.

Add up to 10 stations and set each one's offered load. Switch to EDCA to give each station an access category. Turn on Hidden node, then RTS/CTS, to see collisions nobody could hear coming and how the handshake removes most of them. Change the frame size and PHY rate to see airtime change.

On a computer or tablet, Present opens this simulator full screen for a projector: Space plays or pauses, the Right arrow steps one slot, R resets, Up and Down change the speed, F switches full screen, ? lists the keys and Esc exits.

inputs.name: Stations
inputs.range: 1 to 10

inputs.name: Access category
inputs.range: EDCA only; Legacy DCF gives every station DIFS and a contention window of 15 to 1023

inputs.name: Offered load
inputs.range: always has a frame, or 50 to 2,000 frames/s with random arrivals

inputs.name: PHY rate
inputs.range: 6 to 54 (legacy OFDM); default 54

inputs.name: Speed
inputs.range: 0.1 ms to 200 ms

medium-access-simulator.algorithm: Timing is 802.11 OFDM at 5 GHz: slot 9 µs, SIFS 16 µs, DIFS = SIFS + 2 slots = 34 µs, AIFS = SIFS + AIFSN x slot. A station waits for the medium to be idle for AIFS, then counts down a backoff drawn at random from 0 to CW, one per idle slot. If the medium goes busy the count freezes, and it resumes later without a new draw. At zero the station transmits. A clean frame gets an ACK after SIFS and CW resets to CWmin. No ACK means CW = 2(CW + 1) - 1, capped at CWmax, and a new draw; after 7 failed tries the frame is dropped. A station that heard a frame it could not decode waits EIFS (SIFS + DIFS + an ACK at 6 Mbps = 94 µs) in place of DIFS. Frame airtime = 20 µs + 4 µs x ceil((16 + 8 x bytes + 6) / (rate x 4)).
medium-access-simulator.example: A 1,500-byte frame at 54 Mbps takes 20 + 4 x ceil(12,022 / 216) = 244 µs, and its ACK at 24 Mbps takes 28 µs. One station alone spends 34 µs of DIFS, 67.5 µs of backoff on average, 244 µs of data, 16 µs of SIFS and 28 µs of ACK per frame, about 390 µs, so it delivers about 31 Mbps from a 54 Mbps rate. Each station you add brings collisions that eat into that.
fieldNotes: Timing is legacy OFDM (802.11a/g). Newer PHYs (802.11n, ac, ax, be) have longer preambles and send many frames per access by aggregating them, so the numbers differ. The lesson about contention is the same.
Only uplink is modeled: every station sends to the AP, and the AP answers only with ACK or CTS. Rate adaptation and the NAV reset rule are not modeled.
RTS/CTS removes most hidden-node data collisions, not all of them. A hidden station whose own RTS overlaps the AP's CTS never hears that CTS, so it can still talk over the data frame that follows.
Runs are seeded, so the same settings give the same run every time.
The Wireless Classroom is designed for tablets and computers, and on a phone some views are cramped.
medium-access-simulator.source: IEEE 802.11 channel access rules (DCF and EDCA, clause 10) and OFDM PHY timing (clause 17), with the default EDCA parameters for a non-AP station. The simulation runs on your device.

teaching.teaches: Wi-Fi is half duplex and shared, so stations take turns by counting down a random backoff; collisions double the contention window, more stations mean more waiting, and EDCA lets voice win because it waits less.

controls.control: Play / Pause
controls.does: Runs or freezes the simulated clock. The tool always opens paused at time zero.
controls.why: It opens paused and keeps Step working (reduced motion), so the instructor decides when the clock starts.

controls.control: Step 1 slot
controls.does: Advances one 9 µs slot.
controls.why: Backoff counts down one slot at a time and freezes when the medium goes busy. Stepping lets the room call each count and catch the freeze and resume.

controls.control: Reset
controls.does: Replays the same run from time zero.
controls.why: Runs are seeded, so the same settings give the same run. A demo you rehearsed plays the same collisions live.

controls.control: Speed (air time per real second)
controls.does: 0.1, 0.5, 2, 20 or 200 ms per second; opens at 0.1 ms per second.
controls.why: The slow end shows single slots; the fast end lets the throughput and collision numbers settle.

controls.control: Zoom: Slots / Frames / Wide
controls.does: Changes the timeline's time scale. While paused, drag the timeline sideways to look back.
controls.why: Slots shows the countdown cells; Wide shows many frames so the pattern of turns is visible.

controls.control: Add station / Remove
controls.does: 1 to 10 stations; opens with 3. Each station row also has its own remove button.
controls.why: "More stations mean more waiting and more collisions" is a stated goal of the lesson.

controls.control: Access category (per station)
controls.does: Voice, Video, Best effort or Background. Only live in EDCA.
controls.why: The EDCA table gives Voice AIFSN 2 and CW 3 to 7 against Best effort's AIFSN 3 and CW 15 to 1023: priority traffic wins because it waits less.

controls.control: Offered load (per station)
controls.does: Always has a frame, or 50, 200, 500, 1,000 or 2,000 frames/s with random arrivals.
controls.why: Saturated stations show contention at its worst; light loads show how rarely it bites when the channel is quiet.

controls.control: Per-station table
controls.does: CW, backoff, delivered and dropped for every station.
controls.why: The tool asks for current CW per station, so the class can watch 15 become 31, then 63, after each collision.

controls.control: Channel access: Legacy DCF / EDCA
controls.does: DCF gives everyone DIFS and CW 15 to 1023; EDCA applies each station's access category.
controls.why: The tool builds a DCF mode for everyone as the baseline, then EDCA to show voice getting through first.

controls.control: Hidden node
controls.does: Stations A, C, E cannot hear B, D, F; everyone still reaches the AP. Needs two or more stations.
controls.why: Shows collisions nobody could hear coming: the stations never freeze on each other, so frames overlap at the AP.

controls.control: RTS/CTS
controls.does: Every exchange becomes RTS, CTS, data, ACK; anyone who hears the CTS sets its NAV.
controls.why: The fix for the hidden node.

controls.control: Frame size
controls.why: The tool makes frame size and PHY rate user controls so the class sees airtime per frame change. The help says the same.

controls.control: PHY rate
controls.does: 6 to 54 Mbps (legacy OFDM); default 54.
controls.why: Same as frame size. The Frame card underneath shows the airtime formula with your numbers in it.

demo: Set up: the defaults. Three stations, Legacy DCF, 1,500 bytes at 54 Mbps, speed 0.1 ms per second.
Ask the room: "Two stations reach zero in the same slot. What happens to both frames, and what does each station do next?"

Reveal: press Right until a red collision block appears, then open the per-station table: both colliding stations' CW has gone from 15 to 31. Press Up a few times to speed up, Play, and read the collision rate and throughput. Add stations up to 10 and watch the collision rate climb and throughput fall. The help puts one station alone at about 31 Mbps delivered on a 54 Mbps link.
Optional follow-up: switch to EDCA, set station A to Voice and the rest to Best effort, and compare average access delay. Or turn on Hidden node, watch the collisions, then turn on RTS/CTS.
teaching.pairsWith: Voice Priority, End to End (runs on this engine), Airtime Anatomy, Channel Utilization Meter, Rate Adaptation. Teacher's Guide sequences "Why is the Wi-Fi slow?" and "QoS and contention".
teaching.leftOut: timing is legacy OFDM (802.11a/g, 9 µs slots, 20 µs preamble); newer PHYs have longer preambles and aggregate frames, and the contention lesson is the same. Uplink only: the AP sends only ACK or CTS. No rate adaptation, no aggregation, no NAV reset rule. RTS/CTS removes most hidden-node collisions, not all: a hidden station whose RTS overlaps the AP's CTS never hears that CTS.

voice-priority.name: Voice Priority, End to End
voice-priority.purpose: Follows one voice packet toward a phone on Wi-Fi and shows which of the AP's four queues it waits in. The caller's app marks the packet EF (Expedited Forwarding), a DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point) value. The access point (AP) turns the DSCP into an 802.11 user priority (UP), and the UP picks one of the four WMM (Wi-Fi Multimedia) queues, or access categories. The call gets the Voice queue only if EF survives every hop before the AP and the AP maps it to UP 6.
voice-priority.whyHere: Turning on WMM does not make calls good, and a priority mark set on your own network does not carry across the internet. The AP chooses the queue from the mark it receives, so a tunnel that does not copy the mark outward, a provider that resets it, or an AP that ignores it all put the call in Best effort, behind whatever else is downloading. The Medium Access Simulator shows how the four queues contend for the air; this tool is about whether the mark gets there, and it reuses that simulator's engine for the wait on the Wi-Fi hop.
howToUse: Read the top card: the queue the call waits in, and one sentence saying why.

Pick where the marking is lost: nowhere, at the AP mapping, at the tunnel, or at the internet provider. The path shows the mark each hop passes on, and the hop that loses it says Marking lost here. Press Send the packet, or Next hop, to move the packet toward the phone.

Read the AP's four queues and the Wait on the Wi-Fi hop bars. With the download running, the call in Best effort sits behind the download's frames and waits far longer than in Voice. Turn the download off and the queues come out within a tenth of a millisecond of each other.

Switch the AP mapping to Top three bits to see the older default: EF (46, binary 101110) becomes UP 5, the Video queue, even when nothing on the path loses the mark. Change how many download frames sit ahead in Best effort (illustrative).

Predict, then reveal: Ask the class loads the question (the provider resets the mark while a download runs: which queue does the call wait in?) and hides the answer on the stage; pick an answer, then press Reveal.

On a computer or tablet, Present opens this simulator full screen for a projector: Space sends the packet or pauses, the Right arrow moves it one hop, R resets, Up and Down move where the marking is lost, D starts or stops the download, M switches the AP mapping, P asks, reveals and closes the question, F switches full screen, ? lists the keys and Esc exits.

inputs.name: Where the marking is lost
inputs.range: Nowhere (default), at the AP mapping, at the tunnel, or at the internet provider

inputs.name: How the AP maps DSCP to user priority
inputs.range: RFC 8325 table (default, recommended) or top three bits (older default)

inputs.name: A download is running
inputs.range: On (default) or Off

inputs.name: Download frames ahead in Best effort
inputs.range: 0 to 256; default 64 (illustrative; used only when the call lands in Best effort while a download runs)

voice-priority.algorithm: The packet leaves the caller's app marked EF (46). The tunnel gateway copies the mark to the outer header, or leaves the outer mark at 0 when the loss is at the tunnel, and then no later hop can see EF. The internet provider passes the mark, or resets it to 0 when the loss is there. The home router and switch pass it unchanged. The AP maps the DSCP it sees to a user priority: the RFC 8325 table sends EF to UP 6 and 0 to UP 0; the top-three-bits mapping sends EF to UP 5; when the loss is at the AP mapping, the AP sends every frame as UP 0. UP 6 and 7 are Voice (AC_VO), 4 and 5 Video (AC_VI), 0 and 3 Best effort (AC_BE), 1 and 2 Background (AC_BK). The wait on the Wi-Fi hop comes from the Medium Access Simulator's engine, unchanged: legacy OFDM timing, 1,500-byte frames at 54 Mbps and the default client EDCA (Enhanced Distributed Channel Access) settings, with a voice flow of one packet every 20 ms (illustrative) and, while the download runs, a best-effort flow that always has a frame. Each run is seeded and covers 2 s of air time. In Voice or Video the call has its own queue, so its wait is the engine's mean time from the head of its queue to the ACK. In Best effort the call shares the download's queue, so it waits for the frames ahead to leave, one best-effort frame time each, then for its own turn: wait = (frames ahead + 1) x the mean best-effort frame time.
voice-priority.example: Defaults (nothing lost, RFC 8325 mapping, download running, 64 frames ahead): the call gets UP 6, Voice, and waits 0.48 ms on the Wi-Fi hop. With the loss at the internet provider, the AP sees 0 and the call lands in Best effort: 65 x 0.398 ms = 25.9 ms, 54 times as long. With nothing lost and the top-three-bits mapping, the call gets UP 5, Video, and waits 0.59 ms. With the download off, the three queues wait 0.30, 0.32 and 0.36 ms.
fieldNotes: RFC 8325 notes that the common default of copying the top three DSCP bits puts EF in the Video queue, and recommends mapping EF to UP 6. The DSCP / QoS Markings card holds its full table.

Whether a tunnel copies the inner mark to its outer header is set by the device and its configuration (RFC 4301), so on a real network it depends on the device. Wi-Fi Calling and VPN (virtual private network) traffic both travel in tunnels.
A network you do not run may re-mark or ignore the DSCP at its boundary (RFC 2475). RFC 8325 calls resetting untrusted marks bleaching.

The Wi-Fi hop uses the Medium Access Simulator's simplifications: legacy 54 Mbps timing, one frame size for every frame, no aggregation, and the default client EDCA settings; an AP's own settings can differ. Inside one AP the standard gives the higher queue the win when two of its queues finish counting down together; here the download and the call contend as two transmitters.

Illustrative: a voice packet every 20 ms, and how many download frames sit ahead in Best effort, which depends on the AP's buffer. Wired hops add delay too, and the tool does not put a number on them.
Not modeled: the call's upstream direction, where the phone picks the user priority itself, and how the AP maps the upstream frame back to a DSCP.
The Wireless Classroom is designed for tablets and computers, and on a phone some views are cramped.
voice-priority.source: RFC 8325 (Mapping Diffserv to IEEE 802.11), sections 2.3 and 4.2.1; RFC 4301 (Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol), section 5.1.2.1 and the Bypass DSCP setting; RFC 2475 (An Architecture for Differentiated Services). The Wi-Fi hop runs on the Medium Access Simulator's engine (IEEE 802.11 clause 10 channel access, clause 17 OFDM timing). Computed on your device.

teaching.teaches: a call gets the Voice queue on Wi-Fi only if its EF marking survives every hop before the AP and the AP maps it to UP 6; turning on WMM alone does not do it.

controls.control: Send the packet / Pause
controls.does: Moves the voice packet along the path toward the phone.
controls.why: Lets the class watch the mark each hop passes on.

controls.control: Next hop
controls.does: Moves the packet one hop.
controls.why: Stops the packet at the hop that says "Marking lost here" so you can talk about that device.

controls.control: Reset
controls.does: Back to the defaults, packet at the caller, no question showing.
controls.why: Returns to the starting state between demos.

controls.control: Where the marking is lost: Nowhere / At the AP mapping / At the tunnel / At the internet provider
controls.does: Picks the hop that resets EF to 0. A dropdown on a phone, where four segments truncate.
controls.why: The one control that matters: the visible change is the call dropping from Voice to Best effort while a download runs. It corrects "turning on WMM makes my calls good" and "QoS works across the internet".

controls.control: How the AP maps DSCP to user priority: RFC 8325 table (recommended) / Top three bits (older default)
controls.does: RFC 8325 maps EF to UP 6 (Voice); top three bits turns EF (46) into UP 5 (Video).
controls.why: RFC 8325 notes that the common default of copying the top three bits puts EF in the Video queue, and recommends UP 6. This shows the call landing in the wrong queue with nothing on the path at fault.

controls.control: A download is running
controls.does: On by default.
controls.why: With the download off, the four queues come out within a tenth of a millisecond of each other (help). Priority only matters when something else is queued.

controls.control: Download frames ahead in Best effort (illustrative)
controls.does: 0 to 256 in steps of 8; default 64. Live only when the call lands in Best effort with the download on; locked while the class predicts.
controls.why: The queue depth depends on the AP's buffer, so the help labels it illustrative. The default is 64 frames × 0.398 ms = 25.9 ms against 0.48 ms in Voice.

controls.control: Ask the class / Voice / Video / Best effort / Reveal / close
controls.does: Loads the question (the provider resets the mark while a download runs), hides the answer, takes a guess, reveals.
controls.why: The house "predict, then reveal" pattern, built into the tool.

controls.control: Open Medium Access Simulator / Open DSCP / QoS Markings
controls.does: Links to the related tools.
controls.why: EDCA is not rebuilt here (the Medium Access Simulator shows it), and the DSCP / QoS card holds the RFC 8325 table.

demo: Set up: the defaults. Marking lost Nowhere, RFC 8325 mapping, download running.

Ask the room: press P. "The phone has WMM on and the app marks its voice EF. Your provider resets the mark to 0. While a download runs, which queue does the call wait in?" Take votes on Voice, Video and Best effort.
Reveal: press P again. Best effort, behind the download: about 25.9 ms of waiting at the default 64 frames, against 0.48 ms in Voice.

Optional follow-up: press P to close, set the loss back to Nowhere and press M. The call lands in Video with nothing on the path losing the mark. Then press D to stop the download and show the queues come out nearly equal.
teaching.pairsWith: Medium Access Simulator, the DSCP / QoS Markings card, Power Save (U-APSD and the voice-call traffic pattern).
teaching.leftOut: the Wi-Fi hop uses the Medium Access Simulator's simplifications (legacy 54 Mbps timing, one frame size, no aggregation, default client EDCA settings). The download and the call contend as two transmitters, not two queues inside one AP. Whether a tunnel copies the mark outward depends on the device (RFC 4301). Wired hops add delay the tool does not number. The upstream direction, where the phone picks the UP itself, is not modeled. The voice packet every 20 ms and the download queue depth are illustrative.

fspl-simulator.name: FSPL Simulator
fspl-simulator.purpose: Draws free-space path loss, or the received power it leaves, against distance for 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz on one chart. A cursor reads out each band at any distance, and a Why panel splits each band's loss into the part every band shares and the part that changes with frequency.
fspl-simulator.whyHere: Higher bands lose more at the same distance, and the common explanation (the air absorbs 6 GHz more) is wrong. The extra loss comes from the receive antenna: a shorter wavelength makes a smaller antenna that catches less energy. Seeing the two parts side by side makes that stick, and a measured point shows how far a real room sits from the free-space best case.
howToUse: Turn bands on and off with the chips at the bottom of the screen (on a wide screen, the panel on the right). Each band has its own line style: 2.4 GHz solid with a circle, 5 GHz dashed with a square, 6 GHz dotted with a triangle.

Drag across the chart or tap it to move the cursor, or use the Cursor slider under it. The table under the chart shows path loss and received power for each band at that distance, and the difference between bands.

Switch the chart between Received and Path loss, and the distance axis between 100 m and 1 km. In the Received view, dashed lines mark design targets. By default they are the -67 dBm voice and -70 dBm HD video targets from the Signal Thresholds tool.

Open the controls (the tune button) to pick any 20 MHz channel per band, set Tx power, both antenna gains and other losses, turn on the indoor log-distance model and set its exponent, or enter a measured RSSI and the distance it was taken at. The measured point plots as a diamond with its gap to the free-space curve in dB.

Under Design targets in the controls, set each line's level in dBm and a short label, add a line (up to four) or remove one. A line with no label reads as its level, for example -72 dBm. Your lines are saved on this device for every lesson, and Reset to -67 voice / -70 HD video puts the defaults back.
On a computer or tablet, Present opens this simulator full screen for a projector: Up and Down double and halve the cursor distance, F switches full screen, ? lists the keys and Esc exits.

inputs.name: Bands
inputs.range: 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz, all on by default

inputs.name: Channel
inputs.range: any 20 MHz channel in the band; defaults 6 (2437 MHz), 100 (5500 MHz), 37 (6135 MHz)

inputs.name: Tx power
inputs.range: 0 to 30; default 20

inputs.name: Tx and Rx antenna gain
inputs.range: -5 to 15; default 0 (isotropic)

inputs.name: Other losses
inputs.range: 0 to 30; default 0

inputs.name: Path-loss exponent n
inputs.range: 2.0 to 4.0; default 3.0; indoor model only

inputs.name: Design targets
inputs.range: up to 4 lines, each -100 to -30 dBm with a label of up to 24 characters; default -67 dBm voice and -70 dBm HD video

fspl-simulator.algorithm: FSPL (dB) = 20 log10(4 pi d / lambda), with lambda = c / f and c = 299,792,458 m/s. With d in meters and f in MHz this is 20 log10(d) + 20 log10(f) - 27.55. It splits exactly into spreading loss 10 log10(4 pi d^2), the same at every frequency, plus the aperture term -10 log10(lambda^2 / 4 pi), which depends only on frequency. Received power = Tx power + Tx gain + Rx gain - path loss - other losses. The band difference at equal distance is 20 log10(f2 / f1). The indoor model is PL(d) = FSPL(1 m) + 10 n log10(d / 1 m).
fspl-simulator.example: At 10 m on channel 6 (2437 MHz): spreading loss 10 log10(4 pi x 100) = 31.0 dB, aperture term 29.2 dB, total 60.2 dB. With 20 dBm Tx and 0 dBi antennas the received power is -40.2 dBm. Channel 100 (5500 MHz) loses 20 log10(5500 / 2437) = 7.1 dB more at every distance, and all of that difference is in the aperture term.
fieldNotes: Free space is the best case: no walls, no floor reflection, no people, no fading. Real indoor readings are usually well below the curve.
Every doubling of distance costs 6 dB, so going from 1 m to 2 m costs as much as going from 50 m to 100 m.
The indoor overlay is a model with an exponent you choose, not a measurement. n = 2 reproduces free space.
The aperture term assumes an isotropic (0 dBi) receive antenna. A higher-gain antenna has a larger effective area and wins some of the difference back.
Measured points are typed in by hand. Nothing is read from the Wi-Fi adapter.
The Wireless Classroom is designed for tablets and computers, and on a phone some views are cramped.
fspl-simulator.source: The Friis transmission equation and the free-space path loss formula derived from it. Design targets are read from this app's Signal Thresholds tool. Everything is calculated on your device.

teaching.teaches: every doubling of distance costs 6 dB in free space, and higher bands lose more because the receive antenna is smaller at a shorter wavelength, not because the air absorbs more.

controls.control: 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, 6 GHz (band chips, all on)
controls.does: Show or hide each band's curve.
controls.why: Puts the bands on one chart so the gap between them is visible. Each band has its own line style and marker (solid circle, dashed square, dotted triangle) because the design system has no categorical colors, so the class can tell them apart without color.

controls.control: Received / Path loss (toggle, default Received)
controls.does: Plots received power in dBm, or free-space path loss in dB.
controls.why: Path loss is what the formula gives; received power is the unit a design target is written in, and the target lines only appear in Received.

controls.control: 100 m / 1 km (300 ft / 3,000 ft in imperial)
controls.does: Sets the end of the distance axis.
controls.why: Keeps the default view on indoor distances while a point measured past 100 m (330 ft), or an outdoor link, can still land on the chart.

controls.control: Log / Linear (toggle, default Log)
controls.does: Switches the distance axis.
controls.why: Log shows the straight 6 dB-per-doubling lines; linear shows the curve people are used to. Same numbers either way.

controls.control: Drag or tap the chart; Cursor (slider)
controls.does: Move the distance cursor. The table under the chart reads path loss and received power per band, and the difference between bands.
controls.why: The readout makes the second lesson checkable: the difference between two bands is the same at every distance.

controls.control: 2.4 GHz channel, 5 GHz channel, 6 GHz channel (pickers; defaults 6, 100, 37)
controls.does: Set each band's center frequency.
controls.why: The band gap is 20 log10(f2/f1), so it depends on the channel, not just the band: 6 GHz channel 37 and channel 117 differ by about 0.5 dB.

controls.control: Tx power (0 to 30 dBm, default 20)
controls.does: Raises or lowers every received curve.
controls.why: Received power = Tx power + gains - path loss - losses; moving it shifts every band equally and leaves the gap alone.

controls.control: Tx antenna gain, Rx antenna gain (-5 to 15 dBi, default 0)
controls.does: Add antenna gain at either end.
controls.why: 0 dBi is the isotropic antenna the aperture term assumes. A higher-gain receive antenna has a larger effective area and wins some of the high-band loss back.

controls.control: Other losses (0 to 30 dB)
controls.does: Subtracts a fixed loss from every curve.
controls.why: A stand-in for cable, body or wall loss without modeling any of them.

controls.control: Show log-distance curves (switch); Path-loss exponent n (2.0 to 4.0, default 3.0, off until the switch is on)
controls.does: Overlays the indoor log-distance model.
controls.why: Free space is the best case; this shows how much faster an indoor path loses. Labeled a model with a chosen exponent, not a measurement; n = 2 reproduces free space.

controls.control: Measured point: RSSI, Distance, Measured on (band), Clear measured point
controls.does: Plots a reading you type as a diamond, with its gap to the free-space curve in dB.
controls.why: The gap between the model and a measurement is where the design work happens. Manual entry only; nothing is read from the Wi-Fi adapter.

controls.control: Design targets: Level, Label, remove (x), Add line (up to 4), Reset to -67 voice / -70 HD video
controls.does: Edit the dashed target lines in the Received view. Saved on the device for every lesson.
controls.why: The lines are editable with a number and a label. The defaults are read from the Signal Thresholds tool so the two tools cannot drift apart.

controls.control: Show controls / Hide controls (tune button, phone only)
controls.does: Opens the controls sheet under the chart.
controls.why: Phone first: the chart owns the screen and the controls collapse to one row of band chips.

demo: Set up: all three bands on, Received, Log, cursor at 10 m (33 ft). On channel 6 the path loss is 60.2 dB and, with 20 dBm and 0 dBi antennas, received power is -40.2 dBm.
Ask the room: "Move twice as far away, to 20 m (66 ft). How much signal do we lose?"

Reveal: press Up. Every band drops 6.0 dB. Press it again at 40 m (131 ft): another 6 dB, the same as the first doubling. Then point at the Why panel: the spreading bar is identical for every band; only the aperture bar changes, and channel 100 sits 7.1 dB under channel 6 at every distance.

Optional follow-up: turn on Show log-distance curves at n = 3 and press Up again. A doubling now costs about 9 dB. Or switch to Linear to show the steep drop near the AP is the same 6 dB per doubling, squeezed into the first few meters.
teaching.pairsWith: Decibels in Your Head before it. Wi-Fi Through a Wall and 6 GHz Power and PSD after it (the "Why 6 GHz behaves differently" sequence). Rate vs Range and Uplink vs Downlink for the link budget. Lab: the FSPL lab.
teaching.leftOut: Free space has no walls, floor bounce, people or fading, so real readings usually sit below the curve. The aperture term assumes a 0 dBi receive antenna. The indoor curve is a model with an exponent you choose. Measured points are typed in by hand.

airtime-fairness.name: Airtime Fairness
airtime-fairness.purpose: Shows why one slow client drags every fast client down under plain Wi-Fi contention, and how airtime fairness fixes it. Build a cell of 1 to 8 clients, then compare packet fairness (every client gets the same number of turns) with airtime fairness (every client gets the same share of time).
airtime-fairness.whyHere: A PHY rate is not a throughput. Every turn on the air pays a fixed overhead before any data moves, and under plain contention a 6 Mbps client holds the air for milliseconds each turn while an 867 Mbps client needs well under one. Seeing the airtime share and the throughput side by side explains the performance anomaly and why APs offer airtime fairness.
howToUse: Pick the sharing rule: Packet, Airtime, or Compare to see both. The line under the switch states the result in numbers and changes as you edit.

Read the airtime share bar (who holds the air), the throughput bars (what each client and the whole cell get), and the round (each transmission drawn as wide as its airtime, with the overhead outlined and the frames filled). Replay round runs the animation again.

Edit the clients: a PHY rate from the presets or a custom rate, and the number of frames sent per turn (aggregation). Legacy clients send one frame per turn. Add up to 8 clients, and change the payload per frame to see small frames waste the air.

On a computer or tablet, Present opens this simulator full screen for a projector: Space plays or pauses the round, the Right arrow steps one transmission, R empties the round, Up and Down change the sharing rule, F switches full screen, ? lists the keys and Esc exits.

inputs.name: Clients
inputs.range: 1 to 8; default three at 867 Mbps with 32 frames per turn plus one legacy client at 6 Mbps

inputs.name: PHY rate
inputs.range: 6, 24, 54 (legacy); 150, 300 (HT); 433, 867 (VHT); 600, 1201 (HE); or a custom rate from 1 to 10,000 with a legacy or HT-or-newer preamble

inputs.name: Frames per turn
inputs.range: 1 to 64; always 1 for legacy clients

inputs.name: Payload per frame
inputs.range: 64 to 1,500; default 1,500

airtime-fairness.algorithm: Airtime of one turn T = AIFS 43 µs + average backoff 67.5 µs + preamble (20 µs legacy, 40 µs HT or newer) + SIFS 16 µs + ACK 28 µs (or Block Ack 32 µs when frames are aggregated) + 8 x frames x (payload + 34) / rate. Packet fairness: each client gets one turn per round, so throughput = 8 x frames x payload / (sum of every client's T). Airtime fairness: each client gets 1/N of the time, so throughput = (1/N) x 8 x frames x payload / T. The total is the sum over clients.
airtime-fairness.example: Defaults: an 867 Mbps client sending 32 frames takes about 651 µs per turn; the 6 Mbps client sending one frame takes about 2.22 ms. Under packet fairness the round lasts about 4.17 ms and the slow client holds 53% of it, so each fast client gets 92.0 Mbps, the slow one 2.87 Mbps, 278.9 Mbps in total. Under airtime fairness each client holds 25% of the air: the fast clients get 147.4 Mbps each, the slow one 1.35 Mbps, 443.4 Mbps in total.
fieldNotes: This is a teaching model: one AP sending downlink to every client, every client always has data waiting, no collisions, no retries and no rate adaptation. Airtime Anatomy does the exact per-PHY airtime.
The 40 µs preamble is one teaching value for HT, VHT and HE. Real preambles vary with the PHY, the number of streams and the frame format.
The limits on how many frames or bytes one aggregate may carry are not enforced.
Airtime fairness costs the slow client throughput. That is the point: it stops paying for its slow turns with everyone else's time.
The Wireless Classroom is designed for tablets and computers, and on a phone some views are cramped.
airtime-fairness.source: IEEE 802.11 EDCA and OFDM timing, and M. Heusse, F. Rousseau, G. Berger-Sabbatel and A. Duda, Performance Anomaly of 802.11b, IEEE INFOCOM 2003. The calculation runs on your device.

teaching.teaches: under plain contention every client gets the same number of turns, not the same amount of time, so one slow client drags every fast client down; airtime fairness gives each client an equal share of time instead.

controls.control: Sharing rule: Packet / Airtime / Compare
controls.does: Packet fairness (equal turns), airtime fairness (equal time), or both side by side. Opens on Compare.
controls.why: The fairness switch and compare view: the performance anomaly (Heusse et al., 2003) against its fix.

controls.control: Replay round
controls.does: Runs the round animation again.
controls.why: The animated round: each transmission drawn as wide as its airtime, so the slow client's block visibly dominates under packet fairness.

controls.control: Play / Pause, Step, Reset (Present mode)
controls.does: Plays the round, steps one transmission, empties it.
controls.why: Same round, paced by the presenter.

controls.control: Payload per frame
controls.does: 64 to 1,500 bytes; default 1,500.
controls.why: The lesson: every transmission pays a fixed overhead, so small frames waste most of the air.

controls.control: Add client
controls.does: Up to 8 clients. Opens with three at 867 Mbps and one legacy at 6 Mbps.
controls.why: The default cell, chosen to show the anomaly on sight.

controls.control: PHY rate (per client)
controls.does: Presets 6, 24, 54 (legacy); 150, 300 (HT); 433, 867 (VHT); 600, 1201 (HE); or Custom rate.
controls.why: The preset list, one per generation, so the class can build a realistic mixed cell.

controls.control: Custom rate and Preamble: Legacy / HT or newer
controls.does: Any rate from 1 to 10,000 Mbps with a 20 µs or 40 µs preamble.
controls.why: The tool uses 20 µs legacy and 40 µs as a single teaching value for HT, VHT and HE.

controls.control: Frames per turn (aggregation)
controls.does: 1 to 64; legacy clients always 1.
controls.why: The aggregation count: fast clients recover airtime by sending many frames per turn.

controls.control: Remove (per client)
controls.does: Removes that client.
controls.why: Build the cell down as well as up.

demo: Set up: the defaults, then set the sharing rule to Packet.
Ask the room: "If one client drops to 6 Mbps, what happens to everyone else?" (the Teacher's Guide's own example question).

Reveal: play the round. The 6 Mbps block fills most of the round. Read the takeaway line under the switch, which states the slow client's share of the air and what every client gets. Press Up or Down to switch to Airtime: the fast clients recover, the slow client gets less, and the total rises.
Optional follow-up: set every client to 867 Mbps. Packet and airtime fairness give identical results (one of the tool's tests), which shows the anomaly needs mixed rates.
teaching.pairsWith: the Airtime Fairness lab, four exercises from "A PHY rate is not a throughput" to "Modern clients, same problem". Also Airtime Anatomy, Legacy Protection Cost (a slow device that costs airtime while silent), Rate Adaptation. Teacher's Guide sequences "Why is the Wi-Fi slow?" and "Troubleshooting slow or unstable Wi-Fi".
teaching.leftOut: one AP sending downlink to every client; every client always has data; no collisions, no retries, no rate adaptation. The 40 µs preamble is one teaching value for HT, VHT and HE. Aggregate size limits are not enforced. Airtime Anatomy does the exact per-PHY timing.

airtime-anatomy.name: Airtime Anatomy
airtime-anatomy.purpose: Draws one transmit opportunity (TXOP) to scale, microsecond by microsecond: the wait (AIFS plus backoff), optional RTS/CTS, the preamble, the data, SIFS and the acknowledgment. Two scenarios stack on one axis so you can compare them, and the readouts show the PHY rate, total airtime, throughput and how much of the air carried data. A Structure view opens the PSDU (physical layer service data unit, the bytes the data symbols carry) and draws what is inside it: one MPDU (MAC protocol data unit), an A-MSDU, an A-MPDU, or an A-MPDU of A-MSDUs. Corrupt one MSDU (MAC service data unit, one packet of your data) and it shows what the receiver can report and what the sender has to send again.
airtime-anatomy.whyHere: A PHY rate is the speed of the data symbols only. Every frame also pays for waiting, a preamble and an acknowledgment, and those costs do not shrink as the rate goes up. Seeing them to scale shows why one 1,500-byte frame at 867 Mbps delivers about 56 Mbps, and why aggregation recovers airtime that a faster MCS cannot. Aggregation is not one thing. An A-MSDU (aggregate MAC service data unit) puts several packets under one MAC header and one FCS (frame check sequence), so one bad bit throws all of them away. An A-MPDU (aggregate MAC protocol data unit) gives every subframe its own header and FCS, so the Block Ack bitmap can name the one that failed and only that one is sent again.
howToUse: Read the bars. Hatched blocks are waiting (AIFS and the average backoff), the gray block is the preamble, lime is the data symbols, the dashed box is SIFS and the outlined block is the ACK or Block Ack. Very short segments get a label under the bar with a leader line.
Tap or hover a segment, or pick a duration in the table below the bars, to see how long it is, its share of the TXOP, and the formula with your numbers in it.

Pick a preset or change the inputs. Compare with scenario B stacks a second TXOP on the same scale; Edit scenario chooses which one the inputs change. More settings holds encryption, access category, RTS/CTS, control frame rate and the HE packet extension.

Watch the Check line. It flags combinations the standard does not allow, such as VHT at 6 GHz or a VHT MCS, width and stream count with no whole number of data bits per symbol. It also enforces the standard's limits on size as well as duration: a PPDU over 5.484 ms, and an aggregate the Structure view marks over a maximum, such as an HT A-MPDU of 64 frames of 1,500 bytes (99,328 bytes, over HT's 65,535). The line names the size and the limit, and when a scenario breaks both the time limit and a size limit, it names both. A flagged scenario is not drawn.

Switch the view to Structure to open the PSDU of the scenario you are editing. Arrangement picks Single MPDU, A-MSDU, A-MPDU or A-MPDU of A-MSDUs; MSDUs per A-MSDU sets how many packets share one header (2, 3 or 4). The A-MPDU arrangement is the same aggregate the time view draws, and the line under the inputs says so, with its bytes and its time.

Turn on Corrupt one MSDU, tap a lime block, or use the arrow buttons to move the damage. Each box in the PSDU is one MPDU drawn to scale in bytes (lime is payload, gray is overhead), and the one that fails is outlined and marked with a cross. Under it are the parts of that MPDU, the Block Ack bitmap with a 0 for the failed subframe (or, for a lone MPDU, the ACK that never comes), what is resent in bytes and in time, the limits from the standard for this PHY, the bytes part by part, and all four arrangements side by side. Amber in the limits means the frame fits only a receiver that advertises a larger setting; red means it is over the maximum.

On a computer or tablet, Present opens this tool full screen for a projector: the Right arrow walks the TXOP one segment at a time (in the Structure view it moves the damage to the next MSDU), Up and Down change the rate of the scenario you are editing, V switches between Time and Structure, A steps through the arrangements, C corrupts one MSDU or repairs it, F switches full screen, ? lists the keys and Esc exits.

inputs.name: Band

airtime-anatomy.algorithm: AIFS = SIFS + AIFSN x 9 µs slot. Average backoff = CWmin / 2 x 9 µs. Data bits per symbol N_DBPS = data subcarriers x bits per subcarrier x coding rate x streams (Legacy: rate x 4); HE rounds it down. Symbol time: Legacy 4 µs, HT/VHT 3.2 µs + GI, HE 12.8 µs + GI. MPDU = payload + 26-byte QoS header + 4-byte FCS + encryption; each A-MPDU subframe adds a 4-byte delimiter and pads to 4 bytes. VHT and HE always send an A-MPDU; Legacy and a single HT frame do not. One frame is acknowledged with an ACK, two or more with a Block Ack. Symbols: Legacy/HT/VHT ceil((16 + 8 x PSDU bytes + 6) / N_DBPS); HE ceil((16 + 8 x PSDU bytes) / N_DBPS). Preamble: Legacy 20 µs; HT 20 + 8 + 4 + 4 per HT-LTF; VHT 20 + 8 + 4 + 4 per VHT-LTF + 4; HE 20 + 4 + 8 + 4 + HE-LTFs x (6.4 + GI), or x 16 µs at a 3.2 µs GI (4x HE-LTF). Data: symbols x 4 µs, or with a 0.4 µs GI 4 x ceil(3.6 x symbols / 4); HE symbols x symbol time + packet extension; plus 6 µs at 2.4 GHz. Control frames: 20 + 4 x ceil((16 + 8 x bytes + 6) / (rate x 4)) µs with ACK 14, Block Ack 32, RTS 20 and CTS 14 bytes. Throughput = payload bits / total airtime. Structure view: an MPDU is the 26-byte MAC header, the encryption bytes, the body and a 4-byte FCS. An A-MSDU body is a run of subframes, each a 14-byte subframe header (destination address 6, source address 6, length 2) and one MSDU, every subframe but the last padded to a 4-byte boundary, all under one MAC header and one FCS. An A-MPDU is a run of subframes, each a 4-byte MPDU delimiter, one whole MPDU and padding to a 4-byte boundary. An A-MPDU of A-MSDUs puts one A-MSDU in each A-MPDU subframe. The PSDU is every byte added up, delimiters, headers, padding and FCS included, and the time view uses the same sizes and the same rule for when the PSDU is an A-MPDU. One bad bit fails the FCS of the MPDU it sits in: in an A-MPDU the Block Ack bitmap marks that subframe 0 and only it is resent; a lone MPDU or A-MSDU gets no ACK and is resent whole. The resend is timed as a new PPDU (physical layer protocol data unit) of exactly the resent bytes, preamble plus data, with the same formulas. Limits checked: an HT A-MSDU is at most 3,839 or 7,935 bytes; an MPDU inside an HT A-MPDU is at most 4,095 bytes, 2^12 - 1, because the delimiter's MPDU Length field has 12 bits (14 in VHT and later), so an unencrypted A-MSDU there is at most 4,065; a VHT MPDU is at most 3,895, 7,991 or 11,454 bytes; an A-MPDU is at most 2^(13 + exponent) - 1 bytes, 65,535 for HT and 1,048,575 for VHT; an HE A-MPDU is at most 6,500,631 bytes, the HE PSDU maximum; and preamble plus data is at most 5.484 ms (aPPDUMaxTime), the longest time a legacy station can read from L-SIG: 4,095 bytes at 6 Mbps.
airtime-anatomy.example: HE at 6 GHz, 80 MHz, MCS 11, 2 streams, 0.8 µs GI, 32 frames of 1,500 bytes: 16,333 data bits per symbol in 13.6 µs is 1,200.96 Mbps. The TXOP is AIFS 43 + backoff 67.5 + preamble 50.4 + data 340 + SIFS 16 + Block Ack 32 = 548.9 µs, so 384,000 payload bits deliver 699.6 Mbps, 58.3% of the PHY rate. The same 1,500 bytes sent alone over VHT at 866.67 Mbps take 214.5 µs, ACK included, and deliver 55.9 Mbps. In the Structure view the same 32 frames are 32 A-MPDU subframes of 1,552 bytes (delimiter 4 + MAC header 26 + security 16 + MSDU 1,500 + FCS 4 + padding 2), 49,664 bytes in all. Corrupt MSDU 5 and bit 5 of the Block Ack is 0: 1,552 bytes, 3.1% of the PSDU, go again in a 64 µs PPDU. Pack three of those MSDUs into one A-MSDU instead and one bad bit costs all 4,596 bytes. Pack three of them into each A-MSDU of a 64-frame HT A-MPDU and every MPDU is 4,592 bytes, more than the 4,095 an HT delimiter can describe.
fieldNotes: One station, no contention, no retries. Backoff is the average of a draw from 0 to CWmin; with other stations contending, waits are longer.
HT and VHT are modeled with one BCC encoder (6 tail bits). At the highest rates the standard uses more encoders and a few more tail bits, under one symbol.
HE uses LDPC with pre-FEC padding ignored, so the symbol count can be one short. HE-LTFs are 2x (6.4 µs + GI), or 4x (16 µs) at a 3.2 µs GI. It models the single-user PPDU, not OFDMA resource units.
Control frames go at the legacy rate you choose, and the slot is the 9 µs short slot of an all-OFDM network.
The Check does not catch every VHT MCS exclusion (for example 80 MHz, MCS 6, 3 streams). Confirm unusual combinations in the MCS Index tool.
Airtime on data symbols leaves out the HE packet extension and the 2.4 GHz signal extension: both are padding, not data.

The Structure view checks the limits two sources agree on: the HT Maximum A-MSDU Length (3,839 or 7,935 bytes, HT Capabilities element), 4,095 bytes for an MPDU inside an HT A-MPDU, the VHT Maximum MPDU Length (3,895, 7,991 or 11,454 bytes, VHT Capabilities element), the A-MPDU maximum (HT 65,535, VHT 1,048,575, HE 6,500,631 bytes) and the 5.484 ms PPDU duration. At most MCS values time runs out before bytes do. The time view's Check applies the same limits to the aggregate it draws, so the two views agree: an aggregate the Structure view marks as over a maximum is refused in the time view too.

Not checked: the HE Maximum MPDU Length, and the smaller A-MPDU limit an HE receiver can advertise, which the sources pin only in part, and not at all for HE in 2.4 GHz. EHT (Wi-Fi 7) is not modeled; its exact A-MPDU maximum differs between sources.

The Block Ack bitmap counts MPDUs, one bit each: 64 in the compressed Block Ack since HT, 256 in HE, 512 or 1,024 in EHT. A 1,024-bit bitmap is not new in Wi-Fi 7: the original Basic Block Ack had one, for 64 MSDUs of up to 16 fragments each. What EHT added is 1,024 MPDUs.

Every A-MPDU subframe pads to 4 bytes, the last one included, as the time view counts it. The security header and MIC (message integrity check) are drawn as one block, the HT Control field is left out, and a damaged delimiter, where the receiver searches for the next one, is not modeled.
A resend is timed as preamble plus data for exactly the resent bytes. The new wait, the larger contention window after a failure and the acknowledgment are not added.
The Wireless Classroom is designed for tablets and computers, and on a phone some views are cramped.
airtime-anatomy.source: The IEEE 802.11 PHY transmit-time equations (802.11-2020 clauses 17, 19 and 21; 802.11ax-2021 clause 27) and the default EDCA parameter set, as built into the WLAN Pros Airtime Calculator. Computed on your device. Frame structure and limits: IEEE 802.11-2020 clauses 9.3.2.2 (A-MSDU format), 9.7.1 (A-MPDU format), 9.3.1.8 (BlockAck frame format), 9.4.2.55 (HT Capabilities element), 9.4.2.157 (VHT Capabilities element), 10.12.2 (A-MPDU length limit rules) and 10.13 (PPDU duration constraint). The values themselves come from the Linux kernel 802.11 headers, ns-3, MathWorks, CWNP and INET, with two agreeing sources for every limit checked.

teaching.teaches: a PHY rate is only the speed of the data symbols; every transmission also pays for waiting, a preamble and an acknowledgment, and aggregation recovers the airtime that a faster MCS cannot.

teaching.leftOut: one station, no contention, no retries; backoff is the average of a draw from 0 to CWmin. HT and VHT use one BCC encoder; HE uses LDPC with pre-FEC padding ignored, so the symbol count can be one short. Single-user HE only, not OFDMA. The Check line misses some VHT MCS exclusions. EHT (Wi-Fi 7) is not modeled. A resend is timed as preamble plus data only, without the new wait or the larger contention window.

multipath-simulator.name: Multipath Simulator
multipath-simulator.purpose: Shows why the signal changes when you move a few centimeters. A receiver hears the direct signal plus copies that bounced off walls. Each copy travels a different distance, so it arrives with a different phase, and the copies add like arrows placed head to tail. In phase they reinforce; out of phase they cancel.
multipath-simulator.whyHere: One RSSI reading taken in one spot can be several dB off from a reading a hand width away, and a survey or a troubleshooting call that trusts it is trusting luck. Seeing the arrows add and cancel explains the dips, why they repeat every half wavelength, and why a second antenna rarely sits in a dip at the same spot as the first.
howToUse: Pick a scene. One wall shows the direct copy and one reflection, seen from above. Standing wave puts the receiver between a distant access point and a wall. Many paths blocks the direct copy and adds 2 to 30 reflections from random places.
Pick a band. The dips repeat every half wavelength: 6.2 cm at 2.4 GHz, 2.7 cm at 5.5 GHz and 2.3 cm at 6.5 GHz.

In One wall and Standing wave, pick the wall material (metal, thick concrete, drywall) or set the reflection strength yourself. Drag the receiver in the picture or on the plot, or use the slider, and watch the reflected arrow swing around the direct one.

In Many paths, set the number of reflectors and how far away they are, and press New layout for a different room. Move antenna A along the 2 m track and set how far antenna B sits from it, from 0 to 1 wavelength. The readout shows how often each antenna is more than 10 dB below the average and how often both are at once.

Still in Many paths, Combine shows what the receiver does with its antennas: A only, Selection (use the stronger antenna at each spot) or MRC (maximal ratio combining: add every antenna, lined up in phase). The combined signal is drawn as a third, bold line. Antennas sets 2 or 4; with 4 they sit one spacing apart. The Diversity gain card gives the textbook gain at 1% for both methods and what this track shows.
The delay list shows how late each copy arrives. A copy more than 0.8 microseconds late, about 240 m of extra path, spills past the guard interval into the next symbol.

On a computer or tablet, Present opens this simulator full screen for a projector: Up and Down move the receiver a sixteenth of a wavelength, C steps Combine through A only, Selection and MRC in Many paths, F switches full screen, ? lists the keys and Esc exits.

inputs.range: Metal 1.0, Thick concrete 0.39, Drywall 0.1, or Custom 0 to 1

inputs.range: 0 to 100 along the track (One wall); 0 to 40 from the wall (Standing wave); 0 to 200 (Many paths)

inputs.range: 10, 60 or 300 (Many paths)

inputs.range: 2 or 4 (Many paths)

inputs.name: Combine
