rate-vs-range.algorithm: Received power = AP EIRP + client antenna gain - path loss, with path loss = free-space loss at 1 m + 10 n log10(d). Each ring radius is the distance where received power equals that MCS's minimum sensitivity plus the margin: d = 10^((EIRP + G - FSPL(1 m) - sensitivity - margin) / 10n). Minimum sensitivity at 20 MHz, MCS 0 to 13: -82, -79, -77, -74, -70, -66, -65, -64, -59, -57, -54, -52, -49, -46 dBm, and 3 dB higher for each doubling of width up to 320 MHz. Noise floor = -174 dBm/Hz + 10 log10(BW in Hz) + a 7 dB noise figure. The cell edge uses the 20 MHz floor of the basic rate. Who can associate: a client must support every basic rate, or it is refused with status 18, REFUSED_BASIC_RATES_MISMATCH (IEEE 802.11-2024 Table 9-80). Beacons go at one of the basic rates (10.6.5.1); the model uses the lowest, a common vendor choice rather than a rule, and with no basic rates, a mandatory rate. The ACK goes at the highest basic rate not faster than the frame it answers, in the same modulation; if none fits, at the highest mandatory rate not faster (10.6.6.5.2). Mandatory rates: 6, 12 and 24 Mbps for OFDM; 1, 2, 5.5, 6, 11, 12 and 24 for 802.11g (ERP). An HT, VHT or HE frame first converts to a non-HT reference rate by its modulation and coding (10.6.11, Table 10-10: 64-QAM 5/6 is 54). In the Supported Rates element a basic rate has its top bit set, in units of 500 kb/s: 6 Mbps basic is 8C (9.4.2.3). Beacon airtime comes from the SSID Airtime tool's calculator (802.11ax beacon size, one AP on the channel, no MBSSID). Data rates come from the MCS Index tool (802.11be, 800 ns guard interval).
rate-vs-range.example: At 5 GHz (5500 MHz) with 20 dBm EIRP and n = 3, free-space loss at 1 m is 47.3 dB. The MCS 0 ring reaches 66.8 m at 20 MHz and 42.2 m at 80 MHz. MCS 13 reaches 4.2 m at 20 MHz. A client at 20 m receives -66.3 dBm, just short of MCS 5 (-66 dBm), so it gets MCS 4, with an SNR of 27.7 dB over a -94.0 dBm noise floor. Raising the basic rate from 6 to 24 Mbps pulls the cell edge in from 66.8 m to 36.2 m, and four SSIDs' beacons drop from 2.19% to 0.61% of airtime.
fieldNotes: The model's readings, where the standard is silent: when the highest basic rate below a frame is of the other modulation (1, 2, 5.5 or 11 Mbps answering an OFDM frame), the model keeps the modulation and answers from the mandatory OFDM rates; HE frames are answered in OFDM; an 802.11b device, which has no OFDM receiver, cannot decode a beacon sent at an OFDM rate. Rows decided this way are marked.

A star marks a mandatory rate but does not lock it: the standard says what a device must support, not what an access point must keep on. No status code is shown when a client lacks a required PHY, because none is pinned for that case.
These sensitivities are conformance floors, the least a radio must manage to pass. Real radios do several dB better, so real rings are larger.

Only 6 Mbps has a published floor of its own, -82 dBm, equal to MCS 0. 12 to 54 Mbps use the floor of the MCS with the same modulation and coding (24 Mbps is MCS-equivalent to MCS 3, -74 dBm), so they are labeled MCS-equivalent. 9 Mbps and the 2.4 GHz DSSS rates have no sourced floor, so they draw no cell edge.
The path-loss exponent is a model with a chosen value, not a measurement. Walls, people and furniture make real rings uneven.
The width is held fixed. A real AP may send a narrower transmission to a far client, which reaches as far as the 20 MHz rings.
The beacon bar counts beacons only, as time on the air. It leaves out probe responses, the wait for the medium, and other APs on the same channel, all of which the SSID Airtime tool can add.
The Wireless Classroom is designed for tablets and computers, and on a phone some views are cramped.
rate-vs-range.source: Minimum receiver sensitivity per MCS and width as published for IEEE 802.11 conformance (Rohde & Schwarz 802.11be white paper Table 6-4, matched by a second source). Path loss uses the same Friis math as the FSPL Simulator; beacon airtime uses the SSID Airtime tool's calculator; data rates use the MCS Index tool. Rate sets, status 18, beacon and ACK rates: IEEE Std 802.11-2024, 9.4.2.3, Table 9-80, 10.6.5.1, 10.6.6.5.2, 10.6.10 (Table 10-9), 10.6.11 (Table 10-10), 17.1.1 and 18.1.2. Everything is calculated on your device.

teaching.teaches: rate falls with distance in steps, one ring per MCS; a wider channel shrinks every ring, and a higher minimum basic rate shrinks the cell edge and the beacon airtime. The Rate set card adds: a client must support every basic rate or the AP refuses it with status 18, and the lowest basic rate is not a floor for ACKs.

controls.control: Drag or tap on the rings; Client (slider, logarithmic, default 20 m (66 ft))
controls.does: Moves the client. The label and readout give received power, noise floor, SNR, MCS and data rate.
controls.why: Read the MCS a client gets at any distance and see the step at each ring edge.

controls.control: Band (2.4 / 5 / 6 GHz, default 5)
controls.does: Changes the frequency path loss is taken at (2437, 5500 or 6135 MHz) and the widths on offer.
controls.why: Higher bands lose more in free space, so every ring is smaller.

controls.control: Channel width (MHz) (20 or 40 at 2.4 GHz, up to 160 at 5 GHz, up to 320 at 6 GHz; default 20)
controls.does: Changes every MCS threshold by 3 dB per doubling.
controls.why: Doubling the width raises the noise floor 3 dB, so every ring shrinks. The view never rescales, so the shrink is visible.

controls.control: Spatial streams (rate labels only) (1 to 4, default 2)
controls.does: Changes the data rates on the labels, not the rings.
controls.why: Streams multiply the rate but do not change the signal each MCS needs, so the rings stay where they are.

controls.control: AP EIRP (0 to 36 dBm, default 20)
controls.does: Raises or lowers the downlink level everywhere.
controls.why: More radiated power pushes every ring out by the same number of dB.

controls.control: Client antenna gain (-5 to 6 dBi, default 0)
controls.does: Adds the client's antenna to the link.
controls.why: A worse client antenna shrinks every ring as surely as a weaker AP.

controls.control: Path-loss exponent (model) (2.0 to 4.0, default 3.0)
controls.does: Sets how fast the signal falls with distance.
controls.why: n = 2 is free space, indoors is usually 3 to 4. Labeled a model with a chosen value, not a measurement.

controls.control: Margin (0 to 20 dB, default 0)
controls.does: Adds a safety margin to every MCS threshold.
controls.why: Shows how much coverage a design margin costs, ring by ring.

controls.control: Rate set: 12 chips, 1, 2, 5.5, 11 (2.4 GHz only), 6, 9, 12, 18, 24, 36, 48, 54 Mbps; each tap cycles off, supported, basic; a star marks mandatory rates. Default 6, 12, 24 basic, the rest supported
controls.does: Sets which rates the AP offers and which every client must have. The minimum basic rate is no longer picked: it is the lowest basic rate, and the dashed cell edge and the beacon bar follow it.
controls.why: Raising the lowest basic rate shrinks the cell edge and cuts beacon airtime (6 to 24 Mbps moves the edge from -82 to -74 dBm at 20 MHz). Only 6 Mbps has a published floor; when 9 Mbps or a DSSS rate is the lowest basic rate no cell edge is drawn, because neither has a sourced floor. The star marks, it does not lock: the standard says what a device must support, not what an AP must keep on.

controls.control: Client asking to associate (802.11b only; 802.11g, least it must support; 802.11g; Wi-Fi 6, default)
controls.does: Picks the client the verdict is about. Every type is also listed.
controls.why: A missing basic rate means status 18, REFUSED_BASIC_RATES_MISMATCH. An 802.11b device against OFDM basic rates also cannot decode the OFDM beacons, so it never sees the network. The "least it must support" 802.11g device (1, 2, 6 Mbps) is refused by the default 6, 12, 24 basic set.

controls.control: Network also requires (nothing; HT; HE)
controls.does: Adds a BSS membership selector.
controls.why: A client without the PHY cannot associate. No status code is shown, because none is pinned for that case.

controls.control: ACK table (readout)
controls.does: For every rate that is on, and HE MCS 0 to 11 for a Wi-Fi 6 client, the rate its ACK goes at, and whether a basic rate or the mandatory fallback answered.
controls.why: With only 24 basic, a frame at 12 is acknowledged at 12, not 24. Rows marked * are the model's reading where the standard is silent (a DSSS basic rate below an OFDM frame).

controls.control: SSIDs on this AP (1 to 16, default 4)
controls.does: Scales the beacon airtime bar.
controls.why: Every SSID sends its own beacons at the basic rate, so the airtime cost multiplies.

demo: Set up: the defaults: 5 GHz, 20 MHz, 2 streams, AP EIRP 20 dBm, n = 3, client at 20 m (66 ft). The client receives -66.3 dBm, just short of MCS 5, so it gets MCS 4.
Ask the room: "Widen the channel from 20 to 80 MHz. What happens to the edge of coverage?"
Reveal: set 80. The MCS 0 ring pulls in from 66.8 m (219 ft) to 42.2 m (138 ft), and every other ring shrinks with it.

Optional follow-up: back to 20 MHz, tap the 6 and 12 chips off (leaving 24 basic). The cell edge pulls in from 66.8 m to 36.2 m (119 ft) and four SSIDs' beacons drop from 2.19% to 0.61% of airtime. Now ask: "A client sends at 12 Mbps. What rate does the ACK go at?" Open the ACK table: 12, because no basic rate is at or below 12, so the mandatory rate answers.
teaching.pairsWith: FSPL Simulator, Uplink vs Downlink (the other direction of the same rings), 6 GHz Power and PSD, the SSID Airtime and MCS Index tools. The "RF math and the link budget" and "From bits to rate" sequences.
teaching.leftOut: The sensitivities are conformance floors, the least a radio must manage; real radios do several dB better, so real rings are larger. The path-loss exponent is a chosen value, and walls, people and furniture make real rings uneven. The width is held fixed, where a real AP may send a narrower transmission to a far client. The beacon bar counts beacons only: no probe responses, contention or other APs. The beacon rate is the lowest basic rate, a common vendor choice; the standard asks only for one of the basic rates. Only the legacy rate set is modelled: no Basic HT-MCS, VHT or HE MCS sets.

uplink-downlink.name: Uplink vs Downlink
uplink-downlink.purpose: Shows both directions of one Wi-Fi link at once, from above. The downlink runs from the AP to the client and the uplink from the client to the AP. A solid ring marks how far the client can still decode the AP, a dashed ring how far the AP can still decode the client, and the shaded band between them is the asymmetry zone. Two arrows between the AP and the client carry each direction's received level and its MCS (modulation and coding scheme, the data-rate step).
uplink-downlink.whyHere: Every Wi-Fi link is two links, each with its own transmitter and receiver. The client usually transmits less power than the AP and usually has the worse antenna, so there is a zone where the client hears the AP well enough to stay connected while the AP barely hears the client. That asymmetry is normal, not a fault. Turning the AP down to "match" the client shrinks the cell on the side that was already stronger and does nothing for the uplink: the client is the weak end of the link and needs the AP's extra power.
howToUse: Drag or tap on the floor to move the client, or use the Client slider under the view. The readout gives the level, MCS and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) each way, the imbalance in dB and the width of the asymmetry zone in meters.

Set the AP and client transmit powers and both antenna gains in the controls (below the view on a phone, in the panel on the right on a wide screen). The values are illustrative. Watch the uplink move with the client's power and the AP's antenna, and never with the AP's power.

Pick a regulatory rule. US 6 GHz Standard Power and GVP (geofenced variable power) hold the client 6 dB below the AP's authorized power, so the client follows the AP as you move it. US 6 GHz LPI (low power indoor) gives the client a flat limit, and the EU gives AP and client the same limit. Custom applies no rule. Every rule is a 6 GHz rule, so another band returns to Custom.

Press Turn AP down to match to set the AP's transmit power to the client's. The solid ring shrinks, the dashed ring does not move, and the readout says what changed and what did not. Press it again to put the AP back.
Predict, then reveal asks: the client shows four bars; can the AP hear it? Reveal the answer, then put the client in the zone to see it.

On a computer or tablet, Present opens the tool full screen for a projector: Up and Down move the client out and in, R resets, P reveals the answer, M turns the AP down to match and back, F switches full screen, ? lists the keys and Esc exits.

inputs.name: Regulatory rule
inputs.range: Custom, US 6 GHz Standard Power, US 6 GHz GVP, US 6 GHz LPI or EU 6 GHz LPI; default Custom

inputs.name: Band
inputs.range: 2.4, 5 or 6; default 5. Path loss is taken at 2437, 5500 or 6135 MHz

inputs.name: Channel width
inputs.range: 20 or 40 at 2.4 GHz, up to 160 at 5 GHz, up to 320 at 6 GHz; default 20

inputs.name: AP transmit power
inputs.range: 0 to 30; default 20 (illustrative)

inputs.name: Client transmit power
inputs.range: 0 to 24; default 14 (illustrative). Under a rule, the rule sets it

inputs.name: AP antenna gain
inputs.range: 0 to 8; default 4 (illustrative)

inputs.name: Client antenna gain
inputs.range: -5 to 3; default -2 (illustrative, a phone-class antenna)

inputs.name: Path-loss exponent
inputs.range: 2.0 (free space) to 4.0; default 3.0

uplink-downlink.algorithm: Downlink level = AP transmit power + AP antenna gain - path loss + client antenna gain. Uplink level = client transmit power + client antenna gain - path loss + AP antenna gain. Path loss = free-space loss at 1 m + 10 n log10(d), the same both ways, so downlink minus uplink always equals AP transmit power minus client transmit power. Each direction's MCS is the highest whose minimum receiver sensitivity the level meets (MCS 0 needs -82 dBm at 20 MHz, 3 dB more per doubling of width), and each ring is where that direction falls to the MCS 0 floor. Noise floor = -174 dBm/Hz + 10 log10(BW in Hz) + a 7 dB noise figure at both ends. Rules, in equivalent isotropically radiated power (EIRP, transmit power plus antenna gain): US Standard Power, AP up to 36 dBm and client up to 6 dB below the AP's authorized power; US GVP, AP up to 24 dBm and client 6 dB below; US LPI, AP 5 dBm per MHz up to 30 dBm and client -1 dBm per MHz up to 24 dBm; EU LPI, AP and client both 10 dBm per MHz up to 23 dBm. Under a rule the client transmits at its limit.
uplink-downlink.example: At 5 GHz (5500 MHz), 20 MHz and n = 3, with the illustrative AP at 20 dBm and 4 dBi and the client at 14 dBm and -2 dBi, a client 20 m away hears the AP at -64.3 dBm (MCS 6) while the AP hears the client at -70.3 dBm (MCS 3): a 6 dB imbalance. The client can decode the AP out to 78 m, but the AP can decode the client only out to 49 m, so the asymmetry zone is 29 m wide. Turning the AP down to 14 dBm to match pulls the solid ring in from 78 m to 49 m, and the uplink stays at -70.3 dBm.
fieldNotes: The imbalance is set by the two transmit powers alone. Each antenna's gain counts in both directions, so the AP's better antenna helps it hear the client as much as it helps the client hear it.
Under a rule the client is set to the most it may transmit. The rule is a ceiling: many clients transmit less, which widens the gap.

The US LPI numbers sit 6 dB apart, but that is a coincidence of two flat limits. Only Standard Power and GVP tie the client to its AP, and they tie it to the AP's authorized power: turning the AP's transmitter down does not change its grant, so the client's limit stays put.

Both ends use the same receiver floors, the conformance minimums for each MCS. Real radios do better, and many APs gain more on receive from extra antennas and receive chains, which this model leaves out.
A client's bars come from the downlink only. They cannot tell you whether the AP hears the client.
For one direction in detail, with cable losses and fade margin, use the Link Budget tool.
The Wireless Classroom is designed for tablets and computers, and on a phone some views are cramped.
uplink-downlink.source: Client power rules from the US Code of Federal Regulations, 47 CFR 15.407(a)(4) to (a)(8), and the European standard EN 303 687, Tables 2 and 3, as carried by the 6 GHz Power and PSD tool. Receiver sensitivity per MCS and width and the log-distance path loss are the Rate vs Range tool's. Everything is calculated on your device.

teaching.teaches: every Wi-Fi link is two links, the client usually transmits less than the AP, so there is a zone where the client hears the AP but the AP cannot hear the client, and turning the AP down to "match" fixes nothing on the uplink.

controls.control: Drag or tap on the floor; Client (slider, default 20 m (66 ft))
controls.does: Moves the client. The readout gives each direction's level, MCS and SNR, the imbalance and the width of the asymmetry zone.
controls.why: Put the client inside the shaded zone and read both directions at once.

controls.control: Regulatory rule (picker): Custom (no rule applied), US 6 GHz Standard Power, US 6 GHz Geofenced Variable Power (GVP), US 6 GHz Low Power Indoor (LPI), EU 6 GHz Low Power Indoor (LPI); default Custom
controls.does: Applies a rule to the client's power. Every rule is a 6 GHz rule, so picking another band returns to Custom.
controls.why: Regulations set the client relative to the AP (Standard Power, GVP), as a flat number (US LPI) or the same as the AP (EU). Standard Power and GVP are separate entries because their AP caps differ.

controls.control: Band (2.4 / 5 / 6 GHz, default 5)
controls.does: Sets the frequency path loss is taken at.
controls.why: Path loss is the same both ways on any band; the imbalance comes from the radios.

controls.control: Channel width (MHz) (default 20)
controls.does: Moves each direction's MCS thresholds 3 dB per doubling, and the per-MHz limits under the LPI rules.
controls.why: Under US LPI the limits are per MHz, so at 20 MHz the AP is 18 dBm and its client 12; the flat 30 and 24 appear only at 320 MHz.

controls.control: AP transmit power (0 to 30 dBm, default 20, illustrative)
controls.does: Moves the downlink only.
controls.why: The uplink never moves with the AP's power.

controls.control: Client transmit power (0 to 24 dBm, default 14, illustrative); reads "set by the rule" under a rule
controls.does: Moves the uplink only. Under a rule the client transmits at its limit.
controls.why: The client is the weak end of the link; its power sets the uplink. The rule is a ceiling, and many clients transmit less.

controls.control: AP antenna gain (0 to 8 dBi, default 4), Client antenna gain (-5 to 3 dBi, default -2, a phone-class antenna)
controls.does: Add each antenna's gain.
controls.why: Each antenna counts in both directions, so the AP's better antenna helps it hear the client as much as it helps the client hear it. The imbalance is set by the two transmit powers alone.

controls.control: Path-loss exponent (model) (2.0 to 4.0, default 3.0)
controls.does: Sets how fast the signal falls with distance.
controls.why: Stretches or shrinks both rings without changing the dB imbalance between them.

controls.control: Turn AP down to match / Put the AP back to (power)
controls.does: Sets the AP's transmit power to the client's, and back.
controls.why: AP and client power rarely match and should not be made to. The solid ring shrinks, the dashed ring does not move, and the readout says what changed and what did not. The tool never tells you to equalize the two.

controls.control: Reveal the answer / Hide the answer; Put the client in the zone
controls.does: Answers "The client shows four bars. Can the AP hear it?" and moves the client into the asymmetry zone.
controls.why: Bars come from the downlink only and cannot tell you whether the AP hears the client.

demo: Set up: the defaults: Custom, 5 GHz, 20 MHz, AP 20 dBm with 4 dBi, client 14 dBm with -2 dBi, client at 20 m (66 ft).
Ask the room the question on screen: the client shows four bars. Can the AP hear it?

Reveal: press P. At 20 m the client hears the AP at -64.3 dBm (MCS 6) and the AP hears the client at -70.3 dBm (MCS 3), a 6 dB imbalance. Press Put the client in the zone: between 49 m (161 ft) and 78 m (256 ft) the client still decodes the AP while the AP cannot decode the client.

Optional follow-up: press M. The solid ring pulls in from 78 m to 49 m and the uplink stays at -70.3 dBm: the AP gave up its reach and the uplink gained nothing. Then pick US 6 GHz Standard Power on 6 GHz and move the AP slider: the client follows the AP's authorized power, 6 dB lower.
teaching.pairsWith: Rate vs Range (the same thresholds and path loss), 6 GHz Power and PSD (the same client rules), Body Loss, Link Budget. The "RF math and the link budget" and "Why clients misbehave" sequences.
teaching.leftOut: All radio values are illustrative. Both ends use the same conformance receiver floors, where many APs hear better with extra antennas and receive chains. Under a rule the client is set to the most it may transmit. No walls or bodies; path loss is the log-distance model. For one direction in detail, with cable losses and fade margin, use Link Budget (the tool has a button).

body-loss.name: Body Loss
body-loss.purpose: Shows what people cost a Wi-Fi signal, from above. An auditorium floor holds one AP on the front wall, a person holding a device (the holder) and up to 50 other people. A straight line runs from the AP to the device, and every person that line passes through is numbered. The readouts give the received level, the loss from the holder's own body, the loss from the crowd, the difference between the empty and the occupied room, and the MCS (modulation and coding scheme, the data-rate step) the level supports. Every body-loss value is an illustrative setting, not a measurement.
body-loss.whyHere: A person between the device and the AP costs decibels, and the person holding the device often costs the most, because their body sits right next to its antenna. Facing the AP with the device in front costs little; turning your back puts your body in the path. Crowds add up: a room full of people is a room full of obstacles that are mostly water, which is why a survey of the empty building reads better than the same building in use. Higher bands generally lose more to the body.
howToUse: Turn the holder with the Holder facing slider, the Face the AP and Back to the AP buttons, or by tapping the floor: the holder turns toward the spot you tap. Watch the loss from the holder rise from nothing to the full value as the back turns toward the AP.
Drag the holder to move them, or use the Holder slider under the view. Drag any person to place them on or off the line.
Set the body losses in the controls (below the view on a phone, in the panel on the right on a wide screen). Each is labeled illustrative: set them to match what you measure.
Switch the building between Empty and Occupied, change how many people are in the room, and press Scatter the crowd for a new arrangement. The same arrangement always comes back for the same seed.
Predict, then reveal asks: you surveyed the auditorium empty on Saturday; what happens Monday at 9 a.m.? Reveal the answer, then switch between Saturday and Monday.

On a computer or tablet, Present opens the tool full screen for a projector: Left and Right turn the holder, Space empties or fills the room, Up and Down change the crowd size, R resets, P reveals the answer, F switches full screen, ? lists the keys and Esc exits.

inputs.name: Band
inputs.range: 2.4, 5 or 6; default 5. Path loss is taken at 2437, 5500 or 6135 MHz

inputs.name: Holder facing
inputs.range: 0 to 360, 0 up the page and 90 to the right; default facing the AP

inputs.name: Holder body loss at 2.4 GHz
inputs.range: 0 to 20; default 8 (illustrative)

inputs.name: Loss per person on the line at 2.4 GHz
inputs.range: 0 to 10; default 4 (illustrative)

inputs.name: 5 GHz body-loss multiplier
inputs.range: 1.0 to 2.0; default 1.2 (illustrative)

inputs.name: 6 GHz body-loss multiplier
inputs.range: 1.0 to 2.0; default 1.3 (illustrative)

inputs.name: Building
inputs.range: Empty or Occupied; default Occupied

inputs.name: People in the room
inputs.range: 0 to 50; default 30

body-loss.algorithm: Received level = 20 dBm radiated by the AP - path loss - holder loss - crowd loss, with a 0 dBi device antenna (decibels over an isotropic antenna). Path loss = free-space path loss at 1 m + 10 x 3 x log10(d), the log-distance model at the Roaming Walk default exponent, with d the distance from the AP to the device. Holder loss = the holder setting x the band multiplier x a turn share: 0 while the holder faces anywhere within 120 degrees of the AP, rising along a raised-cosine curve over the last 60 degrees to 1 with the back square to the AP (illustrative). Crowd loss = the per-person setting x the band multiplier x the number of people the straight line from the AP to the device passes through, each body taken as 0.5 m wide seen from above; it is zero while the building is empty, and empty vs occupied changes nothing else. The band multipliers are 1.0 at 2.4 GHz and, by default, 1.2 at 5 GHz and 1.3 at 6 GHz, an illustrative trend, not a measured table. The MCS is the highest whose minimum receiver sensitivity the level meets at 20 MHz (MCS 0 needs -82 dBm). The device is held 0.3 m in front of the body. The crowd is placed at random from a seed, at least 0.7 m apart.
body-loss.example: At 5 GHz with the illustrative defaults, the device is 14 m from the AP and the holder faces the AP. Empty, it reads -61.8 dBm (MCS 7). With 30 people in the room, 2 stand on the line, each costing 4 x 1.2 = 4.8 dB, so the occupied room reads -71.4 dBm (MCS 3): 9.6 dB worse than the survey of the empty room. Turn the holder's back to the AP and the body adds 8 x 1.2 = 9.6 dB more: -81.6 dBm, MCS 0.
fieldNotes: Every body-loss value in this tool is an illustrative, adjustable setting. No measured body-loss figure stands behind the defaults, so treat the numbers as a way to see the shape of the effect, not as a design value.
The holder counts first. A device held against the body loses the most when the back turns toward the AP, which is why a reading can change just by turning around.
A survey walked in an empty building measures a building nobody uses that way. Leave margin for the people who will fill it.
Only people on the straight line count here. Real signals also arrive by reflections around a crowd, which this model leaves out, so it shows the direct path only.
For walls and building materials rather than people, use RF Attenuation (RF: radio frequency) and Wi-Fi Through a Wall.
The Wireless Classroom is designed for tablets and computers, and on a phone some views are cramped.
body-loss.source: No primary source was read for any body-loss figure; every loss value is an illustrative setting. Receiver sensitivity per MCS and the log-distance path loss are the Rate vs Range tool's. Everything is calculated on your device.

teaching.teaches: people cost decibels, the person holding the device often costs the most when they turn their back to the AP, and a crowd on the line is why an empty-building survey reads better than the building in use.

controls.why: Higher bands generally lose more to the body, shown as an illustrative trend.

controls.why: Orientation matters: facing the AP with the device in front costs little; turning your back puts your body in the path.

controls.does: Moves the holder.
controls.why: Changes the path loss and which people stand on the line, so the class can find a clear spot.

controls.does: Places a person on or off the line.
controls.why: Shows that only the people on the straight line count in this model.

controls.control: Holder body loss at 2.4 GHz (illustrative) (0 to 20 dB, default 8)
controls.does: Sets the holder's full loss with the back square to the AP.
controls.why: No primary source was read for any body-loss figure, so every loss is a labeled, adjustable setting; set it to match what you measure.

controls.control: Loss per person on the line at 2.4 GHz (illustrative) (0 to 10 dB, default 4)
controls.does: Sets what each person on the line costs.
controls.why: Same reason: illustrative, adjustable, labeled so.

controls.control: 5 GHz body-loss multiplier (illustrative) (1.0 to 2.0, default 1.2), 6 GHz body-loss multiplier (illustrative) (1.0 to 2.0, default 1.3)
controls.does: Scale the losses at 5 and 6 GHz.
controls.why: The band trend applies to the crowd as well as the holder, because a crowd is bodies.

controls.control: Building: Empty / Occupied (default Occupied)
controls.does: Removes or restores the crowd. Nothing else changes.
controls.why: The Saturday survey against the Monday room.

controls.control: People in the room (0 to 50, default 30)
controls.does: Sets the crowd size.
controls.why: Crowds add up, one body on the line at a time.

controls.control: Scatter the crowd
controls.does: Places the people in a new arrangement from a new seed.
controls.why: The same number of people costs more or less depending on how many land on the line.

controls.control: Reveal the answer / Hide the answer; Show Saturday, empty / Show Monday, occupied
controls.does: Answers "You surveyed the auditorium empty on Saturday. What happens Monday at 9 a.m.?" and switches between the two.
controls.why: Predict, then reveal, on the tool's question.

demo: Set up: the defaults: 5 GHz, Occupied with 30 people, the holder 14 m (46 ft) from the AP, facing it. Two people stand on the line.
Ask the room the question on screen: surveyed empty on Saturday, what happens Monday at 9 a.m.?
Reveal: press P, then Space to empty the room: -61.8 dBm (MCS 7). Space again to fill it: -71.4 dBm (MCS 3), 9.6 dB worse, from two people at 4.8 dB each.

Optional follow-up: press Right one step at a time. The first eight presses change nothing; after that the holder loss ramps in, and with the back square to the AP the level is -81.6 dBm, MCS 0. Then compare 2.4 and 6 GHz.
teaching.pairsWith: Why Two Devices Disagree (body as one part of a reading), Uplink vs Downlink, Wi-Fi Through a Wall and RF Attenuation for walls rather than people.
teaching.leftOut: Every body-loss value is an illustrative setting with no measured figure behind the defaults, so use it for the shape of the effect, not as a design value. Only people on the straight line count; real signals also reach around a crowd by reflection. Bodies are 0.5 m wide seen from above, and the device is held 0.3 m in front of the holder. Path loss is the log-distance model at n = 3.

db-rules.name: Decibels in Your Head: the Rules of 3 and 10
db-rules.purpose: Shows why a few dB is a big change. One dB (decibel) slider moves a signal from -80 to -60 dBm (decibels relative to one milliwatt) against a fixed -70 dBm reference. Above the slider's dB ruler, a linear bar shows the same power in milliwatts, full length at -60 dBm, and a line joins each whole dB to its place on the bar. The readouts give the power of both, the difference as a ratio, and that ratio built from the rules of 3 and 10 beside the exact figure.
db-rules.whyHere: dB is a ratio, so equal steps in dB are equal multiplications of power. +3 dB doubles the power and +10 dB multiplies it by ten. That makes -67 dBm about twice the power of -70 dBm, which the dBm numbers hide. Together the two rules reach any whole number of dB, so a signal difference can be read in your head. This is the dBm-to-milliwatt arithmetic in the CWNA (Certified Wireless Network Administrator) exam objectives.
howToUse: Predict, then reveal asks: is -67 dBm a little or a lot stronger than -70 dBm? Decide, reveal the answer, then press Show -67 dBm against -70 dBm to see the bar double.
Move the Signal level slider. Every 3 dB up doubles the linear bar, and every 10 dB up makes it ten times longer. At -80 dBm the bar is 1% of its length, at -70 dBm 10%, and at -60 dBm all of it.
The step buttons add or take away 3 dB or 10 dB, one rule at a time. A step that would leave the -80 to -60 dBm range is turned off.
Read the rules path. +1 dB, for example, is +10 -3 -3 -3: ten times, then halved three times, 1.25x against the exact 1.259x.

On a computer or tablet, Present opens the tool full screen for a projector: Up and Down move the signal 1 dB, Right adds 3 dB and Left takes 3 dB away, Page Up and Page Down move 10 dB, Space shows -67 dBm against -70 dBm, P reveals the answer, R resets, F switches full screen, ? lists the keys and Esc exits.

inputs.name: Signal level
inputs.range: -80 to -60 in whole dB; default -70, the same as the reference

inputs.name: Reference
inputs.range: Fixed at -70

db-rules.algorithm: Power in milliwatts = 10^(dBm / 10), the dBm / Watt Converter's formula; picowatts (pW, trillionths of a watt) = milliwatts x 10^9. The power ratio of a difference of D dB = 10^(D / 10), so +3 dB = 10^0.3 = 1.995 and +10 dB = 10 exactly. The rules path writes D as 10a + 3b with the fewest steps (10 and 3 share no factor, so every whole D has one) and estimates the ratio as 10^a x 2^b. The linear bar's length is the signal's milliwatts divided by the milliwatts of -60 dBm.
db-rules.example: -70 dBm is 100 pW. -67 dBm is 199.5 pW: +3 dB, 1.995 times the power, about double. -60 dBm is 1,000 pW, ten times the reference. -69 dBm is +1 dB: +10 -3 -3 -3 by the rules, x10 /2 /2 /2 = 1.25x, against the exact 1.259x.
fieldNotes: +3 dB is 1.995 times the power, so say about double. +10 dB is exactly ten times.
The same rules hold for losses: -3 dB halves the power and -10 dB leaves a tenth of it.
dB compares two powers, and dBm is one power compared with one milliwatt. The difference between two dBm levels is in dB.
For a level outside -80 to -60 dBm, or a conversion to watts, use the dBm / Watt Converter. The dB Reference lists the common ratios in a table.
Every number here is arithmetic. Nothing is measured and nothing is illustrative.
The Wireless Classroom is designed for tablets and computers, and on a phone some views are cramped.
db-rules.source: The rules of 3 and 10 for dBm-to-milliwatt conversion are objective 1.2.7 of CWNP's CWNA-109 exam objectives. The arithmetic is the definition of the decibel, 10 log10 of a power ratio, the same formula the dBm / Watt Converter uses. Everything is calculated on your device.

teaching.teaches: dB is a ratio, so +3 dB doubles the power and +10 dB multiplies it by ten, which makes -67 dBm about twice the power of -70 dBm.

controls.control: Signal level (slider, -80 to -60 dBm in whole dB, default -70)
controls.does: Moves the signal against a fixed -70 dBm reference. The linear milliwatt bar, the lines from the dB ruler and the readouts follow it.
controls.why: One control, one visible change: a dB slider over a linear bar that doubles every 3 dB. The range was chosen so -80, -70, -67 and -60 dBm fill 1%, 10%, 20% and 100% of the bar; a wider range would have shrunk the -70 vs -67 comparison to a few pixels.

controls.control: -10 dB, -3 dB, +3 dB, +10 dB (buttons)
controls.does: Step the signal by one rule. A step that would leave -80 to -60 dBm is turned off.
controls.why: Lets you act out the rules path the readout prints (+1 dB is +10 -3 -3 -3) one press at a time on the bar.

controls.control: Reset
controls.does: Returns the signal to -70 dBm and hides the answer.
controls.why: Puts the signal back on the reference (1x, the same power) so the next question starts from zero difference.

controls.control: Reveal the answer / Hide the answer
controls.does: Shows the answer to "Is -67 dBm a little or a lot stronger than -70 dBm?"
controls.why: The house predict-then-reveal pattern: the room commits to a guess before the screen answers.

controls.control: Show -67 dBm against -70 dBm (appears after the reveal)
controls.does: Sets the signal to -67 dBm.
controls.why: Puts the prediction on the bar: 10% of the length becomes 20%, the step the dB ruler hides.

controls.control: Open dBm / Watt Converter, Open dB Reference
controls.does: Open the two calculator tools.
controls.why: For any level outside -80 to -60 dBm or a conversion to watts; this tool is the picture, those are the calculators.

demo: Set up: open the tool as it starts, signal at -70 dBm, answer hidden.
Ask the room: "Is -67 dBm a little or a lot stronger than -70 dBm?" Many will say a little: it is only 3.
Reveal: press P, then Space. The bar goes from 10% to 20% of its length: 100 picowatts to 199.5, about double.

Optional follow-up: from -70, press Page Up. The bar goes to full length, ten times. Then ask what -69 dBm is and read the rules path: +10 -3 -3 -3, ten times then halved three times, 1.25x against the exact 1.259x.
teaching.pairsWith: FSPL Simulator, next on the shelf, where every doubling of distance costs 6 dB. dBm / Watt Converter and dB Reference for the numbers.
teaching.leftOut: Nothing here is measured or illustrative; it is arithmetic. +3 dB is 1.995 times, not exactly 2, which the readouts show beside the rule. The range stops at -80 and -60 dBm so the bar stays drawable; outside that, use the dBm / Watt Converter. It says nothing about noise or SNR.

rate-adaptation.name: Rate Adaptation
rate-adaptation.purpose: Runs one Wi-Fi link frame by frame under Minstrel-style rate control, the kind Linux uses, and shows it learning. A strip draws every attempt of the last 5 ms to scale, colored and numbered by MCS, with failures marked. A chart shows the chosen rate over the last 20 s against the rate the SNR supports, and a table shows what the radio has learned about each rate, updated every 50 ms.
rate-adaptation.whyHere: A radio does not know the best rate. It learns it by trying rates and keeping statistics, and every retry costs more airtime than the first try: the contention window doubles, and a retry at a lower rate takes longer to send. Walking the client away and back shows the chosen rate step down as the signal falls and climb again as sampling finds the higher rates.
howToUse: Press Play, or Step to send one frame with all its retries. The link opens paused with every rate untried. Restart starts a new link that has learned nothing.

Pick a path: Walk (away to 60 m and back to 2 m every 20 s), Steady (4 m) or Fading (12 m, with the signal swelling and fading by up to about 8 dB). The SNR offset slider adds or removes signal on top of the path.

Watch the table. Each rate shows its smoothed success, its throughput estimate and its place in the retry chain: 1st and 2nd are the best and second-best throughput, P is the best probability, low is the lowest rate.
Change the sampling share, the EWMA weight, the retry chain, the retry limit and the ACK timeout while it runs. Set sampling to 0% and Restart to see a link that never finds its higher rates.

On a computer or tablet, Present opens this simulator full screen for a projector: Space plays or pauses, the Right arrow steps one frame, R restarts, Up and Down move the SNR offset, F switches full screen, ? lists the keys and Esc exits.

inputs.name: Path
inputs.range: Walk (away and back), Steady or Fading; default Walk

inputs.name: SNR offset
inputs.range: -20 to +20; default 0

inputs.name: Sampling share
inputs.range: 0 to 30; default 10

inputs.name: EWMA weight on history
inputs.range: 50 to 95; default 75

inputs.name: Retry chain
inputs.range: On, or Off (every attempt stays at the first rate); default On

inputs.name: Retry limit
inputs.range: 7 (short) or 4 (long); default 7

inputs.name: ACK timeout
inputs.range: 45 or 50; default 45

inputs.name: Speed
inputs.range: 1/50, 1/10, 1/4 or real time; default 1/4

rate-adaptation.algorithm: The link is fixed: 5 GHz, 802.11ax, 20 MHz, one spatial stream, 0.8 µs guard interval, 1500-byte frames, best effort, ACK at 24 Mbps, MCS 0 to 11. SNR comes from the path with the Rate vs Range math (20 dBm EIRP, path-loss exponent 3, 5500 MHz) over a -94.0 dBm noise floor. The SNR an MCS needs is its minimum sensitivity minus that noise floor, 12.0 dB for MCS 0 up to 42.0 dB for MCS 11. Each attempt succeeds with a chance from a teaching curve, 90% at that SNR and 10% about 4.4 dB lower. Every 50 ms each rate's success ratio folds into an EWMA (75% on history by default). Throughput estimate = min(success, 90%) x 12,000 bits / the time of one attempt, and rates under 10% success are ignored. About 10% of frames sample a random other rate. Each frame follows a retry chain: best throughput, second best, best probability, lowest rate; a sample frame puts the sample rate first, or second when it is slower than the best rate. Attempts are split over the chain as evenly as they go (7 = 2, 2, 2, 1). Each attempt costs AIFS (43 µs) + mean backoff (CW / 2 x 9 µs) + TXTIME from the Airtime Anatomy calculator + SIFS and ACK, or the ACK timeout. CW is 15 on the first try and doubles per retry (31, 63, ...) up to 1023.
rate-adaptation.example: With the client steady at 4 m the SNR is 48.7 dB, above the 42.0 dB MCS 11 needs, and the rate control settles on MCS 11 (143.4 Mbps) within a second or two, with an estimate of 36.9 Mbps: one first try there takes 292.9 µs of air. At MCS 7 a first try that is delivered takes 347.3 µs. If it fails (348.3 µs with a 45 µs timeout) and the retry goes out at MCS 6, the retry alone takes 432.9 µs, because the mean backoff has grown from 67.5 to 139.5 µs and MCS 6 sends for longer.
fieldNotes: The success curve is a teaching model, not a measured error curve. The sensitivity table it is anchored to is a set of conformance floors; real radios do better.
This follows the published outline of Minstrel. Real drivers differ in detail: minstrel_ht samples on a timer with typed sample sets and sizes each chain stage by a time budget rather than a count.

Delivered throughput is far below the PHY rate here because every frame waits, sends a preamble and waits for its ACK on its own. Aggregation (A-MPDU) and Block Ack, which real links use, are left out.
There is one station, so there are no collisions, and backoff is the mean rather than a random draw. The Medium Access Simulator shows contention.
The ACK timeout is SIFS + slot + a receive delay of about 20 to 25 µs. The sources disagree on the exact constant, so it is a setting.
The Wireless Classroom is designed for tablets and computers, and on a phone some views are cramped.
rate-adaptation.source: Minstrel rate control as described in the Linux wireless documentation (EWMA with 75% history weight, 10% sampling, the multi-rate retry chain); IEEE 802.11 retry limits (dot11ShortRetryLimit 7, dot11LongRetryLimit 4) and contention-window doubling; ACK timeout from the 802.11 formula SIFS + slot + receive start delay. Sensitivity from the Rate vs Range tool, airtime from the Airtime Anatomy tool. Computed on your device.

teaching.teaches: a radio does not know its best rate; it learns it by trying rates and keeping statistics, and every retry costs more airtime than the first try.

controls.control: Play / Pause
controls.does: Runs the link frame by frame. Opens paused with every rate untried.
controls.why: The play control; opening untried shows the learning from zero.

controls.control: Step
controls.does: Sends one frame with all its retries.
controls.why: Shows one retry chain in full: which rates it tried and in what order.

controls.control: Restart
controls.does: Starts a new link that has learned nothing.
controls.why: The help pairs it with sampling at 0%: restart to see a link that never finds its higher rates.

controls.control: Speed (air time per second)
controls.does: 1/50 (watch single frames), 1/10, 1/4, Real time; default 1/4.
controls.why: The tool lists speed with play and step. The slow end shows single frames, the fast end the trend.

controls.control: Path: Walk / Steady / Fading
controls.does: Walk goes out to 60 m and back to 2 m every 20 s; Steady holds 4 m; Fading holds 12 m with up to about 8 dB of swell and fade.
controls.why: The lesson: as the client walks away the rate steps down, and on the way back sampling finds the higher rates again.

controls.control: SNR offset
controls.does: -20 to +20 dB on top of the path; default 0.
controls.why: The SNR slider: move the whole link up or down the rate table.

controls.control: Sampling share
controls.does: 0 to 30% of frames; default 10%.
controls.why: A small share of frames sample other rates. At 0% the link never discovers a better rate.

controls.control: EWMA weight on history
controls.does: 50 to 95%; default 75%.
controls.why: The smoothing, 75% weight on history: lower it and the table reacts faster and noisier.

controls.control: Retry chain: On / Off, same rate
controls.does: On uses best throughput, second best, best probability, then lowest rate; Off keeps every attempt at the first rate.
controls.why: The retry chain order. Off shows why falling back to a safer rate matters.

controls.control: Retry limit (attempts): 7 (short) / 4 (long)
controls.does: Attempts before the frame is dropped.
controls.why: The two retry limits.

controls.control: ACK timeout: 45 µs / 50 µs
controls.does: How long the sender waits for an ACK that never comes.
controls.why: The sources disagree on the exact constant, so the help makes it a setting.

demo: Set up: the defaults. Walk path, 10% sampling, speed 1/4.
Ask the room: "This link has never sent a frame. How does it find the right rate, and when the client walks to 60 m, does the rate slide down smoothly or in steps?"

Reveal: Play. The chart shows the chosen rate stepping down against the rate the SNR supports, and the table shows what the radio has learned about each rate, updated every 50 ms. On the walk back, sampling finds the higher rates again.
Optional follow-up: set Sampling share to 0% and press Restart. The link stays low. Or press Down several times to cut the SNR and watch retries pile up.
teaching.pairsWith: Medium Access Simulator (contention and the doubling CW), Airtime Anatomy (why a lower rate takes longer), What an Interferer Costs (failed frames that rate control can mistake for a weak link). Teacher's Guide sequence "Why is the Wi-Fi slow?".
teaching.leftOut: the success curve is a teaching model anchored to the conformance-floor sensitivity table, not a measured error curve; real radios do better. It follows Minstrel's published outline; minstrel_ht samples on a timer and sizes chain stages by a time budget. No A-MPDU or Block Ack, so delivered throughput sits far below the PHY rate. One station, no collisions, mean backoff instead of a random draw.

ham-band-plan.name: US Amateur Band Plan
ham-band-plan.purpose: The corrected US amateur radio band plan from HF through SHF: each band's frequency range, the Technician / General / Amateur Extra privileges, the maximum power, and the key mode segments, grouped by HF / VHF / UHF / SHF and searchable.
ham-band-plan.whyHere: A Wi-Fi pro who also holds (or is studying for) an amateur license needs the privileges-by-class and power limits in one place. The 13 cm and 5 cm bands also overlap Wi-Fi, so the band edges matter for the Part 15 versus Part 97 picture.
howToUse: Scroll the bands grouped by region, or type a band name or frequency in the search box to filter (for example "20 m" or "14.2").
Each band card shows the frequency range, the Technician / General / Amateur Extra privileges (or a single line where all classes share access), the max power, and any mode notes.
The 60 m channel detail card lists the 4 channels (by center, with the USB dial annotation) plus the 9.15 W ERP segment.
Use Copy results to put the whole plan, the 60 m channels, and the power / data / 9 cm notes on the clipboard as a table.

inputs.name: Search
inputs.range: band name or frequency; empty shows all bands

ham-band-plan.example: Search "60 m" to see the corrected channel plan: 4 channels at 100 W ERP plus the 5351.5-5366.5 kHz segment at 9.15 W ERP. General class runs 1500 W PEP on 80/40/15/10 m; only 30 m (200 W PEP) and 60 m are lower.
fieldNotes: Power column rebuilt from 47 CFR 97.313: a 1500 W PEP general ceiling, with 30 m = 200 W PEP, 60 m = 100 W ERP (channels) / 9.15 W ERP (segment), 2200 m = 1 W EIRP, 630 m = 5 W EIRP, and a Technician on any HF band = 200 W PEP.
60 m is current as of 13 Feb 2026 (4 channels plus the 9.15 W ERP segment); older 5-channel charts are wrong.
There is no symbol-rate (baud) column: the HF baud limit was removed (FCC 23-93) and replaced by a 2.8 kHz bandwidth limit.
9 cm (3.3-3.5 GHz) is omitted: it is in sunset and does not overlap Wi-Fi. Novice and Advanced classes are closed to new applicants and are omitted.
US (FCC) Part 97. Verify current rules before operating; this band plan is a reference, not legal advice.
ham-band-plan.source: A built-in reference table compiled from FCC Part 97, current as of 13 Feb 2026.

ham-band-wavelengths.name: Band Names & Wavelengths
ham-band-wavelengths.purpose: The translation between the two ways of naming the same spectrum: amateur band names (wavelength in meters or centimeters, like 160 m, 2 m, 13 cm) and their actual frequency ranges, with the wavelength = 300/frequency explainer and a worked example each direction.
ham-band-wavelengths.whyHere: Hams name bands by wavelength; Wi-Fi pros name them by frequency. This is the lookup that lets you cross between the two vocabularies, including the Wi-Fi crossover (2.4 GHz sits in the 13 cm band, 5 GHz in the 5 cm band).
howToUse: Read the two-column table: each amateur band name maps to its frequency range and region tag.
The formula card gives the exact wavelength in meters = 299.792458 / frequency in MHz, plus the wavelength ≈ 300 / frequency working approximation.
The worked examples show name-to-frequency, frequency-to-name, and the Wi-Fi crossover.
ham-band-wavelengths.algorithm: Wavelength in meters is 299.792458 divided by the frequency in MHz (and the reverse gives frequency from wavelength). As a quick working approximation, wavelength is about 300 divided by the frequency, which is within roughly 0.07 percent.
ham-band-wavelengths.example: 146 MHz gives a wavelength of 299.792458 / 146 = 2.05 m, which is the "2 m" band. 2442 MHz (Wi-Fi channel 7) gives 12.28 cm, which is the "13 cm" amateur band.
fieldNotes: The wavelength is the nominal band name; the listed range is the actual amateur allocation, not a literal 300/frequency conversion of the edges.
9 cm (3300-3500 MHz) is shown for completeness but is in sunset; it does not overlap Wi-Fi 5 GHz.
ham-band-wavelengths.source: A built-in reference table with wavelengths derived from frequency using the speed of light.

band-designations.name: Spectrum Band Designations
band-designations.purpose: The ITU decade-band designations (HF / VHF / UHF / SHF) with the propagation behavior each implies, plus the non-amateur neighbors a Wi-Fi pro should recognize: the VHF aviation airband (108-137 MHz AM) and the military UHF airband (225-400 MHz AM).
band-designations.whyHere: Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz lives in UHF and 5/6 GHz in SHF. Knowing the band names and their propagation explains why a 2.4 GHz signal behaves nothing like an HF one, and who else shares the spectrum with you.
howToUse: Read each ITU band card: its frequency and wavelength span and what its propagation means in practice.
The neighbors card lists the aviation and military airbands and the ISM / U-NII bands that overlap amateur allocations.
Copy results puts both tables on the clipboard.
band-designations.example: HF (3-30 MHz) is sky-wave / ionospheric skip, the talk-around-the-world bands. SHF (3-30 GHz) is strict line-of-sight, where Wi-Fi 5/6 GHz lives and rain fade begins.
fieldNotes: Each ITU band is ten times the previous one. Below HF: MF (300 kHz-3 MHz) and LF (30-300 kHz). Above SHF: EHF (30-300 GHz).
121.5 MHz is the civil aviation emergency Guard frequency; 243.0 MHz is the military Guard.
Airband and military allocations are confirmed against the FCC Table of Frequency Allocations.
band-designations.source: A built-in reference table based on ITU band designations and the FCC Table of Frequency Allocations.

part15-part97.name: Part 15 vs Part 97
part15-part97.purpose: Where the amateur 13 cm and 5 cm bands overlap the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz Wi-Fi bands, mapped to the Wi-Fi channel grid, and the rule-by-rule comparison between Part 15 (unlicensed Wi-Fi) and Part 97 (licensed amateur): license, power, station ID, encryption, and commercial use.
part15-part97.whyHere: The same 802.11 chipset can run under Part 15 or Part 97. Amateur mesh networks like AREDN run everyday Wi-Fi hardware on the overlapping channels under Part 97 for the higher power ceiling, giving up encryption and commercial use in exchange. This is the signature Wi-Fi-to-ham bridge.
howToUse: The overlap card maps each amateur band to the Wi-Fi band it covers and the Wi-Fi channels that fall inside it.
The comparison card lines up Part 15 and Part 97 rule by rule; each side is always spelled out in words.
The AREDN card is the real-world example.
part15-part97.example: Amateur 13 cm (2390-2450 MHz) covers Wi-Fi channels 1-6 fully. Under Part 15 you are capped at 4 W EIRP, with encryption allowed and no ID required; under Part 97 you may run far more power but must ID by callsign every 10 minutes and run no encryption.
fieldNotes: Part 15 limits are 47 CFR 15.247 / 15.407; Part 97 conduct rules are 47 CFR 97.113 / 97.119 / 97.313.
9 cm (3.3-3.5 GHz) is being sunset and does NOT overlap Wi-Fi 5 GHz; don't confuse it with the 5 cm band.
Part 97 prohibits encryption that hides the meaning of a message, so amateur mesh traffic must travel in the clear.
part15-part97.source: A built-in reference table drawn from FCC Part 15 and Part 97 rules.

ham-study-resources.name: Ham Radio Study Resources
ham-study-resources.purpose: A vetted, offline list of where to study for the US amateur-radio exams: hamstudy.org, the ARRL license manuals, FCC Part 97, and AREDN, each credited, with the stable exam structure and the two currency caveats that shape how to read any older chart.
ham-study-resources.whyHere: The exam-physics and band material is best served by pointing to the current, maintained study platforms rather than freezing a static notes sheet. This curates the strongest pointers and bakes in the two landmines: the new Technician question pool and the 60 m rule change.
howToUse: Read the two currency caveats at the top first; they govern everything below.
Each resource card shows what it's for, the classes it covers, how current it is, the credit line, and a vet note. Tap Open website to launch it in your browser.
The exam structure card lists the question count and pass threshold for each element.
ham-study-resources.example: Technician and General are each 35 questions, 26 to pass; Amateur Extra is 50 questions, 37 to pass. hamstudy.org tracks the live question pools, including the 1 Jul 2026 Technician pool.
fieldNotes: A new Technician question pool takes effect 1 Jul 2026. The exam structure is stable at 35 questions / 26 to pass; the pool's question count rotates every four years, so it is deliberately not stated here.
The 60 m rules changed 13 Feb 2026; any chart or notes predating it are wrong on 60 m.
No Morse code requirement since 23 Feb 2007; the FCC application fee is $35.
The ARRL band chart is copyrighted; this app builds its own band plan from FCC Part 97 data and credits ARRL rather than reproducing the chart graphic.
ham-study-resources.source: A curated list of maintained study resources, each credited to its source.

general-license-frequency-chart.name: General License Frequency Chart
general-license-frequency-chart.purpose: A ready-to-read reference card with Keith's corrected frequency chart for a US General-class amateur radio license: which HF, VHF, UHF, and SHF bands you can use, the power limits, and the current 60 m channel plan. It lives inside the app and works offline, and you can pinch to zoom.
general-license-frequency-chart.whyHere: If you hold (or are studying for) a General-class amateur license, this puts the band edges, segment limits, and power ceilings on the phone already in your hand, with no signal needed. The 13 cm and 5 cm amateur bands also overlap Wi-Fi, so those edges matter when you're thinking about where amateur rules end and Wi-Fi rules begin.
howToUse: Open the card; it fits the screen automatically. Pinch or double-tap to zoom in.
Read across each band for its frequency segments, the voice sideband, and the maximum power column. The 60 m detail table lists the four channels by center frequency plus the 9.15 W ERP segment.

This card is a flat printed page, so a screen reader can't read the content inside it. If you need spoken-out or searchable text, use the interactive US Amateur Band Plan reference, which covers the same information.
fieldNotes: Frequency segments follow the FCC General-class rules; the power figures follow the FCC power rules: a 1500 W PEP ceiling overall, with 30 m capped at 200 W PEP, 60 m channels at 100 W ERP (and the 9.15 W ERP segment), 2200 m at 1 W EIRP, and 630 m at 5 W EIRP. A Technician operating on HF is capped at 200 W PEP.

The 60 m information is current as of 13 Feb 2026 (4 channels plus the 9.15 W ERP segment). Older 5-channel charts are wrong. There is no HF symbol-rate (baud) limit anymore; data is governed instead by a 2.8 kHz bandwidth limit.
The 9 cm band (3.3 to 3.5 GHz) is left off because it is being phased out and has no Wi-Fi overlap. This card reflects US (FCC) rules and is a reference, not legal advice.
A screen reader can't read the content inside the card because it's a flat image of a printed page. The card title and the pinch-to-zoom gesture are announced.
Based on Keith Parsons' corrected General License Frequency Chart. The card is stored in the app and displayed offline.
general-license-frequency-chart.source: Keith Parsons' corrected General License Frequency Chart, shown as a bundled reference card that works offline.

ham-radio-general-exam-study-notes.name: Ham Radio General Exam Study Notes
ham-radio-general-exam-study-notes.purpose: A ready-to-read study sheet with Keith's condensed notes for the US amateur radio General-class exam (Element 3): the rules, operating practice, RF safety, antennas, and propagation you need to know, written for someone who already understands RF from Wi-Fi work. It lives inside the app, works offline, and you can pinch to zoom.
ham-radio-general-exam-study-notes.whyHere: If you're a Wi-Fi pro studying for the General upgrade, this gives you one offline notes sheet you can review anywhere, using the RF concepts you already know as the on-ramp to the amateur-specific rules and operating practice.
howToUse: Open the card; it fits the screen automatically. Pinch or double-tap to zoom in.
Use it as a revision sheet alongside a live question pool. Pair it with the Ham Radio Study Resources tile for hamstudy.org and the ARRL manuals.
This card is a flat printed page, so a screen reader can't read the content inside it.
fieldNotes: The General exam (Element 3) has 35 questions, and you need 26 correct to pass. The question pool rotates on a four-year cycle, so these notes focus on the stable concepts rather than memorized pool answers.
Check the current rules before you operate: 60 m changed on 13 Feb 2026 and the Technician question pool changes on 1 Jul 2026. This reflects US (FCC) rules and is a study aid, not legal advice.
A screen reader can't read the content inside the card because it's a flat image of a printed page. The card title and the pinch-to-zoom gesture are announced.
Based on Keith Parsons' Ham Radio General Exam Study Notes. The card is stored in the app and displayed offline.
ham-radio-general-exam-study-notes.source: Keith Parsons' Ham Radio General Exam Study Notes, shown as a bundled reference card that works offline.

eirp.name: EIRP Calculator
eirp.purpose: Works out your EIRP (Effective Isotropic Radiated Power), the real power leaving your antenna once you account for transmitter power, cable and connector loss, and antenna gain.
eirp.whyHere: EIRP is the number regulators cap. Check it against FCC or ETSI limits, and use it as the transmit-side starting point for a link budget.
howToUse: Enter your transmit power and pick its unit (dBm, W, or mW).
Enter cable loss in dB and antenna gain in dBi.
Read the EIRP in dBm, plus a second line in watts or milliwatts.

inputs.name: TX power
inputs.range: In watts or milliwatts it must be greater than 0; a zero or negative value can't be converted and leaves the result blank.

inputs.name: Cable loss
inputs.range: Positive or negative allowed

inputs.name: Antenna gain
inputs.range: Positive or negative allowed

eirp.algorithm: EIRP in dBm is simply your transmit power plus antenna gain minus cable loss. If you enter power in watts or milliwatts, it's first converted to dBm. The result is also shown in watts (or milliwatts when under 1 W) so you can compare against regulatory limits stated either way.
eirp.example: Transmit power 20 dBm, cable loss 1.5 dB, antenna gain 14 dBi gives 20 minus 1.5 plus 14, which is 32.5 dBm, or about 1.78 W.
fieldNotes: Your cable loss figure should include every connector and jumper loss on the transmit chain.

The reference card lists regulatory EIRP ceilings (for example, 2.4 GHz FCC point-to-multipoint at +36 dBm, or 4 W). Treat those as planning anchors; they vary by sub-band, channel width, and power-control rules, so always check current local regulations.
eirp.source: Standard EIRP arithmetic done on the values you enter, right on your device.

fresnel.name: Fresnel Zone
fresnel.purpose: Works out the radius of the first Fresnel zone along a point-to-point path, plus the 60% clearance figure planners treat as the keep-it-clear threshold.
fresnel.whyHere: A clear line of sight isn't enough for a reliable link; the first Fresnel zone needs to be mostly clear too. This tells you how much clearance you need above terrain, rooftops, and trees.
howToUse: Enter the frequency in GHz.
Enter the total path distance in meters.
Optionally, enter a distance from the transmitter to get the radius at that exact point; leave it blank to see just the midpoint (the widest point).
Read the first-zone radius and the 60% clearance, shown in meters with feet alongside.

inputs.name: Frequency
inputs.range: Must be greater than 0

inputs.name: Total path distance
inputs.range: Must be greater than 0

inputs.name: Point from TX
inputs.range: Must fall somewhere between 0 and the total distance to add an at-that-point result; otherwise it's ignored.

fresnel.algorithm: The zone is widest at the midpoint and pinches toward each end. At any point, the radius grows with the wavelength and with how far the point sits from each end of the path. Wavelength comes from the frequency (about 0.3 divided by the frequency in GHz, in meters). The tool always shows the midpoint radius (the worst case) and multiplies it by 0.6 for the 60% clearance figure. Feet come from multiplying meters by 3.28084.
fresnel.example: At 5.8 GHz over a 10,000 m path, the wavelength is about 0.0517 m, the midpoint radius works out to about 11.37 m, and 60% clearance is about 6.82 m.
fieldNotes: The midpoint radius is the worst case along the path, so clearance there is the constraint that binds.
The frequency unit here is fixed to GHz (unlike the FSPL tool, which also offers MHz).
The 60% clearance figure is the common rule of thumb; some designs need more in heavy foliage or reflective environments.
fresnel.source: Standard Fresnel-zone geometry computed from the frequency and distances you enter, right on your device.

cable-loss.name: Cable Loss
cable-loss.purpose: Estimates the total signal loss for a run of coax of a known type, length, and frequency, plus the loss per 100 feet at that frequency.
cable-loss.whyHere: Cable loss comes straight off both your transmit and receive signal. Pick a cable type and length, and the tool tells you how much signal the feedline will eat.
howToUse: Pick the cable type from the list (six LMR types).
Enter the frequency and pick its unit (GHz or MHz).
Enter the run length and pick its unit (feet or meters).
Read the total loss in dB plus the per-100-foot figure.

inputs.name: Cable type
inputs.unit: One of: LMR-100A, LMR-200, LMR-400 (default), LMR-600, LMR-900, LMR-1200

inputs.name: Frequency
inputs.range: Must be greater than 0

inputs.name: Length
inputs.range: Must be greater than 0

cable-loss.algorithm: Times Microwave publishes an attenuation equation on every LMR datasheet: loss per 100 feet equals k1 times the square root of the frequency in MHz, plus k2 times the frequency in MHz, where k1 and k2 are constants for that specific cable. The tool evaluates that equation at your exact frequency, then scales it by your run length (loss per 100 feet times length in feet, divided by 100). Nothing is interpolated between table rows, so there is no frequency at which the tool has to guess. For example, LMR-400 at 2400 MHz is 6.6 dB per 100 feet.
cable-loss.example: LMR-400 at 2.4 GHz over 50 feet: 6.6 dB per 100 feet times 50, divided by 100, is 3.31 dB total.
fieldNotes: These are manufacturer figures at the datasheet's stated conditions (VSWR 1.0, 25 C). Real loss rises with heat and age, and connectors add loss this tool doesn't count.
The equation is Times Microwave's own, so it reproduces their published tables wherever the two overlap, and it stays exact at frequencies they never tabulated (2400 MHz among them).

There is no RG-58, RG-8, RG-213 or RG-214 here, on purpose. "RG" is not one cable: Belden 8259 and Belden 9201 are both stamped RG-58 and differ by 54 percent at 900 MHz, and no manufacturer publishes RG attenuation at Wi-Fi frequencies at all. For an RG run, read dB/100 ft off your actual cable's datasheet by part number.

Five cables are offered (LMR-100A, LMR-200, LMR-400, LMR-600, LMR-900). Times Microwave tabulates all five to 5800 MHz, so the published attenuation equation is only ever used inside its validated range. LMR-1200 is deliberately omitted: Times stops tabulating it at 2500 MHz and the equation under-predicts its loss at Wi-Fi frequencies.
Above 5800 MHz the tool says plainly that it is extrapolating rather than quietly showing a confident number. Treat a 6 GHz result as a lower bound and confirm against your cable's datasheet.
cable-loss.source: Times Microwave LMR datasheet attenuation equations (k1, k2 per cable), evaluated on your device.

architectural-scale.name: Architectural Scale
architectural-scale.purpose: Converts a named drawing scale to its dimensionless ratio and back, and converts a distance measured on a drawing to its real-world length (or the reverse). Covers US architectural fractional-inch scales, engineer's decimal scales, and common metric scales.
architectural-scale.whyHere: WLAN pros work inside plan sets and scaled PDFs they were never taught to read. Every coverage prediction, wall distance, and mounting height is wrong if the scale is wrong. This is the same calibration step Ekahau, Hamina, and iBwave ask for on import.
howToUse: Pick the scale family (Architectural, Engineering, or Metric).
Pick the specific scale, for example 1/4" = 1'-0". Read its ratio (1:48).
In Measure, choose a direction: Drawn → Real, or Real → Drawn.
Set the drawing units (in / mm / cm) and real-world units (ft / m).
Enter your measurement and read the converted length, with a friendly feet-inches or fractional-inch form beneath it.

inputs.name: Scale
inputs.unit: A named scale within the family (default 1/4" = 1'-0")

inputs.name: Measurement
inputs.unit: Drawing units (in / mm / cm) or real-world units (ft / m), per direction
inputs.range: Must be 0 or greater

architectural-scale.algorithm: ratio = real ÷ drawn. Imperial: ratio = 12 ÷ inches-per-foot (1/8" = 1'-0" → 12 ÷ 0.125 = 96 → 1:96). Engineer's: feet-per-inch × 12 (1" = 20' → 240 → 1:240). Metric scales are already ratios. Drawn → real multiplies the measurement by the ratio; real → drawn divides. The ratio is dimensionless, so the conversion runs through a millimetre base and the two ends can carry different units.
architectural-scale.example: 3.5" measured on a 1/8" = 1'-0" (1:96) sheet is 3.5 × 96 = 336 inches = 28 ft. In reverse, a 45 ft hallway at 1/4" = 1'-0" (1:48) draws at 45 ÷ 48 = 0.9375 ft = 11-1/4 inches.
fieldNotes: The result is only as good as the scale. If a PDF has no embedded scale, confirm which scale it is by measuring a known dimension: a 3'-0" door or a 2×4 ft ceiling tile.
Printed and PDF plans are often not to true scale (fit-to-page printing, cropped sheets). Trust a dimensioned callout on the sheet over any measurement.
US-primary: architectural scales use fractional inches, engineer's scales use decimal feet per inch. Metric ratios (1:50, 1:100) are provided for ISO drawing sets.

enclosure-ratings.name: Enclosure Ratings
enclosure-ratings.purpose: A field reference for the two enclosure-rating systems a WLAN pro reads on outdoor and industrial spec sheets: the IP code (IEC 60529, international) and NEMA types (NEMA 250, US). It decodes each IP digit, lists the NEMA types that matter for Wi-Fi, and shows the one-way NEMA-to-IP translation.
enclosure-ratings.whyHere: US spec sheets quote NEMA and international sheets quote IP, so pros translate between them to compare gear on the same terms and spec an enclosure, AP, antenna, or PoE injector to the real hazard at the mount point.
howToUse: Read an IP code left to right: first digit is solids and dust (0 to 6), second digit is water (0 to 9K). Each digit maps to a defined lab test.
Use the common-ratings table to place a code (for example IP66 = dust-tight plus powerful jets, the mainstream outdoor AP rating).
For a US spec sheet, read the NEMA type, then use the NEMA-to-IP table as a minimum floor. The reverse (IP to NEMA) is not valid.
Use the placement table to pick a rating for where the gear mounts.
fieldNotes: X means not tested, not zero: IPX7 is water-rated 7 with the solids digit unrated. Read X as no data, never as fails.
NEMA to IP is valid only as a minimum. NEMA tests corrosion, icing, gasket aging, and oil, which IP never checks, so a NEMA 4X box exceeds IP66 but an IP66 box is not automatically NEMA 4X.
The water ladder is not a clean superset past 6: an IP67 (immersion) device is not guaranteed to pass IP66 (jets). Gear that must survive both is dual-marked, such as IP66/IP67.
IP tests use fresh water only. Salt, detergents, and solvents need separate chemical-resistance verification.
This is a field reference, not code or design guidance. Confirm requirements with the AHJ, the architect of record, and a licensed electrician.
enclosure-ratings.source: IP per IEC 60529; NEMA per NEMA 250.

hazardous-locations.name: Hazardous Locations
hazardous-locations.purpose: A recognize-and-defer field reference for classified (hazardous) areas: the NEC Class and Division system (US, Article 500) and the IEC Zone system (Article 505/506, ATEX, IECEx). It names what the hazard is (Class), how often it is present (Division / Zone), the recognized protection concepts, and the field read, then stops.
hazardous-locations.whyHere: A standard commercial AP is a genuine ignition source in a flammable atmosphere. Mounting one in a classified area is illegal, uninsurable, and dangerous. WLAN pros need to recognize a refinery, grain elevator, fuel depot, or spray booth before quoting, and route the install to rated gear and the AHJ.
howToUse: Read Class as what the hazard is made of: Class I (gases/vapors), Class II (dust), Class III (fibers/flyings).
Read Division as how often it is present: Div 1 during normal operation, Div 2 only under fault. Div 2 is the far larger wireless market.
Map to the IEC Zone system where a facility uses it (Div 1 is roughly Zone 0+1 for gas; Div 2 is roughly Zone 2).
Match a recognized protection concept (Ex d, Ex i, Ex p, Ex e/nR) to the Division or Zone, or keep the AP out and remote the antenna in.
fieldNotes: Never just mount a commercial AP in a classified area. The default move is to keep the AP in the adjacent general-purpose area and remote the antenna into the zone through a rated penetration.

"Class I Div 2 rated" buys permission to install that specific listed device, in that specific Division or Zone, wired per its control drawing. It is not a blanket safe-anywhere stamp; a Div 2 device is not approved for Div 1.
You cannot mix Division and Zone classification in the same installation. Which one is in force is set by the facility area-classification drawing and the AHJ, not the installer.
This is a field reference, not code or design guidance. Confirm requirements with the AHJ, the architect of record, and a licensed electrician.
hazardous-locations.source: Class/Division per NEC Article 500; Zone per NEC 505/506, ATEX, and IECEx.

nec-gotchas.name: NEC Gotchas
nec-gotchas.purpose: A recognize-and-defer field reference for the NEC articles that actually bite a WLAN installer: elevator hoistways (620), plenum air spaces (300.22), the communications-cable rating ladder (800), PoE bundle heat (725.144), antenna and mast grounding (810), firestopping fire-rated assemblies (300.21), and abandoned cable (800.25).
nec-gotchas.whyHere: These are the code articles most likely to surface on an everyday install. Recognizing each one on site, then handing it to the AHJ, a licensed electrician, or the equipment listing, keeps a WLAN pro out of trouble. This is recognize-and-defer, never how-to-comply.
howToUse: Use it to recognize a code issue on site: the hoistway you cannot put an AP in, the plenum that dictates your cable jacket, the PoE bundle that can overheat, the antenna that needs grounding, the fire wall you must not breach, and the dead cable you must pull.
Read the cable-rating ladder as a jacket fire-rating only (CMP plenum, CMR riser, CM/CMG general, CMX limited); substitution runs downhill only.
On the two STOP items (PoE ampacity, firestop assembly), do not eyeball a number or pick an assembly yourself; hand it to the licensed electrician or the listed system.
Then defer to the right authority for the actual requirement.
fieldNotes: STOP on PoE bundle heat (725.144): the exact ampacity and bundle-count numbers come from the code table and the specific install conditions. Do not eyeball them. Size the bundle with a licensed electrician or the cabling designer against the adopted NEC.
STOP on firestopping (300.21): the approved firestop is a specific listed assembly matched to the wall type, penetrant, and opening. Never improvise it and never pick the assembly yourself.
Grounding (810) caveat: nothing survives a direct strike. Bonding and surge protection mitigate nearby strikes and static, not a direct hit. Conductor sizing is an electrician's call.
This is a field reference, not code or design guidance. Confirm requirements with the AHJ, the architect of record, and a licensed electrician.
nec-gotchas.source: Article numbers per the NEC (NFPA 70); confirm against the locally adopted edition.

safety-basics.name: Safety Basics
safety-basics.purpose: A field-awareness reference for the personal protective equipment a general contractor expects before badging you onto an active site, a short note on ESD (protecting the electronics you install, not the person), and the recognize-and-STOP hazards a WLAN pro must hand off rather than work.
safety-basics.whyHere: Half of a WLAN pro's installs happen on a ladder or lift, on an active construction site, around other trades. Knowing the PPE ratings a GC will ask for keeps you from being turned away at the gate, cheap ESD gear prevents latent failures in the gear you install, and the STOP flags keep a routine cable pull from becoming a health or legal incident. This is awareness and lookup, not compliance instruction.
howToUse: Use the PPE ladder to recognize the four common baseline items and the standard each is rated to (hard hat Z89.1, safety-toe F2413, hi-vis ANSI 107, eye protection Z87.1).
Read the ESD note as gear protection: a grounded wrist strap, mat, and static bags under ANSI/ESD S20.20 guard against latent damage to APs, optics, and boards.
On the four recognize-and-STOP hazards (asbestos/lead, arc flash and energized work, confined spaces, seismic bracing), stop and hand it off. Never run any of them as a procedure yourself.
Confirm the site's specific PPE policy with the employer and GC, who own the assessment.
fieldNotes: The four PPE items are the common 'let me on the site' baseline. On a finished office install street clothes are usually fine; on active construction expect the GC to require all four to badge on.
ESD risk is highest in data centers and any time you handle bare optics or boards. For a sealed AP coming out of a static bag, mounted and cabled, the risk is lower but not zero.
The recognize-and-STOP items are named-and-stopped on purpose: the Toolbox names the hazard and tells you to hand it off, and deliberately gives no procedure for working any of them.
This is a field reference, not code or design guidance. Confirm requirements with the AHJ, the architect of record, and a licensed electrician.
safety-basics.source: Standards designators (ANSI/ISEA Z89.1, ASTM F2413, ANSI/ISEA 107, ANSI Z87.1, ANSI/ESD S20.20, NFPA 70E); confirm the site's PPE policy with the employer and GC.

plan-set-literacy.name: Plan-Set Literacy
plan-set-literacy.purpose: A field reference for reading an architectural drawing set: how a sheet number is built (discipline letter, sheet-type digit, sequence), what each discipline designator and sheet-type digit means, why the Reflected Ceiling Plan (RCP) is the sheet for AP placement, the rest of a plan set worth knowing, and US drawing scales.
plan-set-literacy.whyHere: A WLAN designer who can pull the right sheet, read the RCP, and speak in sheet numbers looks like a peer to the other trades instead of a junior. The RCP is where a coverage design meets the physical ceiling, and catching an AP-versus-diffuser conflict on paper is far cheaper than catching it at rough-in.
howToUse: Read a sheet number left to right: discipline letter, sheet-type digit, sequence. A-201 is Architectural, an elevation, sheet 01.
Use the discipline table to find the sheet owner (A architectural, E electrical, T telecommunications; the WLAN and structured cabling usually live on the T sheets).
Use the sheet-type digit to find the drawing kind (1 plans, 2 elevations, 6 schedules), so A-1xx is an architectural plan and E-6xx an electrical schedule.
For AP placement, open the RCP: overlay your AP locations and resolve conflicts with diffusers, troffers, sprinklers, and soffits before rough-in. Never place APs on the floor plan alone.
fieldNotes: The RCP is drawn as if a mirror on the floor reflects the ceiling upward, so it reads in the same left-right orientation as the floor plan; it carries the ceiling grid, mounting heights, and every ceiling-mounted element.
Always build to the latest revision: the revision cloud marks what changed and the delta triangle carries the revision number.
US architectural sheets use fractional-inch scales (1/8" = 1'-0" is 1:96); to get the ratio, invert the fraction and multiply by 12.
Reference only. Confirm drawing conventions, revisions, and responsibility with the architect of record and your contract for the specific project.
plan-set-literacy.source: Conventions per the US National CAD Standard; sheet-numbering practice varies on smaller jobs.
