site-access.name: Site Access
site-access.purpose: A 'Know Before You Go' checklist: eight site types (aerial and man-lifts, rail, hospitals, maritime, warehouse and distribution, schools, data centers, correctional) and the credential, screening, orientation, or escort that can gate you from reaching the work before it even starts.
site-access.whyHere: On many sites you cannot reach the work area without a specific credential, background check, orientation, or escort. That is a quoting and scheduling factor, not just a safety one. Rail screening, a hospital ICRA permit, or lift-operator proof can each add days or weeks between winning a job and touching a cable.
howToUse: Before you quote, scan the checklist for the site type you are bidding and read what may gate you.
Use the 'ask about' column as the questions to put to the GC, site owner, or authority: screening programs, orientations, escorts, flagman, PFD and TWIC, ICRA and ILSM, tool control.
Budget the lead time (rail screening and hospital ICRA in particular run long) into the schedule you promise.
Confirm each requirement with the site, general contractor, and authority before you go to site; the Toolbox certifies nothing and clears no one.
fieldNotes: The pattern across every item: the requirement is set by someone other than you, must be satisfied before work starts, and carries real lead time and cost.
Maritime and over-water work adds PFD and drowning-hazard rules plus heavy salt corrosion, so spec NEMA 4X or high-IP with explicit corrosion resistance.
There is no OSHA-issued 'lift license'; the employer trains and certifies lift operators, and GCs demand documented proof.
This is a field reference, not code or design guidance. The site, general contractor, and authority set every requirement; confirm each one with them before you go to site.
site-access.source: Access requirements are set by the site, GC, and authority having jurisdiction; confirm each before going to site.

cad-bim-formats.name: CAD & BIM Formats
cad-bim-formats.purpose: A field reference for what the building files an architect hands you actually are: the format decode table (DWG, DXF, DGN, IFC, RVT, NWD/NWC, COBie), the Level of Development (LOD 100-500) ladder for how much of a model to trust, and how a building file flows into a Wi-Fi design tool (Ekahau, Hamina, iBwave).
cad-bim-formats.whyHere: You receive these files on every design job. The difference between a clean import and a wasted afternoon is knowing what the format is, what LOD you were handed, which CAD layers to ask for, and that scale calibration is the single step that makes or breaks the whole design. The Toolbox explains these formats; it does not open, render, or convert them.
howToUse: Use the decode table to recognize a format on sight: DWG and DXF are Autodesk CAD, IFC is the open BIM standard, RVT is a Revit model, NWD/NWC are Navisworks coordination files, COBie is asset data.
Read the LOD you were handed before trusting geometry: LOD 100-200 is a massing study (do not derive wall attenuation from it), LOD 300 and up is dimensionally trustworthy.
Follow the import flow: import the CAD or PDF, calibrate the scale on a known distance (get this wrong and every downstream distance is wrong), then assign wall materials and run the prediction.
Ask the architect for a clean layer set (walls, doors, structure; strip furniture, dimensions, title blocks) instead of an unusable 80-layer dump.
fieldNotes: Scale calibration is the step that matters most: draw a line over a known length and enter the real measurement. An error here corrupts every distance, coverage prediction, and attenuation value downstream.
LOI (Level of Information) is the data-completeness sibling of LOD: LOD is geometry, LOI is data.
The boundary: the Toolbox explains DWG, IFC, RVT, and the rest and how they reach the design tools. It is not a CAD or BIM viewer, converter, or editor.
Reference only. Confirm file handling, model reliability, and responsibility with the architect of record and your design-tool documentation.
cad-bim-formats.source: Format and LOD conventions per Autodesk, buildingSMART, and the AIA/AGC LOD framework.

structured-cabling.name: Structured Cabling
structured-cabling.purpose: A field reference for the TIA and BICSI structured-cabling standards that decide where an AP can go and what feeds it: the TIA-568 family, the 90 m permanent link plus 10 m of cords for a 100 m channel, the cable-category ladder (Cat 5e through Cat 8), and the MDF-IDF topology that ties AP locations to telecom rooms.
structured-cabling.whyHere: The 90 m rule and the Cat 6A bar shape real WLAN decisions: they set the outer edge of where you can place an AP and what uplink it can carry, which quietly drives IDF placement, switch selection, and the whole coverage plan. The physical grounding-as-safety side lives in the NEC codes reference; this is the TIA and BICSI infrastructure side.
howToUse: Use the TIA family to know who owns what: 568 is cabling, 569 pathways and spaces, 606 labeling and administration, 607 telecom bonding and grounding.
Apply the 90+10 m channel rule as an AP-cable-run reality check: an AP more than about 90 m of cable-path from the IDF needs an intermediate closet, a different topology, or fiber.
Read the cable-category table for the multi-gig bar: Cat 6A carries 10 Gbps to 100 m and is the practical minimum for Wi-Fi 6, 6E, and 7 APs with multi-gig uplinks.
Coordinate with the RCDD (BICSI's cabling-design credential) whose 90 m constraint ties AP locations to IDF locations.
fieldNotes: The 90 m permanent link is solid horizontal cable from the telecom room to the outlet; add up to 10 m of stranded patch and equipment cords for a 100 m channel maximum. Exceed it and you are outside TIA.
T568A and T568B are the two pin-out standards; a jack is wired to one, so be consistent end to end.
AP count and placement drive IDF count and PoE-switch port budgeting, so the WLAN design and the cabling design have to talk to each other.
Reference only. Confirm cabling design and standards currency with the RCDD, the architect of record, and your contract for the specific project.
structured-cabling.source: Standards per ANSI/TIA-568/569/606/607 and BICSI; confirm the current edition.

aec-process-glossary.name: AEC Process & Glossary
aec-process-glossary.purpose: A field reference for the architecture-engineering-construction workflow you work inside and the shorthand the other trades use: the AIA design phases (Programming, SD, DD, CD, Bidding, CA) and when Wi-Fi should engage, plus the AEC glossary (RFI, submittal, ASI, AHJ, GC, MEP, OAC, AOR/EOR, and more) that trips WLAN pros up. US convention (AIA).
aec-process-glossary.whyHere: Speak the process fluently and you look like a peer in the room instead of the network person who wandered in. The RFI, the submittal, the punch list, and the OAC are the levers that get your coverage design built the way you drew it. Engaging at Schematic Design is the difference between designing Wi-Fi in and retrofitting it later.
howToUse: Use the phase table to engage at the right moment: establish RF requirements and reserve IDF and ceiling access at SD, coordinate AP locations against the RCP at DD, finalize plans and telecom sheets at CD.
Raise an RFI the moment the Reflected Ceiling Plan and your AP plan disagree, so the conflict is resolved on paper before rough-in.
Get your APs, mounts, and cable approved as a submittal (the contractor's proof that what is installed matches the spec).
Treat anything about contractual responsibility as 'confirm with the architect of record and your contract,' never as a ruling.
fieldNotes: The AHJ (Authority Having Jurisdiction) is the building official, fire marshal, or inspector who interprets and enforces code locally; the AHJ's word governs.
An ASI is a minor clarification with no cost or time impact; a Change Order is a formal, signed change to scope, cost, or schedule (what an ASI is not).
The OAC is the recurring Owner-Architect-Contractor coordination meeting; if Wi-Fi matters, someone has to carry it into the OAC.
Reference only. Confirm contractual responsibility, code compliance, and phase deliverables with the architect of record, the AHJ, and your contract for the specific project.
aec-process-glossary.source: Phase and contract vocabulary per US AIA convention.

link-budget.name: Link Budget
link-budget.purpose: A full point-to-point link budget: it adds up transmit power, antenna gains, cable losses, path loss, and any other losses into a received signal level, then compares that against your receiver's sensitivity to give a fade margin.
link-budget.whyHere: This is the tool for deciding whether a link will close, and by how much. Add up all the gains and losses to see the margin before you deploy.
howToUse: Enter your transmit power and pick its unit (dBm, W, or mW).
Enter transmit antenna gain, transmit cable loss, path loss, receive cable loss, receive antenna gain, and receiver sensitivity.
Optionally enter any other or miscellaneous losses (treated as 0 if left blank).
Read the received signal in dBm and the link margin in dB, color-coded by health.

inputs.name: TX power
inputs.range: In watts or milliwatts it must be greater than 0

inputs.name: Other losses
inputs.range: Optional, defaults to 0

link-budget.algorithm: The received signal is your transmit power, plus both antenna gains, minus every loss along the way (transmit cable, path, receive cable, and any miscellaneous). The link margin is that received signal minus the receiver's sensitivity. Margins are graded: 10 dB or more is healthy (green), 0 to 10 dB is marginal (amber), and below 0 is negative (red). Power entered in watts or milliwatts is converted to dBm first.
link-budget.example: Transmit 30 dBm, transmit gain 20, transmit loss 2, path loss 120, receive loss 2, receive gain 20, no misc loss, receiver sensitivity minus 85: received signal is minus 54 dBm, and the margin is 31 dB, which is healthy.
fieldNotes: You supply the path loss yourself; work it out with the FSPL tool, then add real-world margins.
This budget doesn't include rain fade; use the PtP Link Check for that.
A healthy margin of 10 dB or more is the common design target, giving you room to ride out fading and multipath.
link-budget.source: Standard link-budget arithmetic done on the values you enter, right on your device.

shannon-capacity.name: Shannon Capacity
shannon-capacity.purpose: Works out the theoretical maximum data rate a channel can carry, from its bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio, and in reverse the SNR a target rate would demand.
shannon-capacity.whyHere: Every Wi-Fi generation pushes against this ceiling and none of them breaks it. Bandwidth and signal-to-noise decide the maximum, and everything a vendor sells you is an attempt to get closer to it. Put this next to Noise Floor and the Throughput Calculator and you can see how much of the theoretical maximum your link is actually using.
howToUse: Choose whether to solve for capacity or for the required SNR.
Pick the channel bandwidth.
Enter the SNR in dB, or in reverse the capacity you are aiming for in Mbps.
Set the number of spatial streams, because the bound applies to each stream separately.
Read the capacity, the per-stream figure, and the spectral efficiency in bits per second per Hz.

inputs.name: Bandwidth
inputs.range: Choose from 20, 40, 80, 160, or 320 MHz

inputs.name: SNR
inputs.range: Any value, including negative. Wi-Fi really does operate near and below 0 dB at the lowest data rates

inputs.name: Target capacity
inputs.range: Greater than zero (required SNR mode only)

inputs.name: Spatial streams
inputs.range: 1 to 8

shannon-capacity.algorithm: Capacity equals the number of spatial streams times the bandwidth times the base-2 logarithm of one plus the signal-to-noise ratio, with that ratio as a linear power ratio rather than dB. Reversing it gives the spectral efficiency a target rate needs, and from that the SNR it demands.
shannon-capacity.example: At 80 MHz and 25 dB SNR on one spatial stream the ceiling is about 664.8 Mbps, or 8.31 bits per second per Hz. Asked the other way, 1,000 Mbps on one 80 MHz stream needs 12.5 bits per second per Hz, which needs about 37.6 dB. That is why a gigabit demo only works standing under the access point.
fieldNotes: This is a single-channel bound, and Wi-Fi is MIMO. A radio advertising 1,200 Mbps is not beating Shannon: that rate is the sum of parallel spatial streams, each sitting under its own bound. That is why spatial streams are an input here.
The ratio is linear, not dB. Feeding 25 straight into the formula instead of 316 is the most common mistake with this equation, so the screen shows the conversion.
An impossible target is not an error. Asking for 10 Gbps on one 20 MHz stream honestly needs about 1505 dB, and printing that number is the point.
The ceiling assumes perfect coding and no interference, so a real link always lands below it. The gap between the two is the useful part.
shannon-capacity.source: Shannon-Hartley, published by Claude Shannon in 1948. Computed from the bandwidth, SNR, and stream count you enter, on your device.

noise-floor.name: Noise Floor
noise-floor.purpose: Works out the thermal noise floor for a channel, the receiver's noise floor (thermal noise plus its noise figure), and the quick minus 174 dBm per Hz rule-of-thumb value.
noise-floor.whyHere: Signal-to-noise ratio is your signal minus the noise floor. Knowing the noise floor for a given channel width sets the minimum usable signal and frames any link-margin discussion.
howToUse: Pick the channel bandwidth.
Enter the receiver's noise figure in dB.
Optionally adjust the temperature (defaults to 20 degrees C if left blank).
Read the thermal noise floor, the receiver noise floor, and the rule-of-thumb value.

inputs.name: Bandwidth
inputs.range: Choose from 20, 40, 80, 160, or 320 MHz

inputs.name: Noise figure
inputs.range: Must be 0 or more (defaults to 7; a negative or invalid value leaves the outputs blank)

inputs.name: Temperature
inputs.range: Defaults to 20 if left blank

noise-floor.algorithm: Thermal noise rises with both temperature and channel width; wider channels let in more noise. The tool computes the thermal noise floor from those two, then adds your receiver's noise figure to get the receiver noise floor. It also shows a quick rule-of-thumb value: minus 174 dBm per Hz (thermal noise at about 0 degrees C) plus 10 times the log of the bandwidth in Hz.
noise-floor.example: At 20 MHz, noise figure 7 dB, 20 degrees C: the thermal floor is about minus 100.9 dBm, the receiver floor about minus 93.9 dBm, and the rule-of-thumb value about minus 101.0 dBm.
fieldNotes: This is the theoretical noise floor. Real receivers sit higher because of co-channel interference, adjacent-channel leakage, and ambient RF.
The minus 174 rule is a 0 degrees C approximation, so it differs slightly from the temperature-aware thermal value.
noise-floor.source: Standard thermal-noise physics computed from the bandwidth, noise figure, and temperature you enter, on your device.

rain-fade.name: ITU Rain Fade
rain-fade.purpose: Estimates how much rain will weaken a microwave link, using the ITU-R P.838-3 model for specific attenuation and a simplified ITU-R P.530 for effective path length.
rain-fade.whyHere: Above roughly 10 GHz, rain is the biggest cause of fading on outdoor links. This sizes the fade margin a backhaul link needs to keep working through heavy rain.
howToUse: Enter the frequency in GHz.
Enter the rain rate in mm/hr.
Enter the path length and pick its unit (km or mi).
Pick the polarization (Horizontal or Vertical).
Read the total rain attenuation, the specific attenuation, and the effective path length.

inputs.name: Frequency
inputs.range: Must be greater than 0

inputs.name: Rain rate
inputs.range: Must be greater than 0

inputs.name: Path length
inputs.range: Must be greater than 0

rain-fade.algorithm: The tool uses the ITU-R P.838-3 rain model, which sets how strongly rain attenuates the signal based on frequency and polarization. It carries all 116 published rows of the recommendation's Table 5, covering 1 GHz to 1000 GHz, and fills in between them where needed. From those it gets the specific attenuation in dB per km at your rain rate. Heavy rain rarely falls evenly along a long path, so the model also shrinks the path to an effective length before multiplying the two together for the total attenuation.
rain-fade.example: At 23 GHz, 42 mm/hr, 5 km, horizontal polarization: specific attenuation works out to about 5.85 dB per km, the effective path length shrinks to about 3.94 km, and the total rain attenuation is about 23.07 dB.
fieldNotes: The model assumes the rain rate is uniform along the whole path; real storm cells are smaller, which the effective-length reduction partly accounts for.
Choose a rain rate that matches the availability you're targeting (for example, the rate exceeded only 0.01% of the time in your region). The tool doesn't supply regional rain statistics.
Below roughly 10 GHz, rain fade is usually negligible.
rain-fade.source: ITU-R P.838-3 Table 5 (all 116 rows) plus the ITU-R P.530 path reduction, computed from the values you enter, on your device.

ptp-link.name: PtP Link Check
ptp-link.purpose: A complete point-to-point backhaul link budget from end to end: transmit power through antenna gains, cable losses, free-space path loss, and rain fade to the received signal, then compared against sensitivity for a fade margin and a PASS, MARGINAL, or FAIL verdict.
ptp-link.whyHere: The all-in-one decision tool for a microwave or Wi-Fi backhaul link. It combines free-space path loss and rain fade with the link budget, so you get a single go or no-go answer.
howToUse: Enter frequency (GHz), distance (km or mi), transmit power (dBm), transmit gain (dBi), receive gain (dBi), and receiver sensitivity (dBm).
Optionally enter transmit loss, receive loss, rain rate, required margin, and pick the polarization.
Read the EIRP, free-space loss, rain fade, received signal, link margin, and the verdict.

inputs.name: Frequency
inputs.range: Must be greater than 0

inputs.name: Distance
inputs.range: Must be greater than 0

inputs.name: TX power
inputs.range: Positive or negative

inputs.name: RX sensitivity
inputs.range: Positive or negative; sensitivity is usually negative

inputs.name: TX loss
inputs.range: Defaults to 0

inputs.name: RX loss
inputs.range: Defaults to 0

inputs.name: Rain rate
inputs.range: Defaults to 0 (no fade)

inputs.name: Required margin
inputs.range: Defaults to 10

ptp-link.algorithm: First it works out your EIRP (transmit power plus transmit gain minus transmit loss). Then free-space path loss, which grows with both distance and frequency. If you enter a rain rate, it adds rain fade using the same ITU-R rain model as the Rain Fade tool; with no rain rate, rain fade is zero. The received signal is EIRP minus free-space loss minus rain fade, plus receive gain, minus receive loss. The margin is that received signal minus the receiver's sensitivity. The verdict: margin at or above your required margin is PASS, between 0 and required is MARGINAL, and below 0 is FAIL.
ptp-link.example: At 5.8 GHz over 10 km, transmit 20 dBm, transmit and receive gain 23, sensitivity minus 78, no cable losses, no rain, required margin 10: EIRP is 43.0 dBm, free-space loss about 127.7 dB, received signal about minus 61.7 dBm, and the margin about 16.3 dB, so PASS. (Add 1 dB of transmit loss and 1 dB of receive loss and the margin drops to about 14.3 dB, still PASS.)
fieldNotes: This is the most complete link tool in the suite. Prefer it over the plain Link Budget when the link is outdoors and above roughly 10 GHz.
Free-space loss on its own underestimates real-world loss, and the rain-fade leg only covers rain, not fog, foliage, or multipath.
The MARGINAL band (the link closes but sits below your required margin) is the tool's own warning state; the pass or fail underneath it is purely whether the margin meets what you required.
ptp-link.source: Standard link-budget, free-space-loss, and ITU-R rain-fade math, computed from your inputs on your device.

throughput-calc.name: Throughput Calculator
throughput-calc.purpose: Works out the PHY rate and an estimated real-world throughput for a Wi-Fi connection from the standard, channel width, MCS index, number of spatial streams, and guard interval.
throughput-calc.whyHere: Turns a client's negotiated connection settings into expected data-rate numbers, and sets realistic expectations for what speed you should actually see.
howToUse: Pick the Wi-Fi standard (802.11n, ac, ax, or be).
Pick the channel width, MCS index, number of spatial streams, and guard interval (the choices narrow to what's valid for the standard you picked).
Read the modulation, PHY rate, and estimated real throughput in Mbps.

inputs.name: MCS index
inputs.range: Maximum per standard: 802.11n up to 7, 802.11ac up to 9, 802.11ax up to 11, 802.11be up to 13

inputs.name: Spatial streams
inputs.range: Up to 4 for 802.11n; up to 8 for 802.11ac, ax, and be

throughput-calc.algorithm: The PHY rate goes up with three things: how many data subcarriers fit in the channel width, how many bits each subcarrier carries (set by the MCS index), and how many spatial streams you're running. Wider guard intervals stretch each symbol out slightly, which lowers the rate a little. To estimate real throughput, the tool trims the PHY rate by a flat efficiency factor for overhead: about 70% for 802.11n, 72% for 802.11ac, 76% for 802.11ax, and 80% for 802.11be.
throughput-calc.example: 802.11ax, 80 MHz, MCS 11, 2 spatial streams, 0.8 microsecond guard interval: the PHY rate is about 1201.0 Mbps, and estimated real throughput is about 912.7 Mbps (1201.0 times 0.76).
fieldNotes: The efficiency factors (70% to 80%) are flat per-standard estimates of overhead, not measured for your environment. Real throughput depends on contention, retries, frame aggregation, and airtime sharing.
The PHY rate is the theoretical peak for a single, clean link. Treat the real-throughput number as an optimistic ceiling.
throughput-calc.source: Standard Wi-Fi PHY-rate math with per-standard efficiency estimates, computed from your selections on your device.

downtilt.name: Antenna Downtilt
downtilt.purpose: Tells you how far to tilt an antenna downward so the center of its beam lands on the ground where your users are.
downtilt.whyHere: When you mount a sector or directional antenna up high, you need a tilt angle that aims the main beam at the people below instead of over their heads.
howToUse: Enter the antenna's height above the ground and pick its unit (ft or m).
Enter how far out you want to cover and pick its unit (km, ft, or m).
Read the downtilt angle in degrees.
downtilt.algorithm: It is straight geometry. Picture a right triangle: the antenna height is the vertical side and the coverage distance is the horizontal side. The downtilt angle is the angle whose tangent equals height divided by distance. Everything is converted to meters first (feet times 0.3048, kilometers times 1000).
downtilt.example: An antenna 30 m up aimed at coverage 200 m away needs about 8.53 degrees of downtilt.
fieldNotes: This aims the center of the beam at your target distance. It does not account for how wide the beam is up and down, so use Downtilt Coverage to see the near and far edges.
It is pure geometry. It does not model the antenna's beam shape or any slope in the ground.
downtilt.source: Works out the tilt angle from simple right-triangle geometry using the height and distance you enter.

downtilt-coverage.name: Downtilt Coverage
downtilt-coverage.purpose: Shows where a tilted antenna's beam actually lands on the ground: the near edge, the far edge, and how deep the covered strip is, based on height, tilt, and how tall the beam is.
downtilt-coverage.whyHere: This is the companion to the Downtilt tool. It shows the footprint the beam really covers, so you can spot coverage gaps or signal that overshoots your area.
howToUse: Enter the antenna height above the ground and pick its unit (ft or m).
Enter the downtilt angle in degrees.
Enter the antenna's vertical beamwidth in degrees (how tall the beam is).
Read the near edge, far edge, and coverage depth.

inputs.name: Antenna height (AGL)
inputs.range: must be greater than 0

inputs.name: Vertical beamwidth
inputs.range: must be between 0 and 180 degrees

downtilt-coverage.algorithm: The beam has a top edge and a bottom edge, set by the tilt angle plus or minus half the beamwidth. Each edge, together with the antenna height, forms a right triangle, so the distance to that edge is the height divided by the tangent of the edge's angle below horizontal. The near edge comes from the steeper (lower) beam edge and the far edge from the shallower (upper) one; the depth is the far edge minus the near edge. If the upper beam edge reaches or rises above the horizon, the far edge stretches out with no defined limit, so the tool reports that the beam is above the horizon instead of a distance. It leaves the results blank if the height is not positive or the beamwidth is outside 0 to 180 degrees.
downtilt-coverage.example: At 30 m height, 10 degrees of tilt, and an 8-degree beamwidth: the near edge falls about 120.3 m out, the far edge about 285.4 m out, for a covered strip about 165.1 m deep.
fieldNotes: When the tilt is shallow compared to the beamwidth (say 6 degrees of tilt with a 15-degree beam), the top of the beam clears the horizon and the far edge has no limit. The tool flags this rather than showing a nonsense negative distance.
The edges are the half-power (or stated) beamwidth points. Real coverage fades gradually beyond them rather than stopping cleanly.
downtilt-coverage.source: Uses right-triangle geometry on the top and bottom edges of the beam, worked out from the height, tilt, and beamwidth you enter.

earth-curvature.name: Earth Curvature
earth-curvature.purpose: Tells you the earth bulge, the height of the earth's curvature at the middle of a path, for a given path length and atmospheric K-factor.
earth-curvature.whyHere: On long microwave links the earth's curve, bent a little by the atmosphere, eats into your Fresnel clearance. This shows how much extra antenna height the curvature costs you.
howToUse: Enter the path length and pick its unit (km or mi).
Pick the K-factor.
Read the bulge in both meters and feet.

inputs.name: Path length
inputs.range: miles are converted to kilometers

inputs.name: K-factor
inputs.range: 4/3 standard atmosphere (1.333, default), 1.0 geometric (no bending), 2/3 worst case (0.667), or 2.0 superrefraction

earth-curvature.algorithm: The bulge at the midpoint grows with the square of the path length and shrinks with a larger effective earth radius. In words: take the path length in kilometers, square it, multiply by 1000, then divide by 8 times the earth's mean radius (6371 km) times the K-factor. That gives the bulge in meters; multiply by 3.28084 to get feet. A smaller K-factor means a tighter effective curve and a bigger bulge.
earth-curvature.example: A 20 km path with K = 1.333 gives a bulge of about 5.89 m at the midpoint.
fieldNotes: K = 4/3 assumes a standard atmosphere. K = 2/3 is the conservative worst case for links that have to stay up, and it produces more bulge.
The bulge is the maximum, at the midpoint. Add it to the Fresnel clearance you need when sizing tower heights.
The K-factor shifts with weather and geography, so treat this as a planning number, not a guarantee.
earth-curvature.source: Calculates the midpoint bulge from the path length and K-factor using the standard earth-curvature relationship.

rf-attenuation.name: RF Attenuation
rf-attenuation.purpose: Estimates the total signal loss through building materials by adding up the loss from each layer for the Wi-Fi band you choose.
rf-attenuation.whyHere: For indoor coverage planning. Count the walls, floors, and obstructions between the access point and the client and get a quick total loss in dB to add to your link budget.
howToUse: Pick the band (2.4, 5, or 6 GHz).
Enter how many of each material the signal passes through.
Read the total attenuation in dB.

inputs.name: Band
inputs.range: 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, or 6 GHz

inputs.name: Per-material quantities
inputs.range: only counts greater than 0 add to the total

rf-attenuation.algorithm: Each material has a typical loss per layer that varies by band. Loss climbs with frequency, so a layer costs more at 6 GHz than at 2.4 GHz. For example, drywall runs about 3, 4, and 5 dB at 2.4, 5, and 6 GHz; poured concrete about 13, 16, and 19 dB; a metal door about 20, 26, and 30 dB; foil insulation about 25, 30, and 35 dB. The tool multiplies each material's per-layer loss for your chosen band by how many you entered, then adds them all up.
rf-attenuation.example: At 5 GHz, two sheets of drywall (4 dB each) plus one concrete block (13 dB) come to 21 dB total.
fieldNotes: These are typical figures, not measurements of your building. Real walls vary a lot with construction, moisture, and rebar.
Metal, foil and vapor barriers, and low-E glass are near-total blockers and will dominate the total.
Use this for a first-pass estimate, then confirm with a survey.
rf-attenuation.source: Adds up published typical per-material loss figures for the band you pick and the quantities you enter.

poe-budget.name: PoE Budget
poe-budget.purpose: Checks a PoE switch's total power budget against the power draw of everything plugged into it, and gives you an over, caution, or OK verdict.
poe-budget.whyHere: Before you hang a batch of access points (plus cameras and phones) off a switch, make sure the switch can power them all without blowing past its PoE budget.
howToUse: Enter the switch's PoE budget in watts.
For up to six device rows, enter the watts per device and how many (quantity defaults to 1).
Read the total draw, remaining budget, percent used, and the verdict.

inputs.name: Switch PoE budget
inputs.range: must be greater than 0, or you get no result

inputs.name: Device rows (up to 6)
inputs.unit: watts per device and a quantity
inputs.range: leave a field blank and it counts as 0; quantity defaults to 1

poe-budget.algorithm: For each row it multiplies the watts per device by the quantity, then adds the rows together for the total draw. The remaining budget is the switch budget minus that total, and the percent used is the total over the budget (shown capped at 100 percent). The verdict follows a simple order: if you are over budget it says OVER; otherwise if you are past 80 percent it says CAUTION; otherwise OK.
poe-budget.example: A 370 W budget with six access points at 25.5 W each comes to 153 W drawn, 217 W remaining, 41 percent used, so OK.
fieldNotes: Use each device's worst-case (maximum) draw, not idle, and mind the PoE class.

Budget in PSE watts, not PD watts. PSE is what the switch port must supply; PD is what survives the cable and reaches the device. Twelve Class-4 APs are 306 W of PD but 360 W of PSE: against a 370 W switch that is the difference between comfortable and nearly exhausted. The standards card on this screen shows both columns.
802.3bt Type 4 supplies 90 W (IEEE 802.3-2022, Table 145-11, Class 8 P_Class). The 99.9 W figure sometimes quoted is the PSE power rating band (P_Type, Table 145-16), which is a different quantity.
The percent shown stops at 100 for display, but the OVER verdict triggers on the real negative remaining, so an over-budget case is never hidden.
This checks the switch's total budget only. It does not model per-port limits or power lost over long cable runs.
poe-budget.source: Adds up the draw of every device row and compares it against the switch budget you enter.

metric-conversion.name: Metric Conversion
metric-conversion.purpose: Converts a length between meters, kilometers, miles, feet, centimeters, inches, and nautical miles.
metric-conversion.whyHere: Field work mixes metric and imperial constantly: datasheets in meters, tape measures in feet, link distances in miles. A quick converter saves you from arithmetic slips.
howToUse: Enter a value and pick the unit it is in.
Read it converted into every other unit at once.

inputs.name: Value and source unit
inputs.unit: one of m, km, mi, ft, cm, in, nmi

metric-conversion.algorithm: It converts by way of meters. Each unit has an exact meters-per-unit value: 1 meter, 1000 per kilometer, 1609.344 per mile, 0.3048 per foot, 0.01 per centimeter, 0.0254 per inch, and 1852 per nautical mile. To convert, it turns your value into meters, then divides into the unit you want. Each unit is shown to a sensible number of decimals for its scale.
metric-conversion.example: 1 mile is 1609.344 m, which is 1.609344 km, 5280 ft, and 0.868976 nautical miles.
fieldNotes: It uses the international mile (1609.344 m) and international foot (0.3048 m), not the US survey foot.
The math is exact; the rounding you see is for display only.
metric-conversion.source: Converts every length through meters using exact per-unit conversion factors.

dist-bearing.name: Distance and Bearing
dist-bearing.purpose: Gives you the straight-line-over-the-globe distance between two points, plus the compass bearing to aim from each end to the other.
dist-bearing.whyHere: For aiming point-to-point antennas. You need the distance (for free-space path loss) and the compass bearing (to point the dish) between two sites.
howToUse: Enter the latitude and longitude for point 1 and point 2 in decimal degrees.
Read the distance in km, the forward bearing, and the reverse bearing.
dist-bearing.algorithm: It treats the earth as a sphere with a mean radius of 6371 km and finds the great-circle distance, the shortest path across the curved surface, using the standard haversine method. The forward bearing is the compass heading you would start out on to travel that path from point 1 to point 2; the reverse bearing is simply that heading plus 180 degrees, wrapped to a 0 to 360 range.
dist-bearing.example: San Francisco to Los Angeles works out to about 559.12 km, a forward bearing of 136.5 degrees and a reverse bearing of 316.5 degrees.
fieldNotes: It uses a spherical earth (6371 km mean radius), which is accurate to a fraction of a percent for terrestrial links but not for survey-grade geodesy.
The forward bearing is the starting heading of the great-circle path, and it shifts along the route on long paths.
The reverse bearing is just the forward plus 180 degrees, which is only exact on a sphere.
dist-bearing.source: Uses the haversine great-circle method on a spherical earth to find distance and bearings from the two coordinates.

midpoint.name: Midpoint
midpoint.purpose: Finds the true halfway point along the shortest path over the globe between two coordinates.
midpoint.whyHere: For siting a relay or repeater partway along a long link, or finding the center point of a coverage area between two known locations.
howToUse: Enter the latitude and longitude for point 1 and point 2.
Read the midpoint latitude and longitude.
midpoint.algorithm: It finds the point halfway along the great circle, the shortest curved path across the globe, between your two coordinates, then reports its latitude and longitude wrapped to a normal range. This is a proper spherical calculation, not just averaging the two sets of numbers.
midpoint.example: Halfway between (40, 0) and (40, 90) the point sits well north of the two latitudes, at about (49.88, 45.00), because the shortest path bows toward the pole.
fieldNotes: This is the true great-circle midpoint, not the average of the coordinates. On east-west paths it lands noticeably closer to the pole than a simple average would suggest.
It uses a spherical earth, with the same accuracy caveats as Distance and Bearing.
midpoint.source: Finds the halfway point along the great-circle path between the two coordinates on a spherical earth.

final-point.name: Final Point
final-point.purpose: Given a starting point, a starting bearing, and a distance, it works out the coordinates where you end up.
final-point.whyHere: For projecting where a link points. Given a site, a heading, and a distance, find the coordinates of the far end, for example to check a candidate tower location.
howToUse: Enter the starting latitude and longitude.
Enter the starting bearing in degrees.
Enter the distance and pick its unit (km, mi, or m).
Read the destination latitude and longitude.

inputs.name: Distance
inputs.range: miles and meters are converted to kilometers

final-point.algorithm: Starting from your point, it travels the distance you gave along the great circle in the direction of your starting bearing, treating the earth as a sphere with a 6371 km radius, and reports where that path ends. The longitude is wrapped to a normal range.
final-point.example: From (40, -105) heading due east (90 degrees) for 100 km, you land at about (39.99, -103.83). The latitude dips a hair because a constant starting bearing follows a great circle, not a line of latitude.
fieldNotes: This is a great-circle path on a sphere. The bearing is the starting heading, and the path curves over long distances.
It carries the same spherical-earth accuracy caveats as the other geographic tools.
final-point.source: Projects the endpoint along a great-circle path on a spherical earth from your start point, bearing, and distance.

lat-long.name: Lat / Long Conversion
lat-long.purpose: Converts a coordinate between the three common notations: decimal degrees (DD), degrees and decimal minutes (DDM), and degrees, minutes, and seconds (DMS).
lat-long.whyHere: Different maps and tools write coordinates in different notations. This normalizes between them when you enter a site location.
howToUse: Enter a latitude value (and/or longitude) in decimal degrees.
Read it in DD, DDM, and DMS forms with the correct hemisphere letter.

inputs.name: Latitude
inputs.range: must be within plus or minus 90

inputs.name: Longitude
inputs.range: must be within plus or minus 180

lat-long.algorithm: The sign of your number sets the hemisphere: a positive latitude is North and negative is South; a positive longitude is East and negative is West. To build the other notations, the whole degrees are the part before the decimal, the minutes come from the leftover fraction times 60, and the seconds come from what is left times 60 again. Degrees and decimal minutes just keeps degrees and expresses the rest as minutes with a decimal. Anything out of range or not a real number leaves the output blank.
lat-long.example: 40.7128 degrees latitude shows as DD 40.712800; DMS 40 degrees 42 minutes 46.08 seconds N; and DDM 40 degrees 42.7680 minutes N.
fieldNotes: It checks the ranges (plus or minus 90 for latitude, plus or minus 180 for longitude) and blanks the output if you go outside them.
The sign drives the hemisphere letter, so enter west longitudes and south latitudes as negative numbers.
There is no datum or projection handling. These are plain WGS84-style decimal degrees in, formatted out.
lat-long.source: Splits your decimal-degree coordinate into degrees, minutes, and seconds and formats each notation with the right hemisphere letter.

hex-ascii.name: Hex / ASCII
hex-ascii.purpose: Convert a whole number between decimal, hexadecimal, and binary in real time, and look up any printable ASCII character (codes 32 to 126) in one place.
hex-ascii.whyHere: Handy when you're reading packet captures, MAC and OUI bytes, or hex values in a config and want to flip a number between bases or check an ASCII character without leaving the app.
howToUse: Type a value into any of the three fields (decimal, hexadecimal, or binary) and the other two update instantly.
Scroll the ASCII table to find a printable character and its decimal, hex, and binary codes.

inputs.name: Hexadecimal
inputs.unit: 0-9, a-f, A-F (an optional 0x prefix is ignored)

inputs.name: Binary
inputs.range: Whole numbers of any size, so even very long strings never overflow; leaving a field blank or entering something invalid clears the other two.

hex-ascii.algorithm: It converts a single whole number from whatever base you typed into the other two bases. In the reference table, hex is shown as two uppercase digits and binary as eight bits with leading zeros, and every character is generated from its code so nothing is mistyped.
hex-ascii.example: Enter decimal 65 and you get hex 41 and binary 1000001. In the table, decimal 65 is the letter A, hex 41, binary 01000001.
fieldNotes: Whole numbers only: no negatives, no fractions.
The table covers printable ASCII (codes 32 to 126) only; control characters and extended or Unicode characters are not included.
This converts one number between bases; it does not turn a line of text into its byte sequence.
hex-ascii.source: The result is calculated on your device using standard base conversion.

ipv6-subnet.name: IP Subnet Calculator (IPv6)
ipv6-subnet.purpose: Enter an IPv6 address and prefix length and get back the expanded and compressed forms, the network address, the first and last address in the prefix, the number of hosts, and the address type. It also decodes transition addresses: whether the address you typed carries an IPv4 address inside it, and how a given IPv4 address is written the four ways IPv6 can carry one.
ipv6-subnet.whyHere: IPv6 subnetting and address-type lookups during design and troubleshooting, where doing 128-bit math by hand invites mistakes. The transition section answers a different question: NAT64, 6to4 and IPv4-mapped addresses genuinely turn up in captures and firewall logs, and "what am I looking at" is the moment they cause.
howToUse: Enter an IPv6 address (default 2001:db8::1).
Enter the prefix length (default 32). A link-local address pasted straight off ifconfig or ip -6 addr works as-is, zone index and all: fe80::1%en0 is accepted, and the zone comes back on its own row.
Read the expanded form, compressed form, network and prefix, first and last address, host count, and address type.
Read the transition section at the bottom. It decodes the same address you typed above and names the format, the embedded IPv4, and what that IPv4 actually is.
The IPv4 field in that section runs the other direction: type an IPv4 address and read it as IPv4-mapped, NAT64, a 6to4 prefix, and the deprecated IPv4-compatible form.
Read the solicited-node multicast address and the reverse DNS name at the bottom. Both are derived from the address you already typed.

inputs.name: IPv6 address
inputs.range: only one :: shortcut allowed; an invalid format shows an inline error

inputs.name: Prefix
inputs.range: 0 to 128 (anything outside that shows an error)

inputs.name: Zone index (optional, on the address)
inputs.unit: interface name or ifindex after a %
inputs.range: fe80::1%en0, fe80::1%12, or the %25en0 spelling used inside a URL

inputs.name: IPv4 address (transition section)
inputs.range: four octets, each 0 to 255

ipv6-subnet.algorithm: It expands the address to its full form, works out which bits the prefix fixes, and from that gives you the network address plus the first and last address in the block. It also shows the shortest valid compressed form by collapsing the longest run of zero groups. Host count is 2 raised to the number of host bits (128 minus the prefix); anything above 2 to the 63rd is reported as "More than 2^63" rather than a full number. The address type is identified by matching the address against the well-known IPv6 ranges (unspecified, loopback, link-local, unique-local, multicast, 6to4, IPv4-mapped, documentation, or global unicast). Transition decoding matches the address against five known formats and reports the first that fits: IPv4-mapped (::ffff:0:0/96, RFC 4291), the NAT64 well-known prefix (64:ff9b::/96, RFC 6052), 6to4 (2002::/16, RFC 3056, where the 32 bits after 2002 are the site endpoint), Teredo (2001:0::/32, RFC 4380, where the client address and port are stored with every bit inverted and are shown flipped back), and the deprecated IPv4-compatible form (::/96, RFC 4291), which excludes :: and ::1 because those are not IPv4 at all. Writing an IPv4 address as IPv6 is the same work in reverse.
ipv6-subnet.example: 2001:db8::1 with a /64 gives expanded form 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001, compressed form 2001:db8::1, network 2001:db8::/64, 64 host bits (so the host count shows "More than 2^63"), and type Documentation (2001:db8::/32).
fieldNotes: Host counts above 2 to the 63rd are shown as "More than 2^63" rather than a full number.
The "first address" is the network address itself. IPv6 has no broadcast address and does not reserve the all-zeros host the way IPv4 does.
Address-type detection covers the common well-known ranges, not every reserved block.
This tool lives under Networking Tools in the current menu.
An address literal with a dotted IPv4 tail, such as ::ffff:192.168.1.1, is accepted. That form is legal IPv6 and is how a mapped or NAT64 address is written in a log.

NAT64 is decoded against the well-known 64:ff9b::/96 prefix only. A network can run its own NAT64 prefix at /32, /40, /48, /56 or /64, and the IPv4 bits sit at a different offset in each. That prefix length is not carried in the address, so decoding one without being told which prefix is in use would be guessing. The screen says so rather than guessing.
Teredo stores the client address and port with every bit inverted. Read raw, they look like nonsense. The screen flips them back and says it did.
An address with no IPv4 inside is reported as having none. The screen never invents an embedded address to fill the row.
IPv4-compatible (::a.b.c.d) is deprecated. It is decoded so you can recognize one in an old configuration, and labeled so you do not build on it.
The 6to4 output is a PREFIX for a whole site (a /48), not a host address.

A zone index (the %en0 on fe80::1%en0) names the local interface the scope belongs to, so it sits outside the 128 bits and is set aside before the math runs. The Zone row shows it back, because a character you typed that vanishes with no acknowledgement looks like an input the tool failed to read. A half-typed zone such as fe80::1% is reported as an invalid address.

The solicited-node multicast address (RFC 4291 section 2.7.1) is FF02::1:FF plus the low-order 24 bits of the address. IPv6 neighbor discovery sends its solicitation to that group rather than to all nodes, which is how it avoids waking every device on the link the way ARP broadcast does. When address resolution is failing, whether the node joined the right group is the question, and working the address out by hand is where it goes wrong.
Only the low 24 bits are used, so two addresses in completely different prefixes can share a solicited-node group. It is a useful filter, not a unique identifier.

The reverse DNS name (RFC 3596 section 2.5) is all 32 nibbles in reverse order with the ip6.arpa suffix. No trailing dot is shown, because this is a screen rather than a zone file; add one if you are pasting it somewhere that needs a fully qualified name.
ipv6-subnet.source: The result is calculated on your device.

subnet-planner.name: Subnet Planner (VLSM)
subnet-planner.purpose: Two jobs on IPv4 blocks that span more than one network. Split carves a parent block into right-sized subnets from a list of host counts. Summarize takes a list of networks and gives the single block that covers them all, plus the smallest set of blocks that covers them exactly.
subnet-planner.whyHere: "Here is your /22 for the site, now give me a VLAN for staff, one for guests, one for the IoT gear and a point-to-point link" is a design question the single-subnet calculator cannot answer, because it works on one network at a time. Summarize is the same math in reverse, for when you are writing a route, an ACL, or a firewall rule and want one line instead of nine.
howToUse: Pick Split or Summarize at the top.
Split: type the block you are carving, for example 10.20.0.0/22, then list the subnets you need, one per line, as a name and a host count ("Staff 500") or just a count ("500").
Summarize: paste your networks, one per line. A prefix, a dotted mask, or a bare address all work.
Everything recalculates as you type. Use Copy to take the whole plan with you.

inputs.name: Block to carve up (Split)
inputs.range: any IPv4 block, /0 to /32

inputs.name: Subnets you need (Split)
inputs.unit: one per line, name then host count
inputs.range: 1 host or more per line

inputs.name: Networks to summarize
inputs.range: any IPv4 networks, in any order

subnet-planner.algorithm: Split sorts your subnets largest first, then places each one at the next free address. Because every block size is a power of two and the list runs from largest to smallest, each block lands on its own boundary with no wasted space in between. That ordering is what makes VLSM efficient, and it is why the output is not in the order you typed. Host counts use the classic reservation, so a subnet for 500 hosts gets a /23 (510 usable) and one for 2 hosts gets a /30. Whatever is left over is reported as the largest whole blocks that fit it. Summarize merges your networks into continuous ranges (so an overlap counts once and two touching networks become one), then reports the smallest single block containing all of them and, separately, the smallest set of blocks that covers them exactly.
subnet-planner.example: Split 10.20.0.0/22 for Staff 500, Guest 200, IoT 100 and a 2-host point-to-point link and you get 10.20.0.0/23, 10.20.2.0/24, 10.20.3.0/25 and 10.20.3.128/30, with 124 addresses still free in five blocks. Summarize 10.0.0.0/24 and 10.0.3.0/24 and the covering supernet is 10.0.0.0/22, which also claims 512 addresses that are not in your list: 10.0.1.0/24 and 10.0.2.0/24.
fieldNotes: The Extra count in Summarize is the number that matters. A covering supernet almost always includes addresses you did not ask for, and advertising it pulls in traffic for networks you may not own. The screen names those gaps as blocks so you can see exactly what you would be claiming.
A subnet that does not fit is named and told why, and the ones that do fit are still placed. A plan where the last VLAN overflowed is more useful than no plan at all.

A request for 2 hosts gets a /30 here, because that is what works everywhere. If your gear supports RFC 3021 a /31 carries the same two hosts on a point-to-point link in half the space, and the screen says so.
A request for 1 host gets a /32. That is a single host route with no room for a gateway, so ask for 2 if you meant a device and its router.
A bad line is skipped by line number, not by rejecting the whole paste. Paste a messy list and fix the lines it names.
If a network is typed with host bits set, for example 10.0.0.37/24, it is read as 10.0.0.0/24 and the screen tells you it did that rather than quietly answering a different question.
Fully offline: this is integer arithmetic on the device, and it works on every platform including the web build.
CATALOG NOTE: manual category is Networking Tools; catalog id is subnet-planner with route /tools/subnet-planner.
subnet-planner.source: Calculated on the device; nothing is sent anywhere.

non-wifi-channels.name: Non-Wi-Fi Wireless Channels
non-wifi-channels.purpose: Look up the channel and frequency plans of the common non-Wi-Fi radios that share or sit next to the bands a Wi-Fi pro works in: LoRaWAN, IEEE 802.15.4, Bluetooth Classic, Bluetooth LE, and Zigbee.
non-wifi-channels.whyHere: For when you're chasing interference or co-existence in the 2.4 GHz band, or sizing a sub-GHz IoT deployment, and need to know where these radios actually sit.
howToUse: Each technology has its own section.
LoRaWAN plans marked with a "verify" chip are version-dependent or thinly sourced, so confirm them before you rely on them.

Bluetooth LE rows are listed by actual frequency (not by index) so you can see how the 3 advertising channels are spaced out; an "Advertising" chip marks channels 37, 38, and 39 (2402, 2426, and 2480 MHz).
Zigbee's "common picks" (11, 15, 20, 25, 26) are a convention, not a requirement.
fieldNotes: What it shows: one card per technology. LoRaWAN: regional plan (EU868, US915, AU915, AS923, IN865, KR920, CN470, CN779, RU864), frequency range in MHz, and a channel-plan description. IEEE 802.15.4: band (868 MHz / 915 MHz / 2.4 GHz), channel-number range, spacing, center summary, and region. Bluetooth Classic (BR/EDR): 79 channels, 1 MHz spacing, 2402 to 2480 MHz, about 1600 hops per second, global. Bluetooth LE: all 40 channels in frequency order with index, frequency in MHz, and kind (Advertising or Data). Zigbee: 2.4 GHz channels 11 to 26, sub-GHz bands, and common 2.4 GHz channel picks.
Bluetooth, Bluetooth LE, and 802.15.4 use globally fixed channel grids. LoRaWAN frequency plans are set entirely by region; there is no single global LoRaWAN channel map.

Plans marked "verify" (CN470 is version-dependent, CN779 is deprecated or limited, RU864 is thinly sourced) should be confirmed against the LoRa Alliance RP002 regional parameters and your local regulator.
The Bluetooth LE table lists each channel's true frequency directly rather than using the simple "2402 + 2 x index" formula, which is a common shortcut that produces the wrong frequencies.
The 868 and 915 MHz bands of 802.15.4 are region-restricted; channels 11 to 26 in 2.4 GHz are global.

Data source: cross-checked against the LoRa Alliance RP002, IEEE 802.15.4, the Bluetooth SIG Core Spec, and the CSA/Zigbee spec. The 802.15.4 center frequencies were verified against the standard's formula (channel 0 = 868.3 MHz; channels 1 to 10 = 906 + 2 x (k-1); channels 11 to 26 = 2405 + 5 x (k-11)).
non-wifi-channels.source: Values are cross-checked against the published standards.

channel-map.name: Channel Map
channel-map.purpose: A visual channel-bonding map showing, per band, how 20/40/80/160/320 MHz channels bond together, which primary (center) channel labels each bonded block, and which blocks require DFS.
channel-map.whyHere: For planning channel widths and bonding, so you can see at a glance which 20 MHz primaries fold into a given 80 or 160 MHz channel, and which bonds pull in a DFS sub-channel.
howToUse: Scroll the 5 and 6 GHz maps sideways. Each block's number is its primary (center) channel.

Color and chip legend: No DFS (neutral, just a fact not a warning), DFS (amber, radar detection required), Mixed / DFS (red, a 160 MHz bond that spans both DFS and non-DFS sub-bands, where any DFS sub-channel subjects the whole bond to DFS), and PSC (lime, the 6 GHz preferred scanning channels).
The 6 GHz 320 MHz row shows channel 31 as the primary block and channel 63 as a dashed alternative; they overlap, so only one is used at a time.
fieldNotes: What it shows: a three-way band toggle. 2.4 GHz: the 11 US channels as 20 MHz blocks, with 1, 6, and 11 emphasized (non-overlapping) and the rest faint. 5 GHz: rows for 20/40/80/160 MHz bonded widths, each block labeled with its primary/center channel and tinted by DFS class. 6 GHz: rows for 20/40/80/160/320 MHz across the full US band (channels 1 to 233, UNII-5 through UNII-8), with PSC channels marked.
US by default. The map covers the full US 6 GHz band, channels 1 to 233 (UNII-5 through UNII-8). 6 GHz needs no DFS, and no AFC for low-power indoor (LPI) use.

Data source: US (FCC). 5 GHz DFS: No DFS = UNII-1 (36 to 48), UNII-3 (149 to 165), and UNII-4 (169 to 177); DFS = UNII-2A and 2C. UNII-4 (169/173/177) is included per Keith's RF Channel Allocations chart.
channel-map.source: Values come from the US (FCC) channel plan.

spectrum.name: Spectrum Reference
spectrum.purpose: A per-band fact sheet for the three Wi-Fi bands: total usable spectrum, supported standards, channel counts, non-overlapping counts, channel widths, DFS/radar requirements, common co-existing interferers, and key deployment notes.
spectrum.whyHere: The one-screen "tell me everything about this band" reference: what lives in it, what interferes with it, and what the power and DFS rules are.
howToUse: Pick a band (2.4, 5, or 6 GHz) and read the eight facts top to bottom.
The colored range badge is just a visual pairing with the band label (2.4 GHz amber for congested, 5 GHz blue, 6 GHz green).
The "Co-existence" row names the band's common interferers or managed incumbents.
fieldNotes: What it shows: each band gets a range badge plus eight facts: Total spectrum, Standards, Channels (US), Non-overlapping, Channel widths, DFS / Radar, Co-existence, and Key notes.
US by default; every band carries the footnote "US (FCC) regulatory domain. Verify local rules before deployment."

Includes useful specifics: UNII-1 is indoor-only in some regions; UNII-2A/2C DFS means a 60-second channel availability check before first use (10 minutes for 5600 to 5650 MHz in the EU), and on radar the AP leaves within 10 seconds and stays off for 30 minutes; 6 GHz has four US power modes, namely Standard Power (up to 36 dBm EIRP, AFC required indoors and outdoors), LPI (up to 30 dBm, no AFC), VLP (up to 14 dBm EIRP, no AFC, mobile), and Geofenced Variable Power (up to 24 dBm EIRP, U-NII-5 and U-NII-7 only); and WPA3 is mandatory on 6 GHz.
Data source: US (FCC) regulatory domain. Values: 2.4 GHz = 83.5 MHz (US); 5 GHz = about 580 MHz usable (UNII-1/2A/2C/3); 6 GHz = 1200 MHz (5925 to 7125 MHz).
spectrum.source: Values come from the US (FCC) regulatory domain.

capacity-planner.name: Capacity Planner
capacity-planner.purpose: An informational statement, not a calculator: it explains why Wi-Fi capacity planning cannot honestly be reduced to a few input boxes and a confident AP count.
capacity-planner.whyHere: The tool that used to live here returned an AP-count from a single formula. That math was removed because one formula cannot honor the variables that actually drive capacity. This screen replaces the false precision with an honest explanation and points you to a real plan.
howToUse: There is nothing to enter. Read the statement: capacity planning is a design problem, not a calculation.
For a plan you can trust, bring in a Wi-Fi professional experienced in your kind of environment; a real plan comes from measuring and modeling your specific space and usage.
fieldNotes: This is a read-only disclaimer screen: no inputs, no math, no copyable result. The tile, the /tools/capacity-planner route, and the "Capacity Planner" title are kept so the tile still resolves where users expect.

Real Wi-Fi capacity depends on the applications in use and their airtime cost, client device capabilities and roaming, AP and antenna selection, channel reuse and co-channel interference, band steering, airtime fairness, QoS, and how people move through the space. Change any one and the answer changes.
A confidently wrong number is worse than no number, which is why the calculator was removed rather than kept with a caveat.
capacity-planner.source: Verbatim from Keith's approved disclaimer copy; no external data source (the screen performs no calculation).

mcs-index.name: MCS Index
mcs-index.purpose: Look up the modulation, coding rate, and PHY data rate for any 802.11 MCS index across channel widths, for 802.11n (HT), 802.11ac (VHT), 802.11ax (HE), and 802.11be (EHT / Wi-Fi 7), scaled by the number of spatial streams.
mcs-index.whyHere: For when you see an MCS index in a capture or client stats and want to know the modulation and coding behind it and the rate it should deliver at a given width and stream count.
howToUse: Choose the standard (n, ac, ax, or be) and the stream count; the rates update. 802.11n offers 1 to 4 streams (MCS 0-31 is eight indices across four streams - the standard defines no more); ac, ax, and be offer 1 to 8.
MCS 0 (BPSK 1/2) is the most robust and slowest; higher MCS indices use denser modulation (up to 1024-QAM for ax and 4096-QAM for be) for higher rates but need a better signal.
Cells shown as "N/A" are genuinely invalid combinations, not zero and not made up. Some are invalid only at certain stream counts.
Above 4 spatial streams no rate is shown at all. That is not an "N/A" - it is a gap in the published source. The screen says so explicitly rather than computing a number it cannot source.
fieldNotes: What it shows: two selectors, the 802.11 standard (n, ac, ax, or be) and the number of spatial streams (1 to 8). Columns per standard: 802.11n = 20 LGI, 20 SGI, 40 LGI, 40 SGI; 802.11ac = 20/40/80/160 SGI; 802.11ax = 20/40/80/160 MHz; 802.11be = 20/40/80/160/320 MHz (both at an 800 ns guard interval).

802.11ac MCS 9 at 20 MHz is valid ONLY at 3 spatial streams - it is N/A at 1, 2 and 4. MCS 9 at 40 MHz is valid at every stream count. Two further stream-dependent exclusions: MCS 6 at 80 MHz and MCS 9 at 160 MHz are both invalid at 3 streams.

The source tables publish 1 to 4 spatial streams. Above 4 the app shows no rate, because the per-stream exclusions up there are unpublished and are not derivable from the ones below - a rule that reproduces MCS 9 at 20 MHz exactly still gets MCS 6 at 80 MHz and MCS 9 at 160 MHz wrong. A known gap beats an invented number.

Guard-interval definitions: 802.11n LGI = 800 ns and SGI = 400 ns; 802.11ac uses SGI. 802.11ax and 802.11be define 0.8, 1.6, and 3.2 microsecond guard intervals only - there is no 400 ns short GI above 802.11ac.
The notes card points out that real throughput is typically 50 to 65% of the PHY rate. These rates are PHY-layer maximums, not delivered throughput.

Rates are rounded from the exact PHY value at the chosen stream count, not by multiplying a rounded single-stream figure - so 802.11ac MCS 9 at 160 MHz with 2 streams reads 1733.3, matching the source, not 1733.4.
Data source: Keith Parsons' MCS Index Chart and mcsindex.net (by @VergesFrancois, SemFio Networks), cross-checked against the IEEE 802.11n/ac/ax/be PHY rate tables.
mcs-index.source: Values come from Keith Parsons' MCS Index Chart and mcsindex.net, cross-checked against the IEEE 802.11n/ac/ax/be PHY rate tables.

modulation.name: Modulation
modulation.purpose: Explains what a modulation constellation is on the I/Q plane and why each step up in order (BPSK to QPSK to 16/64/256/1024-QAM) carries more bits per symbol but needs a cleaner link (lower EVM, higher SNR).
modulation.whyHere: The visual companion to the MCS Index table. Reach for it when you want to understand why a higher MCS needs a better signal, or to explain constellations, bits per symbol, and EVM to someone, rather than to look up a spec rate.
howToUse: Read the six constellation diagrams in order; each step doubles the points and adds one bit per symbol while the points pack closer together.
Read the Error Vector Magnitude (EVM) explainer to see what the receiver has to overcome to keep each symbol on the correct side of its decision boundary.
Read the summary card for the order, bits per symbol, and SNR/EVM relationship at a glance.
Tap any diagram to open a full-screen pinch-to-zoom view for the detail-dense planes.
fieldNotes: The SNR and EVM figures on the cards are representative, order-of-magnitude demands, not exact 802.11 MCS thresholds. The relationship, not the precise number, is the point. Use the MCS Index tool for the spec rate and modulation table.

EVM (Error Vector Magnitude) is how far the received symbol lands from the ideal point, expressed as a percentage (or in dB) of the reference amplitude. As the order rises, the decision boundaries shrink, so higher-order QAM needs a lower EVM and a higher SNR.

The diagrams are shown on an always-dark card in both light and dark app themes so they never look inverted. They are marked decorative for screen readers, and the summary card below them carries the same order, bits, SNR and EVM figures as real on-screen text - so nothing in the diagrams is available only to sighted users.
The Copy action exports the same summary table as the screen shows, plus the note that the numbers are representative.

signal-thresholds.name: Signal Thresholds
signal-thresholds.purpose: RSSI and SNR design targets: a recommended quality scale for RSSI, minimum RSSI and SNR by application, and the SNR needed to reach each typical MCS index.
signal-thresholds.whyHere: For validating a survey or troubleshooting a complaint: "is -68 dBm good enough for VoIP?" or "what SNR do I need to hold MCS 7?"
howToUse: RSSI bands carry a colored verdict dot plus the quality word (green = good, amber = marginal/Fair, red = bad/Poor); the word always carries the meaning, never the color alone.
In the application table, read across to the minimum RSSI and minimum SNR your use case needs.
The SNR-to-MCS table tells you the SNR floor to sustain a given rate.
fieldNotes: What it shows: three blocks. RSSI quality scale: Excellent (> -60 dBm) / Good (-60 to -67) / Fair (-67 to -72) / Poor (-73 or weaker). Minimum signal by application: VoIP/real-time, HD video, general browsing, email/basic data, IoT/low-rate, and location/RTLS, each with a minimum RSSI, minimum SNR, and a note. SNR to MCS (80 MHz, 1 spatial stream): the SNR floor for each MCS index (MCS 0 at 5 dB up to MCS 11 at 35 dB) with an indicative rate.
These are recommended design targets, not an industry standard. IEEE 802.11 does not define "good" or "poor" signal levels, and appropriate thresholds vary by site and by customer requirement.
Values vary by client hardware, environment, and AP vendor; treat them as field-planning guidelines, not guarantees.
The SNR-to-MCS rates are indicative (80 MHz, single stream); the MCS 10 and 11 rates are noted as 802.11ax.
signal-thresholds.source: Recommended design targets. Not an industry standard: IEEE 802.11 does not define signal-quality levels.

80211-standards.name: 802.11 Standards
80211-standards.purpose: A PHY-layer comparison of every major 802.11 amendment, from the original 802.11 (1997) through Wi-Fi 7, with year, bands, maximum PHY rate, MIMO, channel widths, and modulation.
80211-standards.whyHere: For settling "which generation does what": the bands it reaches, its maximum rate, its MIMO ceiling, and its modulation.
howToUse: Scan by generation badge (Wi-Fi 4 through Wi-Fi 7).
The band filter answers "which generations reach 6 GHz" (Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7).
Amendments before Wi-Fi 4 (802.11, 802.11b, 802.11a, 802.11g) show a dash for generation, since official Wi-Fi Alliance naming begins at Wi-Fi 4.
fieldNotes: What it shows: one card per amendment with the IEEE designation, a Wi-Fi generation badge, year, and rows for Bands (GHz), Max PHY rate, MIMO, Channel width (MHz), and Modulation. An optional band filter (All / 2.4 / 5 / 6 GHz) narrows the list.

Two footnotes: (1) "Official Wi-Fi Alliance generation naming begins at Wi-Fi 4 (802.11n); earlier amendments are shown by their 802.11 names only"; (2) "Wi-Fi 7 certification began 2024; IEEE 802.11be was published 2025."
The max PHY rate is the theoretical aggregate ceiling; real-world throughput is typically 50 to 60% of it.

Data source: the IEEE 802.11 amendments. Key rows: 802.11ac = Wi-Fi 5 (2013, 6.9 Gbps); 802.11ax = Wi-Fi 6 (2019) and Wi-Fi 6E (2020, adds 6 GHz); 802.11be = Wi-Fi 7 (2024, 23.1 Gbps with MLO, 4K-QAM, up to 320 MHz).
80211-standards.source: Values come from the IEEE 802.11 amendments.

roaming.name: Roaming Parameters
roaming.purpose: The 802.11k/r/v fast-roaming protocols (what each does and what it needs) plus RSSI, SNR, and latency design thresholds for enterprise roaming.
roaming.whyHere: For designing or troubleshooting roaming for VoIP and unified comms, confirming the role of each protocol and the signal-overlap targets that make handoffs work.
howToUse: Each protocol heading shows the designation (lime) and the full name.

In the thresholds table, the scenario word is color-tinted with a dot: green = good (the two design targets), amber = marginal (the overlap zone), red = bad (the sticky-client trigger and the unusable level).
Design rules carry the actionable target (for example, "at least 2 APs at -67 dBm everywhere" or "a second AP at -72 dBm or better across the overlap zone").
fieldNotes: What it shows: a Protocols block covering 802.11r (Fast BSS Transition), 802.11k (Neighbor Report), and 802.11v (BSS Transition Management), each with what it does, its deployment requirements, and a field note. A Thresholds block covers five scenarios (VoIP/UC design target, standard data design target, roaming overlap zone, sticky-client trigger, and unusable), each with a minimum RSSI, minimum SNR, roam latency, design rule, and a status verdict.
The intro notes that targets vary by client hardware and AP vendor: these are design guidelines, not guarantees.

Field notes flag real client behavior: some older clients have 802.11r compatibility issues; Android and iOS generally honor 802.11v, but some Windows drivers ignore BSS Transition Management entirely.
Data source: IEEE 802.11k/r/v. This reference covers exactly these three protocols; OKC is not included.
roaming.source: Values come from the IEEE 802.11k/r/v standards.

frame-exchange.name: Association Sequence
frame-exchange.purpose: Step-by-step maps of how a device joins Wi-Fi and roams between access points, showing the order and direction of every message that passes between the device, the access point, the RADIUS server, and the DHCP server.
frame-exchange.whyHere: When you are reading a capture or explaining how a join happens, this confirms which message should come next and who sends it to whom.
howToUse: Pick a scenario (Open / WPA2-PSK, WPA3-SAE, OWE / Enhanced Open, Passpoint / Hotspot 2.0, WPA2-Enterprise (802.1X/EAP), 802.11r Roam) and read the phases from top to bottom.
Each step is tagged with a plain type: MGMT (management), EAP (EAP / EAPOL key), WIRED (RADIUS/DHCP traveling over the wired network), or DHCP.
The legend at the bottom spells out each tag. The tag is shown as text, so you never have to rely on color to read it.
fieldNotes: What it shows: a picker with six scenarios. Each one is split into named phases (for example Probe & Auth, Association, 4-Way Handshake, EAP Authentication, DHCP), and each step lists a step number, a direction, the message name, a type tag, and a short note.

OWE / Enhanced Open: Open System authentication happens first, then the association exchange carries each side's public key inside a Diffie-Hellman element (the request carries the device's key, the response carries the access point's key). A shared secret is derived from those keys, and a normal 4-Way Handshake follows. No passphrase is used.

Passpoint / Hotspot 2.0: the distinctive part is a query the device makes before it joins, asking which networks an access point can authenticate for. Once that is answered, an ordinary 802.1X/EAP exchange plus 4-Way Handshake runs.

eduroam and OpenRoaming are not separate diagrams. They are behind-the-scenes agreements between networks that run over an exchange already shown here. eduroam is 802.1X/EAP with your home network authenticating you by realm (noted on the WPA2-Enterprise scenario); OpenRoaming is a Passpoint plus EAP arrangement triggered by a matching network identifier (noted on the Passpoint scenario). The 802.11r scenario also notes the roam variant that hands off through the wired network alongside the over-the-air version.

These are representative sequences, not an exhaustive list. Optional and passive-scan paths, and the back-and-forth inside EAP methods, are summarized (for example the WPA3 DHCP phase is shown as one combined line, identical to the WPA2 flow).

Built from IEEE 802.11 join and handshake behavior, cross-checked against published research (RFC 8110 for OWE, the 802.11u query mechanism for Passpoint). It reflects the real exchanges: the WPA3 commit and confirm steps, the way OWE rides its keys inside association, the pre-join query for Passpoint, 802.1X/EAP carried over RADIUS, and both the over-the-air and through-the-wired-network forms of an 802.11r fast roam. General reference, not region-specific.
frame-exchange.source: The sequences reproduce the standard 802.11 join and handshake behavior; nothing is invented.

packet-decode.name: Packet Decode
packet-decode.purpose: Byte-level anatomy of the Layer 3 and 4 headers a capture shows beneath 802.11: the field, its bit offset and width, and what it means, for IPv4, IPv6, TCP, UDP, and ICMP. Plus the TCP control bits, the TCP connection states with the three-way handshake and teardown, a common IP-protocol-numbers table, and the ICMP and ICMPv6 type and code tables.
packet-decode.whyHere: When you are reading a packet in Wireshark and need to confirm which field sits at which offset, what a TCP flag combination means, or what an ICMP type and code is telling you, without leaving the app or going online.
howToUse: Scroll to the header you are decoding. Each header table lists the field, its bit offset (counted from bit 0), its bit length, and a plain-language meaning.
The IPv4 Type-of-Service octet is shown the modern way: DSCP (6 bits) plus ECN (2 bits). The legacy precedence reading is noted beneath.
For TCP, the flags table lists the eight control bits (CWR, ECE, URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN, FIN); the reserved bit that some tools still label NS is shown separately with its history.
The IPv4 Protocol and IPv6 Next Header fields point at the IP-protocol-numbers table. For TCP and UDP port numbers, use the Well-Known Ports reference instead.
Use the copy button in the toolbar to copy every table as tab-separated text, one section per header.
fieldNotes: Bit offsets count from bit 0 of each header, where bit 0 is the first (most-significant) bit. Bit lengths are exact, never approximate. Variable-length fields (IPv4/TCP Options, padding, payload) are labeled variable.

TCP control bits use RFC 9293's canonical layout: a 4-bit reserved field plus 8 control bits. The bit at position 103 that Wireshark historically labels NS is Reserved in RFC 9293. It was NS (Nonce Sum, RFC 3540), which RFC 8311 made Historic, and RFC 9768 reassigns it as AE (Accurate ECN). It is shown for decoder completeness, flagged historic, not as a current flag.
ICMP type 4 (Source Quench) is kept in the table but marked deprecated per RFC 6633.

Every field offset, width, flag, state, type, and code is transcribed from the RFCs and the IANA registries and cited per table: IPv4 (RFC 791, with DSCP/ECN per RFC 2474 and RFC 3168), IPv6 (RFC 8200), TCP (RFC 9293), UDP (RFC 768), ICMP (RFC 792 plus the IANA ICMP Parameters registry), and ICMPv6 (RFC 4443, with NDP per RFC 4861).
packet-decode.source: Every value is transcribed from the primary RFC or IANA registry, cited per table; nothing is invented or approximated.

reason-codes.name: 802.11 Reason Codes
reason-codes.purpose: The 802.11 reason codes (why a device was kicked off) and status codes (why a join succeeded or failed) that show up in captures, with a search box to find one fast.
reason-codes.whyHere: When a capture shows a deauth with reason code 15, or a join response with status 17, and you need the plain-language meaning right away.
howToUse: Type a number or a keyword (for example "15" or "handshake") to filter. A "no match" card appears if nothing fits.
Reason codes show up in Deauthentication and Disassociation frames; status codes show up in Authentication, Association, and Reassociation Response frames.
In the status group, code 0 means success and is shown in green.
fieldNotes: What it shows: reason codes grouped by theme: Common (1 to 9), Capability/Channel mismatch (10 to 11), Security frame/element errors (13 to 14, 17 to 22, 24), Security handshake failures (15, 16, 23), QoS/load management (34 to 39), and Fast Roaming/802.11r (45 to 48). Plus a separate Association Status Codes group (the most common subset, 0 to 104), where code 0 ("Successful") is highlighted in green.
The status-code list is the most common subset, not the full table.
The codes and their meanings come straight from the standard; nothing is invented.
Source and standard: IEEE 802.11-2020, section 9.4.1.7 (reason codes) and section 9.4.1.9 (status codes), cited in the footnote.
reason-codes.source: The codes and meanings are reproduced directly from the IEEE 802.11 standard.

http-status-codes.name: HTTP Status Codes
http-status-codes.purpose: The full set of HTTP response codes, grouped by class, each with a plain-English meaning. A fast offline lookup when a captive portal, web service, proxy, or API returns a code and you need to know what it means.
http-status-codes.whyHere: When a check comes back 403 or 503, or a captive-portal probe returns 511, and you want the meaning without leaving the app or going online.
howToUse: Type a number or keyword (for example "404" or "redirect") to filter. A "no match" card appears if nothing fits.
The filter looks at the code number, the short reason phrase, and the plain-English meaning, so typing "timeout" finds 408 and 504.
Use the copy button in the toolbar to copy the whole reference as tab-separated text, one section per class.
fieldNotes: What it shows: codes grouped by class: 1xx Informational, 2xx Success, 3xx Redirection, 4xx Client Error, 5xx Server Error. Each row is the code number, its reason phrase, and a short meaning.
511 (Network Authentication Required) is the tell-tale sign of a captive portal: the network blocks access until the device signs in.
418 is listed in the official registry as "(Unused)". It is widely known as the "I am a teapot" joke code from RFC 2324; the tool labels it honestly and notes the backstory.

Source: the official IANA HTTP Status Code Registry, fetched 2026-06-04. Most codes are defined by RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics). Code numbers and reason phrases match the registry exactly; the plain-English meanings were written for this tool. Unassigned and retired codes are left out; nothing is invented.
http-status-codes.source: Code numbers and reason phrases come from the official IANA HTTP status registry; the plain-English meanings were written for this tool.

wpa-security.name: WPA Security
wpa-security.purpose: A side-by-side table of Wi-Fi security modes (from WEP through WPA3-Enterprise) showing encryption, key method, protected-management-frame support, and a deploy-or-avoid verdict, plus a rundown of the advanced features that set them apart.
wpa-security.whyHere: When choosing or auditing the security on a network, this confirms a mode's cipher, key method, whether management-frame protection is required, and whether it is recommended, acceptable, or best avoided.
howToUse: Each mode has a colored verdict chip, and the word is always spelled out: WEP and WPA1 read "Do not deploy" / "Deprecated" (red); WPA2-Personal reads "Acceptable" (amber); WPA3-Personal and WPA3-Enterprise read "Recommended" (green); Enhanced Open reads "Open networks" and WPA2-Enterprise reads "Enterprise std" (blue/info).

Below the table, the feature rows explain the mechanisms (for example SAE replaces the older shared-key handshake and adds forward secrecy; OWE encrypts open networks without a password; 6 GHz requires WPA3 or OWE).
fieldNotes: What it shows: security modes: WEP, WPA (WPA1), WPA2-Personal, WPA3-Personal, Enhanced Open, WPA2-Enterprise, WPA3-Enterprise, each with its category, encryption suite, key method, protected-management-frame support (Not supported / Optional / Required), and a verdict chip. Advanced features: SAE, protected management frames (802.11w), OWE, forward secrecy, 192-bit security mode, WPA3-required-on-6-GHz, and the 802.1X/RADIUS roles.
WPA3-Enterprise's 192-bit mode (GCMP-256 with HMAC-SHA-384 and ECDH/ECDSA-384) is noted as required for government and classified deployments. 6 GHz does not allow WPA2 or anything older.
The verdicts are reference guidance reflecting current best practice.
